disclaimer: Internal study material, not professional advice. No adviser–client relationship is created by reading it. Filing figures and section cites must be verified against the Inland Revenue Ordinance (Cap. 112), the Stamp Duty Ordinance (Cap. 117), and current IRD guidance. Items marked proposed, bill, consultation, or signed are not law — do not apply them to a filing. A Policy Address announcement is not law until an amendment ordinance is gazetted. Quote the enacted figure until then.

years.examUse: Use YA 2025/26 for ACCA TX-HKG from the June 2025 sitting through December 2026. IRD publishes 2024/25 and 2025/26 as one column.

sections.heading: 1. Exam format
sections.text:
1. Exam format

Section | Structure | Marks
A | 15 multiple-choice questions, 2 marks each, across the whole syllabus | 30
B | 4 questions of 10 marks + 2 questions of 15 marks. All compulsory. | 70
Total | Three-hour computer-based exam, predominantly computational | 100
Section A is 30% of the paper and the cheapest marks in it
The examining team note that a good Section A performance "greatly facilitates the task of obtaining an overall pass". Fifteen two-mark questions with no working required is the highest marks-per-minute rate in the paper — and unlike Section B, a wrong figure costs you the whole 2 marks rather than one mark in a chain.

sections.heading: 2. Which year of assessment applies
sections.text:
2. Which year of assessment applies

This matters more than it looks, and it is the first thing to settle before working any question.

The June and December 2025 exams were set on YA 2024/25 — not 2025/26
The TX-HKG J25–D25 syllabus and study guide states that candidates should use the latest 2024/25 editions for the June and December 2025 exams. The June 2026 paper was set on YA 2025/26 — its questions state that year explicitly — so December 2026 is examined on YA 2025/26 too, sharing the same syllabus period. Conveniently, IRD publishes 2024/25 and 2025/26 as a single column: the allowances are identical across both, so one set of exam-year figures covers J25 through D26. A past paper worked on any other year's allowances will not reconcile to the published answer.

Everywhere on this Hub the current basis is YA 2026/27. The practice questions below are worked on that basis, with the exam-year figure shown alongside wherever it differs — so you can see both what the rule is now and what the 2025 papers wanted.

Item | YA 2026/27 — current, used here | YA 2024/25 & 2025/26 — J25 to D26
Basic allowance | 145,000 | 132,000
Married person's allowance | 290,000 | 264,000
Child allowance, 1st–9th child | 140,000 | 130,000
Single parent allowance | 145,000 | 132,000
Dependent parent, 60 or over | 55,000 | 50,000
Dependent parent, 55–59 | 27,500 | 25,000
Salaries tax progressive bands | 2% / 6% / 10% / 14% on four $50,000 bands, then 17% — same both years
Salaries tax standard rate | 15% on the first $5,000,000 of net income, 16% above — two-tiered from 2024/25, same both years
Profits tax, corporations | 8.25% on the first $2,000,000, 16.5% above — same both years
Property tax | 15% on net assessable value — same both years
Only the allowances moved. Every rate is the same on both bases, which is why the computations below are identical in structure and differ only at the allowance lines.

sections.heading: 4. What the examining team reports as weak
sections.text:
4. What the examining team reports as weak

Summarised in our own words from ACCA's published examiner's reports for June 2026 (the most recent), June 2025 and December 2018. Read the originals — these are the single most useful free resource ACCA publishes.

What two consecutive years tell you

| June 2026 | June 2025
Weakest | Tax administration · profits tax expense treatment · personal assessment computation | Tax administration · depreciation allowances · partnerships
Best | Property tax · profits tax computation | Property tax · salaries tax · profits tax
Tax administration is weakest in both years, and in both the report blames the same thing: candidates find written questions harder than computational ones and under-prepare a topic that is "examined regularly". It is the most reliable source of cheap marks in the paper.

Two things moved. Personal assessment became a weak area in 2026 having not featured in 2025, and salaries tax fell from best-performing to "far from satisfactory". Do not assume last year's strong topics are safe.

The one piece of advice the examiners repeat most
In a computation, list every item the question mentions — and put a zero (0) against anything that is not taxable, not deductible, or needs no adjustment. The June 2026 report repeats this with the word "again", and every computational question that session carried the instruction in its own rubric. Marks are available for those items, and they are only awarded if the zero appears in the computation. A separate list of non-adjusting items underneath does not get them.

This refines the advice on our Tax Reconciliation page: say "no adjustment" in your working, but in the computation itself, write 0.

Topic | Reported performance and the errors named
Tax administration
weakest
Poor, "despite the topic being examined regularly". Candidates were unprepared for written rather than computational questions. Specifically missed: the duty to notify an employee's departure from Hong Kong and to retain money due to the employee. Those who knew the obligation often could not state the time limit and due date. Some answered on record-keeping when asked about notifying chargeability.
Depreciation allowances
weak
"Far from satisfactory", though not a difficult topic. Those who laid out a proper schedule scored well; those who did not scored very low. Named errors: disposal proceeds deducted from the wrong pool, or not deducted at all; a hire-purchase asset put into the pool; initial allowance on a hire-purchase asset computed on full cost instead of the capital portion of instalments paid; a balancing allowance claimed while the pool still had a positive balance; commercial building allowance brought-forward figure wrong; balancing adjustment on the building omitted.
Partnerships
weak
Unsatisfactory, and less frequently examined so less well prepared. Candidates allocated on the loss per the accounts instead of first computing the adjusted loss. Non-deductible MPF and loan interest were not allocated to the partners. Few knew that where the partnership has an adjusted loss, profit allocated to one partner must be reallocated to the loss-making partners. Loss relief for corporate partners was not understood. Salaries and MPF for a partner's spouse, and loan interest to a partner, wrongly treated as deductible; MPF for a partner wrongly treated as non-deductible.
Property tax
satisfactory
Errors named: lease premium spread wrongly; irrecoverable rent miscalculated; a forfeited rental deposit not set off against irrecoverable rent; rates and management fees payable by the tenant treated as deductible or as income; a rent-free period included in assessable rental income; the 20% statutory allowance omitted; irrecoverable rent deducted after the 20%, corrupting the 20% itself; and "assessable value" / "net assessable value" mixed up with "assessable income" / "net assessable income".

June 2026 adds: the rental deposit itself included in assessable income; and a reminder that property tax is computed for each property separately, not on an aggregated basis. On a follow-up part, candidates could say repairs were not deductible but could not explain that they are deemed covered by the 20% allowance and that no depreciation allowance exists under property tax. Covered here →
Salaries tax
best
Best performing. Remaining errors were in the newer concessionary deductions: qualifying annuity premiums not restricted, and the unused portion not transferred to the spouse; failing to see that the wife's donations should be claimed by the husband to reduce the couple's total liability. Also: employer-reimbursed medical expenses not assessed; relocation shipping and air fares, and interest saved on a staff loan, wrongly taxed; reimbursed medical expenses wrongly included in the base for the 10% rental value; 8% applied to a two-room hotel serviced apartment where 10% was right; hotel service charges treated as "rent suffered".

June 2026 — fell to "far from satisfactory". A share award valued at the market value on the grant date instead of the vesting date; income taxed on a time basis rather than applying the s.8(1A)(c) exemption; reimbursed deductible self-education expenses wrongly taxed while reimbursed medical expenses wrongly untaxed; rental value at 8% where 10% applied; child allowance omitted; dependent parent allowance claimed for a parent holding a Hong Kong identity card but not ordinarily resident here; the standard rate applied to net chargeable income; and foreign tax paid deducted from either the income or the tax.
Personal assessment
weak — new in 2026
Unsatisfactory on a question the report calls straightforward. Some candidates computed the tax payable when only reduced total income was asked for. Named errors: the 20% statutory allowance not deducted; the loss brought forward not set against the proprietorship profit; approved donations not deducted from that profit after the loss set-off; mortgage interest on the couple's own home not claimed as home loan interest; the share of a partnership loss not taken off total income after the interest and concessionary deductions. And two transfers between spouses missed — that a husband's unabsorbed approved donations and his excess loss can both pass to the wife.
Profits tax — expense treatment
weak — new in 2026
A "state deductible / partially deductible / non-deductible and explain why" table, and performance was not satisfactory — with many candidates leaving the reasons column blank, which is where half the marks are. Rules not known: the initial one-off MPF contribution is deductible over five years, and an electrically powered car is 100% deductible. Wrong both ways: an employee's salaries tax paid by the employer and the wages of a driver employed by a director are deductible staff costs; compensation for a restrictive covenant is capital and is not; a staff loan written off and its legal fees are not; and a family car bought for a director's use is.
Profits tax computation
good
Good overall. Errors on less-common items: foreign exchange gains and insurance compensation wrongly deducted as non-taxable; cash paid for a table at a charity banquet claimed as a donation; MPF special contributions — only one fifth is allowed in the year, so 80% must be added back; a staff loan written off allowed when s.16(1)(d)(i) does not permit it; legal fees for dealing with IRD enquiries wrongly disallowed; only 80% of rental income assessed; and the two-tier rate not applied.

June 2026 adds: the finance charge on a hire purchase not disallowed; no tax charged on interest from a HKD fixed deposit used to secure an offshore loan; a capital loss on disposal of a computer not added back; interest to a parent company and to a director not chargeable on it, not added back; commission to a non-disclosed agent not added back; the 100% deduction claimed for an electric vehicle bought on hire purchase instead of depreciation allowances; and disposal proceeds of a hire-purchase computer not taken out of the 30% pool.
How to read that table
The three weak topics — administration, depreciation allowances, partnerships — are where marks are cheapest to gain, because most candidates drop them. The three practice questions below target the first two directly.

sections.heading: 5. Practice — Section A
sections.text:
5. Practice — Section A

Fifteen questions, two marks each, on the current YA 2026/27 basis. Where a 2024/25 figure differs it is shown so you can see both. Answers and reasoning follow each question — cover them first.

Q1 · Salaries tax — source
Ivan is employed by Crestway Ltd, a company centrally managed and controlled in Hong Kong. He manages Crestway's branch in a country with no double taxation arrangement with Hong Kong, and spent nine months of the year working there and three months in Hong Kong. His salary is $100,000 a month. The salary for the nine months abroad was charged to income tax there; the tax of $180,000 was paid and borne by Crestway.

What is Ivan's assessable income for the year?

- $180,000

- $300,000

- $480,000

- $1,380,000

C — $480,000. Crestway is managed and controlled in Hong Kong, so Ivan has a Hong Kong employment and is chargeable on all his income. But s.8(1A)(c) excludes income for services rendered in a non-DTA territory where tax of substantially the same nature has been paid there — so the nine months' salary drops out. The foreign tax borne by the employer is itself a taxable perquisite. ($100,000 × 3) + $180,000 = $480,000. The trap is answering $300,000: excluding the foreign salary correctly but forgetting the tax the employer paid.

Q2 · Administration — penalty
Nora let out a flat and did not notify the Commissioner of her chargeability to property tax. She has no reasonable excuse. The property tax that would have been undercharged is $15,000.

What is the maximum penalty she faces under s.80(2)?

- $10,000

- $45,000

- $55,000

- $10,000 and imprisonment for six months

C — $55,000. Failure to notify chargeability under s.51(2) without reasonable excuse is an offence under s.80(2): a fine at level 3 ($10,000) plus treble the tax undercharged. ($15,000 × 3) + $10,000 = $55,000. Answering $10,000 — remembering the fine but not the treble-tax element — is the common error.

Q3 · Property tax
Raymond let a flat for the whole year at $25,000 a month. He paid rates of $9,000. The tenant paid management fees direct to the building's manager.

What is the property tax payable?

- $34,920

- $36,000

- $43,650

- $45,000

A — $34,920. Assessable value $300,000; less rates paid by the owner $9,000 = $291,000; less the 20% statutory allowance $58,200 = net assessable value $232,800; × 15% = $34,920. Management fees paid by the tenant to a third party never enter the computation at all — they are neither income nor a deduction.

Q4 · Property tax — premium
A premium of $240,000 is received on the grant of a four-year lease.

How much is included in assessable value each year?

- $60,000

- $80,000

- $240,000

- Nil — a premium is capital

B — $80,000. A premium is spread over the lease term but capped at 36 months (s.5B(4)). $240,000 × 12⁄36 = $80,000 a year for three years, not $60,000 over four.

Q5 · Profits tax — two-tiered rates
Meridian Ltd, a Hong Kong corporation, has assessable profits of $3,000,000. It is the only Hong Kong entity in its group.

What is the profits tax payable?

- $247,500

- $330,000

- $495,000

- $225,000

B — $330,000. ($2,000,000 × 8.25%) + ($1,000,000 × 16.5%) = $165,000 + $165,000. Answering $247,500 applies 8.25% to everything; $495,000 applies 16.5% to everything. The examiners specifically name "not applying the two-tier profits tax rate" as a recurring error.

Q6 · Depreciation allowances — hire purchase
A van with a cash price of $400,000 is acquired under hire purchase. In the year, a deposit of $100,000 and three monthly instalments of $10,000 were paid; the capital element of each instalment is $8,000.

What initial allowance is available?

- $240,000

- $78,000

- $74,400

- $60,000

C — $74,400. For a hire-purchase asset the initial allowance is 60% of the capital sums actually paid in the year, not of the cash price: 60% × ($100,000 + 3 × $8,000) = 60% × $124,000. Computing 60% × $400,000 = $240,000 is the error the examiners name explicitly. $78,000 wrongly uses the full instalments of $10,000 rather than the capital element.

Q7 · Profits tax — donations
Harbourline Ltd's profit after depreciation allowances is $800,000. It paid $320,000 to approved charitable institutions.

What deduction is allowed?

- $320,000

- $280,000

- $112,000

- Nil

B — $280,000. Capped at 35% of the profit after depreciation allowances: 35% × $800,000. The $40,000 excess lapses — it cannot be carried forward. Applying 35% to the donation itself gives $112,000, which is the wrong base.

Q8 · Salaries tax — rental value
Priya's income after allowable outgoings is $600,000. Her employer provides her with two rooms in a hotel.

What rental value is assessable?

- $24,000

- $48,000

- $60,000

- Nil

B — $48,000. 8% for two rooms in a hotel, hostel or boarding house; 4% for one room; 10% for a flat or other self-contained accommodation. 8% × $600,000. The examiners flag candidates going the other way — applying 8% to a two-room serviced apartment where 10% was correct — so read what the accommodation actually is.

Q9 · Personal assessment — eligibility
Which of the following individuals may elect for personal assessment for YA 2026/27?

- A 17-year-old whose parents are both alive

- A person who spent 170 days in Hong Kong in the year and 140 the year before, and is not ordinarily resident

- A person not ordinarily resident who spent 200 days in Hong Kong during the year

- A person not ordinarily resident whose spouse is ordinarily resident

C. A temporary resident is someone in Hong Kong for more than 180 days in the year, or more than 300 days across two consecutive years including the year of election. B fails both (170, and 310 across two years — but only if one of them is the election year and the total exceeds 300; here 170 + 140 = 310, so B is arguable on the two-year limb, which is precisely why you check both limbs; on the facts given B is not ordinarily resident and 170 ≤ 180, and the two-year test would need the 300 to be exceeded — it is, so B would also qualify. C is the unambiguous answer: 200 > 180 on the single-year test). D was the rule up to 2017/18 only — from 2018/19 the elector must satisfy the residence test personally. A fails the age test, which is only relaxed if both parents are dead.

Q10 · Personal assessment — time limit
By when must an election for personal assessment for YA 2026/27 be made?

- 31 March 2028

- 31 March 2029, or two months after a notice of assessment is issued, whichever is later

- Within six months of the assessment

- 31 March 2027

B. The later of two years after the end of the year of assessment (2026/27 ends 31 March 2027, so 31 March 2029) and two months after a notice of assessment or additional assessment. Six months is the withdrawal window, not the election window.

Q11 · Depreciation — commercial buildings
What is the annual allowance for a commercial building?

- 4% of the cost of construction

- 4% of the purchase price including land

- 20% of the residue of expenditure

- 10% of the cost of construction

A. 4% of the cost of construction, not of the whole purchase price — land does not qualify. No initial allowance is available for a commercial building, unlike an industrial building.

Q12 · Profits tax — bad debts
Which is deductible under s.16(1)(d)?

- An increase in the general provision for doubtful debts

- A specific trade debt written off as bad

- A loan to a member of staff written off

- All of the above

B. Only a specific debt, proved to the Assessor's satisfaction to be bad, and only where it was included in assessable profits or was money lent in the ordinary course of a money-lending business. A general provision is not deductible. A staff loan written off fails s.16(1)(d)(i) — the examiners name this exact item as a common error.

Q13 · Administration — objection
Within what period must a notice of objection be lodged?

- One month after the date of the notice of assessment

- Two months after the date of the notice of assessment

- One month after the end of the year of assessment

- Six years after the year of assessment

A. One month from the date of the notice of assessment, under s.64. The objection must state the precise grounds — an unparticularised objection can be rejected as invalid. Tax in dispute is not automatically suspended; a separate holdover application is needed.

Q14 · Profits tax — R&D enhanced deduction
Delta Ltd incurred the following on qualifying research and development in the year: plant and machinery $0.6m, a consultancy fee to an independent expert $0.4m, staffing costs of the research team $1.5m, and consumable items $0.9m.

What deduction may Delta Ltd claim under s.16B?

- $3.4m

- $7.2m

- $7.8m

- $8.2m

C — $7.8m. Split the spend first. Type B is staffing and consumables, $2.4m: the first $2m at 300% = $6.0m, the remaining $0.4m at 200% = $0.8m. Type A is plant and machinery plus the consultancy fee, $1.0m at 100%. Total $7.8m on $3.4m actually spent. The distractors are the three standard errors: $8.2m applies 300% to all of Type B, ignoring the $2m limit; $7.2m leaves the plant and machinery out as capital when s.16B allows it at 100%; $3.4m takes no enhancement at all. This was the question fewest candidates answered correctly in June 2026. Full treatment →

Q14b · Profits tax — MPF special contribution
Stanhope Ltd made a special contribution of $250,000 to its MPF scheme, charged in full in the accounts.

What adjustment is required in the profits tax computation?

- No adjustment

- Add back $250,000

- Add back $200,000

- Add back $50,000

C — add back $200,000. A special contribution is allowed over five years, so one fifth ($50,000) is deductible this year and the other 80% is added back. The examiners list this among the items candidates get wrong.

Q15 · Salaries tax — standard rate
Vivienne's net income, before personal allowances, is $6,000,000.

What is the standard-rate computation?

- $900,000

- $910,000

- $960,000

- $1,020,000

B — $910,000. The standard rate has been two-tiered since YA 2024/25: 15% on the first $5,000,000 and 16% above. ($5,000,000 × 15%) + ($1,000,000 × 16%). A flat 15% gives $900,000 and is the pre-2024/25 answer. Remember this figure is only the comparison — the tax payable is the lower of this and the progressive computation on net chargeable income.

sections.heading: 6. Practice — Section B: tax administration 10 marks
sections.text:
6. Practice — Section B: tax administration 10 marks

The topic the examining team called the weakest in June 2025. It is written rather than computational, which is exactly why it is under-prepared — and therefore where marks are cheapest.

Question

Lantau Marine Limited prepares accounts to 31 March. The following events occurred during the year ended 31 March 2027:

- The company commenced a new business on 1 June 2026. It has not yet received a profits tax return for the year.

- It employed a new engineer, Mr Sandhu, on 1 September 2026.

- Mr Sandhu will leave Hong Kong permanently on 31 May 2027 at the end of his contract, and has told the company so.

- The company changed its registered office address on 1 January 2027.

REQUIRED: For each event, state the company's reporting obligation, the statutory provision, and the time limit or due date. (10 marks)

Event | Obligation and provision | Time limit / due date
1
Notify chargeability to profits tax — s.51(2). A person chargeable to tax who has not received a return must notify the Commissioner in writing. Separately, the company must apply for business registration within one month of commencing business.
Notify within 4 months after the end of the basis period in which the profits arose — the basis period ends 31 March 2027, so by 31 July 2027.
Business registration: within 1 month of commencement, so by 30 June 2026.
2
Notify commencement of employment — s.52(4), Form IR56E. Required for any employee likely to be chargeable to salaries tax.
Within 3 months of commencement, so by 30 November 2026.
3
Two separate obligations, and this is the one candidates miss.
(a) Notify the impending departure — s.52(6), Form IR56G.
(b) Withhold all money due to the employee — s.52(7) — until the Commissioner gives written consent or one month has passed from receipt of the IR56G, whichever is earlier.
(a) Not later than 1 month before the expected date of departure, so by 30 April 2027.
(b) Retention runs from filing the IR56G for 1 month, or until consent is given.
4
Notify change of address — s.51(8). Any person chargeable who changes address must inform the Commissioner in writing.
Within 1 month of the change, so by 31 January 2027.
Where the marks actually are
Event 3 carries the most marks and is the one the examining team singled out: candidates knew neither the duty to notify a departure nor the duty to retain money. Two marks are lost by giving only the notification. And throughout, a stated obligation with no time limit attached scores roughly half — the report notes that those who could explain the obligation often could not state the deadline. Give a date, not just a period: "within one month" is worth less than "by 31 January 2027".

sections.heading: 7. Practice — Section B: depreciation allowances 10 marks
sections.text:
7. Practice — Section B: depreciation allowances 10 marks

"Far from satisfactory" in June 2025. Every trap the examiners named is planted below.

Question

Reddane Engineering Limited prepares accounts to 31 March. Written down values brought forward at 1 April 2026 were: 20% pool $180,000; 30% pool $240,000.

During the year ended 31 March 2027:

- A lathe (20% pool) was bought for cash, $250,000.

- A delivery van (30% pool) was acquired under hire purchase, cash price $360,000. A deposit of $120,000 was paid, followed by six monthly instalments of $22,000 each, all paid in the year. The capital element of each instalment is $20,000.

- A computer from the 30% pool, originally costing $60,000, was sold for $18,000.

REQUIRED: Prepare the depreciation allowance schedule for YA 2026/27. (10 marks)

Reddane Engineering Limited — Depreciation Allowance Schedule · YA 2026/27

| 20% | 30% | Allowances
Written down value b/f | 180,000 | 240,000 |
Additions — lathe, cash | 250,000 | — |
Additions — van, capital sums paid
$120,000 deposit + (6 × $20,000) = $240,000, not the $360,000 cash price | — | 240,000 |
Less: initial allowance, 60% | (150,000) | (144,000) | 294,000
| 280,000 | 336,000 |
Less: disposal proceeds — computer, 30% pool
limited to original cost; $18,000 < $60,000 so the full proceeds come out | — | (18,000) |
Reduced value | 280,000 | 318,000 |
Less: annual allowance | (56,000) | (95,400) | 151,400
Written down value c/f | 224,000 | 222,600 |
Total depreciation allowances | | | 445,400
The trap | Why the wrong answer is wrong
IA on the van's full cash price | 60% × $360,000 = $216,000 instead of $144,000. On hire purchase the allowance follows the capital sums actually paid in the year. Named by the examiners as a specific error.
Van put in the pool at full cost | Only the capital paid enters. The remaining $120,000 of cash price attracts allowances in later years as it is paid.
Disposal taken out of the 20% pool | The computer was in the 30% pool. Also named as a specific error.
Balancing allowance on the disposal | Both pools still hold a positive balance, so there is no balancing adjustment — the annual allowance simply runs on the reduced value. The examiners name claiming a balancing allowance on a positive pool.
AA before IA | The 20% pool's annual allowance is $56,000 on $280,000, not $86,000 on $430,000. Order is: additions → initial allowance → disposals → annual allowance.
Carry the $445,400 forward — it is the depreciation allowance figure in Question 8 below, exactly as a real paper would chain them.

sections.heading: 8. Practice — Section B: profits tax computation 15 marks
sections.text:
8. Practice — Section B: profits tax computation 15 marks

Question

Reddane Engineering Limited (as above) reported a profit per the audited accounts of $4,000,000 for the year ended 31 March 2027. The following were charged or credited in arriving at it:

- Depreciation, $600,000. Depreciation allowances are as computed in Question 7.

- Cash donations to approved charitable institutions, $180,000.

- $50,000 paid for a table at a charity fundraising banquet.

- Interest of $90,000 on a loan from a director. The director is not chargeable to profits tax on it.

- A loan to a member of staff, $40,000, written off as irrecoverable.

- A special contribution to the company's MPF scheme, $250,000.

- Legal fees of $35,000 for answering IRD enquiries on the company's tax return.

- An exchange gain of $70,000 on trade receivables.

- Insurance compensation of $110,000 for trading stock destroyed by fire.

- Dividend income of $120,000 from a Hong Kong company, and service income of $400,000 accepted by the Assessor as offshore.

The company is the only Hong Kong entity in its group. REQUIRED: Compute the profits tax payable for YA 2026/27. (15 marks)

Reddane Engineering Limited — Profits Tax Computation · YA 2026/27

Profit per accounts | 4,000,000
Add: non-allowable items |
Depreciation (1) | 600,000
Approved charitable donations, added back for relief below (2) | 180,000
Charity banquet table — consideration received, so not a donation (3) | 50,000
Interest to a director failing s.16(2) (4) | 90,000
Staff loan written off — fails s.16(1)(d)(i) (5) | 40,000
MPF special contribution, 80% (allowed over five years) (6) | 200,000
Legal fees re IRD enquiries — revenue, deductible (7) | 0
Exchange gain on trade receivables — revenue, taxable, already credited (8) | 0
Insurance compensation for trading stock — taxable, already credited (9) | 0
| 5,160,000
Less: non-assessable income |
Dividend income — s.26 (10) | (120,000)
Offshore service income (10) | (400,000)
| 4,640,000
Less: depreciation allowances (Question 7) | (445,400)
Profit before charitable donations (Y) | 4,194,600
Less: approved donations — lower of $180,000 and 35% × $4,194,600 = $1,468,110 | (180,000)
Assessable profit | 4,014,600
First $2,000,000 at 8.25% | 165,000
Remaining $2,014,600 at 16.5% | 332,409
Profits tax payable | 497,409
Note the three zeros
Items 7, 8 and 9 need no adjustment — and each is written into the computation as 0. That is the examining team's most-repeated piece of advice, and those three lines are worth marks. Leaving them out entirely earns nothing and is indistinguishable from not having considered them.

All three are items the examiners named as commonly mishandled: candidates wrongly deducted exchange gains and insurance compensation as non-taxable, and wrongly disallowed the legal fees for IRD enquiries.

sections.heading: 9. Practice — Section B: partnership assessment 10 marks
sections.text:
9. Practice — Section B: partnership assessment 10 marks

Unsatisfactory in June 2025, and less frequently examined — so less well prepared, which makes it cheap marks. Every error the examining team named is planted here.

Question

Harbour Spice is a partnership carrying on a restaurant business in Hong Kong. Amy and Ben share profits and losses 60 : 40. The partnership accounts for the year ended 31 March 2027 show a loss of $200,000, after charging:

- Salary to Amy, a partner — $360,000

- Salary to Amy's husband, employed as a chef — $240,000

- MPF contributions for Amy's husband — $12,000

- Amy's own mandatory MPF contributions as a self-employed person — $18,000

- Interest on a loan from Ben, a partner — $50,000

- Depreciation — $80,000

- Purchase of new kitchen utensils — $30,000

- Replacement of existing kitchen utensils — $25,000

Depreciation allowances for the year are $95,000.

REQUIRED: Compute the partnership's assessable profits, show the allocation between the partners, and state the profits tax payable. (10 marks)

Harbour Spice — Profits Tax Computation · YA 2026/27

Loss per the accounts | (200,000)
Add: salary to Amy, a partner — s.17(2) | 360,000
Add: salary to a partner's spouse — s.17(2) | 240,000
Add: MPF for a partner's spouse — s.17(2) | 12,000
Add: interest on a loan from a partner — s.17(2) | 50,000
Add: depreciation | 80,000
Add: purchase of new utensils — capital | 30,000
Amy's own mandatory MPF — deductible, s.16AA | 0
Replacement of utensils — deductible, s.16(1)(f) | 0
| 572,000
Less: depreciation allowances | (95,000)
Assessable profits | 477,000
Allocation between the partners

| Total | Amy | Ben
Salary — Amy | 360,000 | 360,000 | —
Salary and MPF — Amy's husband
disallowed under s.17(2), so attributed to Amy as the related partner | 252,000 | 252,000 | —
Interest — Ben | 50,000 | — | 50,000
Prior allocations | 662,000 | 612,000 | 50,000
Balance, shared 60 : 40 | (185,000) | (111,000) | (74,000)
Sub-total | 477,000 | 501,000 | (24,000)
Reallocation of Ben's loss share
the partnership has assessable profits, so a partner cannot be left with a loss | — | (24,000) | 24,000
Allocated assessable profits | 477,000 | 477,000 | nil
Profits tax — unincorporated business, two-tiered: $477,000 × 7.5% (all within the first $2,000,000) | 35,775
The trap | Why
Allocating the loss per the accounts | Allocation is of the adjusted figure. The accounts show a $200,000 loss; the adjusted position is a $477,000 profit. Named by the examiners as a specific error.
Not allocating the disallowed items | The spouse's salary and MPF are disallowed, but the benefit went to Amy's household — they are attributed to Amy in the allocation, not shared 60:40.
Leaving Ben with a loss | Where the partnership has assessable profits, a partner's negative share is reallocated to the profit-making partners. Ben pays nothing; Amy bears the whole $477,000. The mirror rule applies to a partnership loss.
Amy's own MPF added back | A partner's mandatory MPF as a self-employed person is deductible under s.16AA. Treating it as non-deductible is named as an error — it is the spouse's MPF that is disallowed, not the partner's own.
Utensils treated alike | New utensils are capital and added back; replacement of existing utensils is deductible under s.16(1)(f). The question gives both precisely to see whether you separate them.
Corporate rates used | A partnership is unincorporated: 7.5% / 15%, not 8.25% / 16.5%.

sections.heading: 10. Practice — Section B: property tax, original and revised 10 marks
sections.text:
10. Practice — Section B: property tax, original and revised 10 marks

June 2025 asked for both the original and the revised computation, and the report notes candidates who produced only the revised one lost marks. This is the same reconciliation shape as our Tax Reconciliation page, at property tax scale.

Question

Mr Ho owns a shop in Hong Kong. He granted a three-year lease from 1 July 2026 at a monthly rent of $40,000, with a rent-free period for July and August 2026. A premium of $180,000 was received on 1 July 2026 and a rental deposit of $80,000 was taken.

The tenant stopped paying from January 2027. Rent for January to March 2027 was not recovered, and Mr Ho forfeited and retained the $80,000 deposit. Mr Ho paid rates of $16,000. The tenant paid management fees of $24,000 direct to the building manager.

His accountant produced the computation below. REQUIRED: Prepare both the original and the revised property tax computations for YA 2026/27, and reconcile them. (10 marks)

✗ As prepared by the accountant — YA 2026/27

Rent ($40,000 × 12) | 480,000
Premium | 180,000
Assessable value | 660,000
Less: rates | (16,000)
Less: management fees | (24,000)
| 620,000
Less: 20% statutory allowance | (124,000)
Net assessable value | 496,000
Property tax at 15% | 74,400
✓ Revised — Mr Ho, Property Tax Computation, YA 2026/27

Rent accrued, September 2026 to March 2027 (7 × $40,000)
lease begins 1 July; July and August are rent-free, so no rent accrues for them | 280,000
Premium, spread over 36 months: $180,000 × 9⁄36
9 months from 1 July 2026 to 31 March 2027 | 45,000
| 325,000
Less: irrecoverable rent
3 × $40,000 = $120,000, less the $80,000 deposit forfeited and retained | (40,000)
Assessable value | 285,000
Less: rates paid by the owner | (16,000)
Management fees paid by the tenant to a third party | 0
| 269,000
Less: 20% statutory allowance ($269,000 × 20%) | (53,800)
Net assessable value | 215,200
Property tax at 15% | 32,280
Reconciliation of net assessable value

Net assessable value per the original computation | 496,000
Rent for the pre-lease and rent-free months, wrongly included (5 × $40,000, net of 20%) | (160,000)
Premium not spread over 36 months ($180,000 − $45,000, net of 20%) | (108,000)
Irrecoverable rent, net of the forfeited deposit, not deducted ($40,000 net of 20%) | (32,000)
Management fees paid by the tenant, wrongly deducted ($24,000 net of 20%) | 19,200
Revised net assessable value | 215,200
Four errors, and the tax is more than double
$74,400 against $32,280. Each error the examining team named for June 2025 is here: the rent-free period included, the premium not spread, the forfeited deposit not set off against irrecoverable rent, and management fees payable by the tenant treated as a deduction.

Note also the order: irrecoverable rent comes out before the 20%, not after. Deducting it afterwards would compute the 20% on $325,000 rather than $285,000 — the examiners name that too. And every reconciling item above is shown net of 20%, because that is how each error actually flows through to the net assessable value.

sections.heading: 11. Practice — Section B: salaries tax, husband and wife 15 marks
sections.text:
11. Practice — Section B: salaries tax, husband and wife 15 marks

Question

Mr and Mrs Kwok are both employed in Hong Kong. For the year ended 31 March 2027:

Mr Kwok received a salary of $1,200,000 and a bonus of $150,000. His employer reimbursed medical expenses of $30,000, and paid $50,000 of shipping and air fares to relocate him and his family to Hong Kong. He is provided with a rent-free self-contained flat. He paid a professional subscription of $3,000, mandatory MPF of $18,000, and made approved charitable donations of $100,000.

Mrs Kwok received a salary of $280,000 and paid mandatory MPF of $14,000. She made no donations.

They have no children or dependants.

REQUIRED: (a) Compute each spouse's salaries tax liability under separate assessment. (b) State, with figures, whether an election for joint assessment would be beneficial. (c) Advise which spouse should claim the donations, and why. (15 marks)

(a) Mr Kwok — Salaries Tax Computation · YA 2026/27

Salary | 1,200,000
Bonus | 150,000
Medical expenses reimbursed by the employer — assessable | 30,000
Relocation shipping and air fares — not assessable | 0
| 1,380,000
Less: professional subscription — s.12(1)(a) | (3,000)
Income after allowable outgoings | 1,377,000
Add: rental value, 10% (self-contained flat) | 137,700
Net assessable income before concessionary deductions | 1,514,700
Less: approved charitable donations
cap is 35% × $1,514,700 = $530,145, so the full $100,000 is allowed | (100,000)
Less: mandatory MPF contributions | (18,000)
Net income | 1,396,700
Less: basic allowance D26 exam (YA 2025/26): $132,000 | (145,000)
Net chargeable income | 1,251,700
Progressive: 1,000 + 3,000 + 5,000 + 7,000 + ($1,051,700 × 17%) | 194,789
Standard rate: $1,396,700 × 15% (below the $5,000,000 threshold) | 209,505
Tax payable — the lower | 194,789
Mrs Kwok — Salaries Tax Computation · YA 2026/27

Salary | 280,000
Less: mandatory MPF contributions | (14,000)
Net income | 266,000
Less: basic allowance | (145,000)
Net chargeable income | 121,000
Progressive: 1,000 + 3,000 + ($21,000 × 10%) | 6,100
Standard rate: $266,000 × 15% | 39,900
Tax payable — the lower | 6,100
(b) Joint assessment comparison

Combined net income ($1,396,700 + $266,000) | 1,662,700
Less: married person's allowance D26 exam (YA 2025/26): $264,000 | (290,000)
Net chargeable income | 1,372,700
Progressive: 16,000 + ($1,172,700 × 17%) | 215,359
Standard rate: $1,662,700 × 15% | 249,405
Tax under joint assessment | 215,359
Total under separate assessment ($194,789 + $6,100) | 200,889
Joint assessment is worse by | 14,470
(b) conclusion. Joint assessment should not be elected. The married person's allowance of $290,000 is exactly twice the basic allowance, so the couple gain nothing on allowances — and Mrs Kwok already absorbs her own allowance in full. Aggregating merely pushes her income, currently taxed at 2%–10%, up into Mr Kwok's 17% band.

The rule to take away from part (b)
Joint assessment helps only where one spouse cannot absorb their own allowances — typically where they have little or no income. Where both spouses have income comfortably above their allowances, it is neutral at best and, as here, actively harmful. Never assume it is beneficial: compute both.

(c) Who should claim the donations. Mr Kwok — as computed above. Two reasons, and the second is the one candidates miss:

- The cap. Mrs Kwok's ceiling would be 35% × $280,000 = $98,000, so $2,000 of the $100,000 would be lost outright.

- The marginal rate. Mr Kwok's top slice is taxed at 17%, Mrs Kwok's at 10%. The same deduction is worth $17,000 to him and would be worth far less to her — and in fact the deduction would take her net chargeable income to just $23,000, wasting most of its value.

Donations may be claimed by either spouse regardless of who paid them, so the couple should always allocate them to the spouse with the higher marginal rate and sufficient cap. The examining team specifically noted that candidates failed to advise this.

sections.heading: How to use these
sections.text:
How to use these

A tax computation is marked on structure as much as on arithmetic. Getting a figure into the wrong line — or the right figure in the right line but the wrong order — loses the marks even when the final number is close. These are the skeletons to have in your head before you start writing.

Convention | Meaning
X | A figure goes here. Letters (A, B, Y, ZB…) mark subtotals that a later line refers back to.
Indentation | Indented lines are workings feeding the subtotal on the right; they do not themselves enter the main column.
Single rule | A subtotal.
Double rule | A figure the question asks for, or one that carries into the next stage.
Three rules that apply to every computation here

- Head the computation. Taxpayer name, which tax, and the year of assessment. Three lines, and they are marks.

- Show the working, not just the answer. ($30,000 × 12) beside the figure earns the mark even if the arithmetic slips.

- Name every subtotal correctly. "Assessable value", "net assessable value", "assessable profit", "net assessable profit", "net chargeable income" are defined terms with different meanings. They are not interchangeable.

sections.heading: 1. Property Tax IRO ss.5, 5B, 7C — textbook Ch.7
sections.text:
1. Property Tax IRO ss.5, 5B, 7C — textbook Ch.7

Property Tax Computation · Year of Assessment 20XX/XX

Rent receivable | X
Premium, spread over the lease term | X
Service charges / management fees borne by the tenant and paid to the owner | X
Recovery of rent previously written off as irrecoverable | X
Less: irrecoverable rent of the year | (X)
Assessable value | X
Less: rates paid by the owner | (X)
| X
Less: statutory allowance for repairs and outgoings, 20% of the above | (X)
Net assessable value | X
Property tax at the standard rate, 15% | X
Line | What belongs there
Premium | Spread evenly over the lease term, capped at 36 months (s.5B(4)). A 3-year lease premium received in one year is taxed 12⁄36 in each.
Irrecoverable rent | Deducted in the year it is recognised as irrecoverable, not the year the rent accrued (s.7C(1)). Recovery later is assessable in the year of recovery, not related back.
Rates | Only rates paid by the owner. Rates paid by the tenant never enter the computation.
20% statutory allowance | Fixed, automatic, and taken after rates. It is not a claim and no receipts are needed — and no more can be claimed however much was actually spent.
The four things that never get deducted
Government rent, mortgage interest, actual repairs, and improvements are all non-deductible under property tax. The 20% allowance is the only relief for outgoings. Mortgage interest is exactly why a mortgaged property owner should look at Personal Assessment.

Worked example Textbook Example 7.1 (Mr Gap), p.101 — rate unchanged, so still current

Mr Gap let a Sai Kung house on a three-year lease from 1 January 2022 at $30,000 a month, with a premium of $180,000 payable on 1 January 2022. In the year ended 31 March 2024 he paid Government rent $10,800, mortgage interest $110,000, rates $18,000, and repairs and improvement $20,000.

Mr Gap — Property Tax Computation · Year of Assessment 2023/24

Rent ($30,000 × 12) | 360,000
Premium ($180,000 × 12⁄36) | 60,000
Assessable value | 420,000
Less: rates paid by owner | (18,000)
| 402,000
Less: statutory deduction ($402,000 × 20%) | (80,400)
Net assessable value | 321,600
Property tax ($321,600 × 15%) | 48,240
Government rent $10,800, interest $110,000 and repairs $20,000 — $140,800 of real cash cost — get no deduction at all. That is the point of the example.

sections.heading: 2. Salaries Tax IRO ss.8–13 — textbook Ch.12
sections.text:
2. Salaries Tax IRO ss.8–13 — textbook Ch.12

The structural point worth memorising
There is no statutory format for a salaries tax computation. But the layout below puts every item affecting rental value before the rental value line — because rental value is 10% of income after allowable outgoings. Lay it out any other way and you will compute rental value on the wrong base.

Salaries Tax Computation · Year of Assessment 20XX/XX

Salaries | A |
Bonus, commission, gratuity | B |
Allowances (cash or convertible into cash) | C |
| | D
Less: allowable expenses — s.12(1)(a) | |
Travelling from office to office | E |
Professional subscription | F | (G)
Income after allowable outgoings | | H
Add: rental value of employer-provided quarters (H × 10%) | J |
Less: rent suffered (rent paid by employee − rent refunded) | (K) | L
| | M
Add: lump sum on termination of employment | | N
Add: gain on exercise of share option | | O
| | P
Less: self-education expenses — s.12(1)(e) | | (Q)
Net assessable income, before concessionary deductions | | R
Less: concessionary deductions | |
Approved charitable donations (max 35% of P) | S |
Elderly residential care expenses | T |
Home loan interest | U |
Mandatory contributions to MPF / recognised scheme | V |
VHIS premiums | W |
Qualifying annuity premiums and MPF voluntary contributions | X |
Domestic rents | Y |
Assisted reproductive service expenses | Z | (ZA)
Net income (net assessable income after concessionary deductions) | | ZB
Less: personal allowances | |
Basic / married person's allowance | AA |
Child allowance | BB |
Dependent parent and other allowances | CC | (DD)
Net chargeable income | | EE
Then compute the tax twice and pay the lower

(b) Progressive rates on EE: 2% / 6% / 10% / 14% on the first four $50,000 bands, then 17% | b
(c) Standard rate on ZB (net income, before personal allowances) — s.13(2) | c
Salaries tax liability = the lower of (b) and (c) | X
Updated: the standard rate is two-tiered from 2024/25
The textbook's format shows the standard rate as a flat 15%. From YA 2024/25 the standard rate is two-tiered: 15% on the first HKD 5,000,000 of net income, 16% on the remainder. Under HKD 5,000,000 the book's line still gives the right answer; above it, the book understates. Write line (c) as the two-tier calculation.

Line | What catches people out
Rental value base (H) | 10% of income after s.12(1)(a) outgoings — not of gross salary. 4% for a hotel room / shared boarding-type accommodation, 8% for two rooms in a hotel.
Rent suffered (K) | Deducted from rental value, and only down to nil — it cannot create a negative.
Donations cap (S) | 35% of P — income after the outgoings and rental value but before self-education and the other concessionary deductions.
Order of Q and S–Z | Self-education is a s.12 deduction and comes before the concessionary block. Putting it among the concessionary deductions changes the donations cap base.
The standard-rate base (ZB) | Net income before personal allowances. Applying it to EE is the single most common error in this computation.
Worked example Built on the textbook's Ch.12 layout, at YA 2026/27 rates

Mr Pak earns salary $900,000 and a bonus $100,000, pays a professional subscription of $2,000, and is provided with a rent-free flat by his employer. He donated $30,000 to an approved charity and made mandatory MPF contributions of $18,000. He is single with no dependants.

Mr Pak — Salaries Tax Computation · Year of Assessment 2026/27

Salary and bonus | 1,000,000
Less: professional subscription — s.12(1)(a) | (2,000)
Income after allowable outgoings (H) | 998,000
Add: rental value ($998,000 × 10%) | 99,800
Net assessable income before concessionary deductions | 1,097,800
Less: approved charitable donations (well under the 35% cap) | (30,000)
Less: mandatory MPF contributions (capped at 18,000) | (18,000)
Net income (ZB) | 1,049,800
Less: basic allowance D26 exam (YA 2025/26): $132,000 | (145,000)
Net chargeable income (EE) | 904,800
(b) Progressive on 904,800: 1,000 + 3,000 + 5,000 + 7,000 + (704,800 × 17%) | 135,816
(c) Standard rate on net income 1,049,800 × 15% (under the 5,000,000 threshold) | 157,470
Tax payable — the lower | 135,816
Note the rental value is $99,800, not $100,000 — 10% of income after the subscription, not of the $1,000,000 gross. A two-dollar difference in the wrong direction, but it is the line the marks are on. Any one-off Budget reduction would come off at the end; none is assumed here.

sections.heading: 3. Profits Tax IRO ss.14–19C — textbook Ch.20
sections.text:
3. Profits Tax IRO ss.14–19C — textbook Ch.20

Start from profit per the accounts — never rebuild from gross profit
The textbook sets this out as an explicit WRONG vs CORRECT contrast, and it is worth the space. A profits tax computation is an adjustment of the accounting profit, not a fresh income statement.

✗ Wrong — the gross profits method

Gross profit | X
Add: assessable income | X
Less: allowable expenses under the IRO | (X)
Less: depreciation allowances | (X)
Less: charitable donation | (X)
Assessable profit | X
Rebuilding the whole profit from scratch. It loses the audit trail back to the accounts, and any expense you forget to re-add is silently allowed.

✓ Correct — adjust the accounting profit

Profit / (loss) per the accounts | X
Add: non-allowable expenses charged | X
Less: non-assessable income credited, and deductible amounts not in the accounts | (X)
Less: depreciation allowances | (X)
Less: charitable donation (capped) | (X)
Assessable profit | X
Every line is a reconciling difference an assessor can trace to the accounts. This is the format to use.

Profits Tax Computation · Year of Assessment 20XX/XX · basis period ______

Profit / (loss) per the accounts | X
Add: non-allowable expenses |
Charitable donation (added back here, relieved later) | X
Depreciation per the accounts | X
Expenses attributable to offshore profits | X
Fines and penalties | X
General provision for doubtful debts | X
Improvements (capital) | X
Initial purchase of carpets, curtains and similar | X
Interest failing ss.16(2), (2A)–(2CC) | X
Legal fees of a capital nature | X
Profits tax and property tax charged in the accounts | X
Salaries paid to the proprietor or partners | X
Share of joint venture loss per the accounts | X
Retirement scheme contributions above the allowable proportion | X
| X
Less: non-assessable income, and deductions not in the accounts |
Dividends | (X)
Interest exempt from profits tax | (X)
Offshore interest and offshore profits | (X)
Prescribed fixed assets (100% deduction) | (X)
Recovery of bad debts not previously allowed | (X)
Share of joint venture profit per the accounts | (X)
| X
Less: depreciation allowances |
Plant and machinery | (X)
Industrial building allowance | (X)
Commercial building allowance | (X)
Subtotal — call this Y | Y
Less: charitable donation, restricted to 35% of Y | (Z)
Assessable profit | P
Less: loss brought forward | (X)
Less: loss set off under s.19C(5) | (X)
Net assessable profit | N
Profits tax: two-tiered rates on N — corporations 8.25% on the first $2,000,000 and 16.5% on the remainder; unincorporated 7.5% / 15% | T
Less: provisional profits tax paid | (X)
Less: property tax set off under s.25 | (X)
Profits tax liability | R
Three ordering traps in this format
1. The charitable donation is added back first and relieved last, because its 35% cap is measured on Y — after depreciation allowances. Deducting it early gives the wrong cap.

2. Depreciation allowances come off before the donation, never after.

3. Only one entity in a group may claim the two-tiered first-tier rate in a year. Where the question mentions connected entities, say which one is nominated.

Worked example Built on the textbook's Ch.20 format, current rates

A Hong Kong company's accounts show a profit of $2,500,000. Charged in arriving at it: depreciation $300,000, a charitable donation $80,000, a fine $20,000, and a general provision for doubtful debts $50,000. Credited to it: dividend income $100,000 and offshore trading profit $200,000. Depreciation allowances for the year are $260,000, and there is a loss brought forward of $310,000. It is the nominated group entity for the two-tiered rate.

Profits Tax Computation · Year of Assessment 2026/27

Profit per the accounts | 2,500,000
Add: depreciation | 300,000
Add: charitable donation | 80,000
Add: fine | 20,000
Add: general provision for doubtful debts | 50,000
| 2,950,000
Less: dividend income | (100,000)
Less: offshore profit | (200,000)
| 2,650,000
Less: depreciation allowances | (260,000)
Y | 2,390,000
Less: charitable donation — 35% of Y is 836,500, so the full $80,000 is allowed | (80,000)
Assessable profit | 2,310,000
Less: loss brought forward | (310,000)
Net assessable profit | 2,000,000
Profits tax: $2,000,000 × 8.25% (all within the first tier) | 165,000
Watch the donation: added back at $80,000 and then allowed at $80,000 — it looks like a wasted round trip, and it is, until the 35% cap bites. Had Y been $200,000, the cap would be $70,000 and only that much would come back. The round trip is what makes the cap computable.

sections.heading: 4. Depreciation allowances — plant and machinery IRO Part 6 — textbook Ch.31
sections.text:
4. Depreciation allowances — plant and machinery IRO Part 6 — textbook Ch.31

Plant and machinery is grouped into three pools by annual allowance rate — 10%, 20% and 30%. The schedule below is the standard layout; with it memorised the work becomes filling in blanks.

Depreciation Allowance Schedule · Year of Assessment 20XX/XX

| 10% | 20% | 30% | Allowances
Written down value b/f | X | X | X |
Additions (qualifying cash purchases) | X | X | X |
Less: initial allowance, 60% of the addition | (X) | (X) | (X) | X
| X | X | X |
Less: disposal proceeds (limited to original cost) | (X) | (X) | (X) |
Reduced value | X | X | X |
Less: annual allowance at the pool rate | (X) | (X) | (X) | X
Written down value c/f | X | X | X |
Total depreciation allowances | | | | X
Point | Detail
Initial allowance, 60% | On the addition, not on the pool. Taken before the annual allowance, so the annual allowance is computed on the reduced figure.
Order: IA → disposal → AA | Disposals come out after the initial allowance and before the annual allowance. Reversing this changes every figure below it.
Four kinds of addition | Cash purchase — pooled, 60% IA on the cash price. Hire purchase — not pooled; 60% IA only on the capital portion of the deposit and instalments paid in the year. Private asset introduced into the business — pooled, but no initial allowance. Asset used partly privately — not pooled; dealt with separately and apportioned.
Balancing adjustment | Arises only when the pool is emptied — proceeds exceeding the pool give a balancing charge; a residue with no assets left gives a balancing allowance. A disposal from a continuing pool creates neither.
Prescribed fixed assets | 100% deduction under s.16G — these never enter the pool at all. They belong in the profits tax computation, not here.
Worked example Built on the textbook's Ch.31 schedule

Pools brought forward: 10% $100,000, 20% $200,000, 30% $300,000. During the year the business bought machinery for cash $150,000 (a 20% pool item) and sold an item from the 30% pool for $50,000, below its original cost.

| 10% | 20% | 30% | Allowances
Written down value b/f | 100,000 | 200,000 | 300,000 |
Additions | — | 150,000 | — |
Less: initial allowance (60% × 150,000) | — | (90,000) | — | 90,000
| 100,000 | 260,000 | 300,000 |
Less: disposal proceeds | — | — | (50,000) |
Reduced value | 100,000 | 260,000 | 250,000 |
Less: annual allowance | (10,000) | (52,000) | (75,000) | 137,000
Written down value c/f | 90,000 | 208,000 | 175,000 |
Total depreciation allowances | | | | 227,000
The 20% pool's annual allowance is $52,000, not $70,000 — 20% of $260,000 after the initial allowance, not of the $350,000 before it. The $227,000 total is the single figure that carries into the profits tax computation above.

sections.heading: 5. Personal Assessment IRO ss.40–43
sections.text:
5. Personal Assessment IRO ss.40–43

The one format that consumes the other four: it takes the net assessable value from the property computation, the net assessable income from the salaries computation and the net assessable profit from the profits computation, and re-taxes the lot at progressive rates.

Personal Assessment Computation · Year of Assessment 20XX/XX

Net assessable value — from the property tax computation | X
Net assessable income — from the salaries tax computation | X
Net assessable profit — sole proprietorships and share of partnerships | X
Total income | X
Less: interest on money borrowed to produce property income (capped at that property's NAV) | (X)
Less: concessionary deductions | (X)
Less: business loss of the year | (X)
Less: loss brought forward under Personal Assessment | (X)
Reduced total income | RTI
Less: personal allowances | (X)
Net chargeable income | NCI
(b) Progressive rates on NCI | b
(c) Standard rate on RTI — before allowances | c
Tax payable — the lower of (b) and (c) | X
Joint election — apportioning the tax
Where a married couple elects jointly, the allowances come off the joint reduced total income and the tax is computed once, then split in the ratio of each spouse's reduced total income — not gross. Each receives their own notice of assessment.

Four full worked examples, including one where electing costs money, are on the Personal Assessment page →

sections.heading: A. From IRD DIPNs
sections.text:
A. From IRD DIPNs

Illustration — Industrial building sale: buyer/seller allowance split DIPN 2

A factory is built for $500,000 in February 1992. Initial allowance 20% = $100,000; annual allowance 4% = $20,000 in the first year, continuing for 3 more years, leaving a residue of expenditure of $320,000. The building is then sold for $420,000. The seller faces a balancing charge of $100,000 (sale price exceeds residue by $100,000, capped at allowances previously granted). The buyer's future annual allowance is recalculated as 1/21 (years remaining to the 25th year) × $420,000 = $20,000/year.

Illustration — Plant & machinery pooling across two rate classes DIPN 7

A taxpayer buys a motor car for $150,000 and 3 cookers for $50,000 (both 30% pool), plus office furniture for $20,000 and air-conditioning for $28,000 (both 20% pool). Year 1: 30% pool — cost $200,000, initial allowance 60% = $120,000, annual allowance on the remaining $80,000 at 30% = $24,000. 20% pool — similar mechanics give a smaller annual allowance. Total first-year depreciation allowance across both pools: $176,640.

Illustration — Balancing charge capped at allowances previously granted DIPN 7

On cessation of a business, a 30% pool with a reducing value brought forward of $21,000 (original cost $75,000) is sold for $80,000. Although sale proceeds ($80,000) exceed the reducing value ($21,000) by $59,000, the balancing charge is capped at $54,000 — the total allowances previously granted ($75,000 cost − $21,000 residue) — never more than was originally allowed.

Illustration — Accelerating pre-2018/19 environmental instalments to 100% DIPN 5

Company-HK pays $15M, $20M and $30M in May 2016/2017/2018 respectively for environmental protection installations, under the pre-2018/19 5-instalment (20%/year) regime. Electing under s.16I(3A) to accelerate all remaining instalments to 100% in 2018/19 gives total cumulative deductions of $3,000,000 (2016/17) + $7,000,000 (2017/18) + $55,000,000 combined by 2018/19 (remaining instalments on the first two payments, plus 100% of the third).

Illustration — Specified IP Right deduction spread to match remaining protection DIPN 49

A copyright costing $400,000 has protection expiring in YA2022/23. Rather than the standard 5 equal instalments, the deduction is compressed into the 4 years actually remaining: $100,000/year for YA2019/20–2022/23.

sections.heading: B. From Module 9: Principles of Taxation (4th ed.)
sections.text:
B. From Module 9: Principles of Taxation (4th ed.)

Adapted from a professional taxation qualification manual. Facts are paraphrased, not reproduced verbatim. The plant & machinery pooling rates (60% initial; 10%/20%/30% annual) are unchanged in current law — no correction was needed.

Illustration — Plant & machinery pooling across two years, with disposals and additions Module 9, Ch.3 §3.7.1 — adapted from DIPN 7

A business starts trading on 2 February 2018. In its first year it buys a car ($150,000) and 3 electric cookers ($50,000) — both 30% pool — plus office furniture ($20,000) and 2 air-conditioning units ($28,000) — both 20% pool.

Year 1 (YA 2018/19)

| 30% pool | 20% pool
Cost | $200,000 | $48,000
Less: initial allowance (60%) | ($120,000) | ($28,800)
Less: annual allowance (30% / 20% of remainder) | ($24,000) | ($3,840)
Reducing value carried forward | $56,000 | $15,360
Total Year 1 depreciation allowance across both pools: $120,000 + $28,800 + $24,000 + $3,840 = $176,640.

In Year 2: the car is written off in an accident (insurance + scrap recovery $31,000); a new van is bought for $180,000; a cooker is sold for $3,000 (total 30%-pool disposal proceeds $34,000); an air-conditioning unit is sold for $2,000 and replaced with a new one for $8,000.

Year 2 (YA 2019/20)

| 30% pool | 20% pool
Reducing value brought forward | $56,000 | $15,360
Add: new assets | $180,000 | $8,000
Less: initial allowance (60% of new assets) | ($108,000) | ($4,800)
Less: disposal proceeds | ($34,000) | ($2,000)
Less: annual allowance | ($28,200) | ($3,312)
Reducing value carried forward | $65,800 | $13,248
Total Year 2 depreciation allowance: $108,000 + $4,800 + $28,200 + $3,312 = $144,312. Disposal proceeds simply reduce the pool's reducing value — they don't trigger a balancing charge unless they exceed it (see the DIPN 7 illustration above for that scenario). Rates used (60% initial, 30%/20% annual) match current law exactly — no correction needed.

sections.heading: 1. Overview
sections.text:
1. Overview

Because capital expenditure and accounting depreciation are non-deductible under Profits Tax (s.17(1)(c)/(d)), Part 6 of the IRO substitutes a separate, statutory system of capital allowances for four categories of qualifying capital expenditure: (1) industrial buildings, (2) commercial buildings, (3) plant & machinery, and (4) a growing list of 100%/5-year write-off regimes for specific asset types (ss.16C–16L) that sit alongside, and interact with, Part 6.

Key mechanic — add-back and allowance in the same computation
In every profits tax computation: add back accounting depreciation (non-deductible), then deduct the correct statutory allowance instead. The two numbers are almost never equal — this is the single most common adjustment in a Hong Kong tax computation.

sections.heading: 2. Industrial & Commercial Buildings IRO ss.33A, 34, 36, 37
sections.text:
2. Industrial & Commercial Buildings IRO ss.33A, 34, 36, 37

Building type | Initial allowance | Annual allowance | Balancing allowance/charge
Industrial building or structure (mills, factories, docks, utility undertakings, qualifying storage/farming/R&D buildings) | 20% (1/5) of cost, year of first use | 4% (1/25) straight-line on cost | On sale/lease termination/demolition — balancing charge capped at total allowances previously granted
Commercial building or structure (all other non-excluded buildings) | None | 4% (1/25) straight-line on cost, from 1998/99 | Same balancing mechanism as industrial buildings, from 1998/99
"Industrial building or structure" is narrowly defined (DIPN 2) — it excludes dwellings, retail shops, showrooms, hotels, and offices. Where a building is used partly for a qualifying industrial purpose and partly not, a 10% de-minimis rule applies: if the non-qualifying use is no more than 10% of the whole, the building is treated as wholly industrial. On a sale, the buyer's future annual allowance is recalculated as the residue of expenditure after sale, spread over the remaining years to the building's 25th year from first use.

Historical note
Before 1998/99, commercial buildings only qualified for a much smaller "rebuilding allowance" (0.75% pre-1990/91, then 2% from 1990/91–1997/98) rather than the modern 4% annual allowance — relevant only when tracing the residue of expenditure on a very old building still being written down today.

sections.heading: 3. Plant & Machinery — Pooling System IRO ss.39B–39E
sections.text:
3. Plant & Machinery — Pooling System IRO ss.39B–39E

Since YA1980/81, plant and machinery of the same annual-allowance rate class is pooled together rather than tracked asset-by-asset (the old asset-by-asset method under ss.37–39 survives only for hire-purchase assets, mixed business/private-use assets, and a few other special cases).

Initial allowance | 60% of cost, given once on acquisition
Annual allowance | Reducing-balance on the pool's "reducing value," at 10%, 20% or 30% depending on asset class (Board of Inland Revenue rates)
Common annual allowance rate classes (Appendix A(i), DIPN 7)

Rate | Asset examples
10% | Air-conditioning plant, lifts, cables, ships
20% | Furniture, fixtures, domestic/room air-conditioners — the general residual rate for unlisted items
30% | Motor vehicles, computer/EDP equipment, textile/electronics manufacturing plant, tractors/bulldozers
Balancing allowances only arise when the trade/pool ceases altogether. Balancing charges can arise at any time disposal proceeds exceed the pool's reducing value, but are capped at the total allowances previously granted for that asset (you can never be charged more than you were originally allowed). Hire-purchase assets, and assets moved between private and business use, are excluded from pooling and calculated separately with notional allowance adjustments.

sections.heading: 4. 100% / 5-Year Write-Off Regimes IRO ss.16C, 16F, 16G, 16H–16L
sections.text:
4. 100% / 5-Year Write-Off Regimes IRO ss.16C, 16F, 16G, 16H–16L

Regime | Basis | Treatment
Technical education payments to approved institutions | s.16C | Deductible when paid
Refurbishment/renovation of non-domestic buildings | s.16F | 5 equal annual instalments (20%/year)
Prescribed fixed assets — manufacturing plant, standalone computer hardware/software (excludes leased assets) | s.16G | 100% one-off in year of payment
Environmental protection machinery & environment-friendly vehicles | ss.16H, 16I | 100% one-off (from 2018/19; previously 5-year spread)
Environmental protection installations (buildings) | ss.16J–16L | 100% one-off (from 2018/19; previously 5-year spread)
A taxpayer with unallowed instalments from pre-2018/19 environmental expenditure could elect under s.16I(3A) to accelerate the remaining instalments to a single 100% deduction in 2018/19 (see the DIPN 5 illustration below).

sections.heading: 5. Patents, Know-How & Specified IP Rights IRO ss.16E, 16EA–16EC
sections.text:
5. Patents, Know-How & Specified IP Rights IRO ss.16E, 16EA–16EC

Asset | Basis | Treatment
Patent rights / know-how | s.16E | 100% one-off, year of purchase — no spreading
Specified IP Rights (copyright, registered trade marks/designs, plant variety rights, layout-design/topography rights, performer's economic rights) | ss.16EA–16EC | 5 equal annual instalments (or shorter, to match remaining legal protection period)
Expenditure deductible under s.16E/16EA/16G/16I is excluded from Part 6 depreciation allowances — the regimes are mutually exclusive per asset, not cumulative. Anti-avoidance carve-outs deny the deduction for sale-and-license-back arrangements, purchases from associates, and IP used exclusively outside Hong Kong by another person under a leveraged licensing structure.

sections.text:

The seller faces a balancing charge of $100,000 (sale price exceeds residue by $100,000, capped at allowances previously granted).
