sections.heading: 1. Overview
sections.text:
1. Overview

These provisions are common infrastructure across Profits Tax, Property Tax and Salaries Tax — a computation is only complete once you know how it gets filed, assessed, and (if needed) disputed or paid provisionally.

sections.heading: 2. Returns & Filing IRO s.51
sections.text:
2. Returns & Filing IRO s.51

The Commissioner issues annual returns (profits tax, salaries tax, property tax, employer's return) which must be completed and filed by the stated due date — extensions are routinely available for corporate profits tax returns filed through a tax representative under the Block Extension Scheme. Every person carrying on a trade, profession or business must keep sufficient records (s.51C) for at least 7 years to enable profits/losses to be readily ascertained.

Practical note
For a newly incorporated company, the first profits tax return is usually issued around 18 months after incorporation or commencement of business — but a company must still notify the Commissioner of chargeability (s.51(2)) within 4 months after the end of the basis period if no return has been issued, even where no return has yet been received.

Block Extension Scheme — 2025/26 returns, "D" code extended
By circular letter of 14 July 2026, the Commissioner further extended the due date for 2025/26 profits tax returns with Accounting Date Code "D" (accounting date falling between 1 and 31 December 2025):

- Paper filing: 17 August 2026 → 31 August 2026

- Electronic filing: 17 September 2026 → 2 October 2026

The extension was granted to help businesses and practitioners adapt to new compliance requirements; the circular still urges representatives to file well before the extended date. Codes "N" and "M" were not changed by this circular. Source: Circular Letter to Tax Representatives — Block Extension Scheme for Lodgement of 2025/26 Tax Returns, 14 Jul 2026.

Business Tax Portal — new Responsible Person capacities (8 Jun 2026)
IRD expanded the capacities in which a Responsible Person may register a business for the Business Tax Portal (BTP). Check the registration capacity before opening a BTP account for a client entity — an account opened in the wrong capacity has to be redone.

sections.heading: 3. Assessment & Estimated Assessment IRO ss.59–60
sections.text:
3. Assessment & Estimated Assessment IRO ss.59–60

The assessor assesses the return as filed, or — where no return is filed, or the assessor is not satisfied with a return — issues an estimated assessment based on the best information available. Estimated assessments are commonly issued precisely to protect the statutory time limit for assessment where a return is outstanding; they are not a final determination and are superseded once the actual figures are agreed (usually via an objection, §4).

Additional assessments may be raised within the statutory time limit (generally 6 years from the end of the relevant year of assessment, extended to 10 years in cases involving fraud or wilful default) where profits/income have been understated or under-assessed.

sections.heading: 4. Objections & Appeals IRO s.64 (objections), s.66 (Board of Review), s.69 (case stated)
sections.text:
4. Objections & Appeals IRO s.64 (objections), s.66 (Board of Review), s.69 (case stated)

Stage | Time limit | Forum
Notice of objection | 1 month from the date of the assessment | Commissioner of Inland Revenue
Appeal against the Commissioner's determination | 1 month from the determination | Board of Review
Case stated appeal on a point of law | 1 month from the Board's decision | Court of First Instance, then Court of Appeal / Court of Final Appeal
An objection must state precisely the grounds of objection — a bare, unparticularised objection can be rejected as invalid. Tax under dispute is not automatically suspended; the taxpayer must separately apply to hold over payment of the tax in dispute (or the portion in dispute) pending resolution.

sections.heading: 5. Provisional Tax & Holdover IRO ss.63A–63U, 71
sections.text:
5. Provisional Tax & Holdover IRO ss.63A–63U, 71

Provisional profits tax, provisional salaries tax, and provisional property tax are each charged in advance, generally based on the immediately preceding year's assessable profits/income, and later set off against the final assessment for that year once it issues. A taxpayer may apply to hold over payment of the whole or part of provisional tax where, for example, the current year's profits/income are objectively likely to be significantly lower than the prior year's, or personal allowances have increased, or an objection is pending on the immediately preceding year's assessment.

Practical note
Holdover applications have their own strict statutory deadlines (broadly, the later of 28 days before the provisional tax is due, or 14 days after the provisional tax notice is issued) — missing the window forfeits the holdover regardless of the merits.

sections.heading: 6. Late Payment of Tax — Surcharge and Recovery IRO s.71; Part 12
sections.text:
6. Late Payment of Tax — Surcharge and Recovery IRO s.71; Part 12

The consequence almost every taxpayer actually meets, and the one most often confused with the penalties in §7. A surcharge under s.71 is not a penalty for an offence — it is automatic, needs no intent, no reasonable-excuse enquiry and no hearing. Miss the date and it is imposed.

When | What happens | Provision
The due date passes
A 5% surcharge is imposed on the tax unpaid. Recovery action may begin immediately and without prior notice.
s.71(5)
6 months after the due date
A further 10% surcharge on the amount still unpaid — including the 5% already imposed.
s.71(5A)
The 10% is charged on the tax plus the first surcharge — so it is not 15%
On tax of $100,000 left unpaid for over six months:

Tax due | 100,000
Add: 5% surcharge — s.71(5) | 5,000
Amount unpaid after the due date | 105,000
Add: further 10% on $105,000 — s.71(5A) | 10,500
Total payable | 115,500
Total surcharge $15,500 — 15.5% of the original tax, not 15%. The second surcharge compounds on the first.

The instalment trap

Where a demand note is split into two instalments, missing the first makes the second immediately due, and the 5% is then charged on the whole outstanding balance — not just on the instalment that was missed.

Demand note of $100,000: first instalment $70,000, second $30,000

First instalment paid on time, second missed — 5% × $30,000 | 1,500
First instalment missed — the second accelerates, so 5% × $100,000 | 5,000
Cost of missing the earlier date rather than the later one | 3,500
Left unpaid for six months, that same note reaches $115,500.

Recovery of tax in default IRO Part 12

IRD does not wait for the six-month mark before acting. Its own notice states that other than imposing the 5% surcharge it "will also immediately commence other recovery actions without prior notice":

Action | What it means in practice
Recovery notice to a third party
s.76
Served on anyone who owes or holds money for the defaulter — employer, bank, tenant, debtor, customer. That person must pay the money to IRD instead, and is discharged to the extent they do. This is why a tax default can become visible to an employer or banker.
Civil proceedings
s.75
Tax in default is recoverable as a civil debt in the District Court. A judgment carries the usual consequences, including costs and interest on the judgment debt.
Departure prevention order
s.77
The Commissioner may apply to a District Judge for a direction stopping a defaulter from leaving Hong Kong until the tax is paid or security given.
Joint and several liability
property tax co-owners
Co-owners are liable jointly and severally: IRD may pursue any one of them for the whole amount, not merely their share. Once one pays in full, recovery against the others stops. Tax is never collected twice, and any overpayment is refunded.
Applying to pay by instalments does not stop the surcharge
A taxpayer in genuine financial difficulty may apply to settle by instalments. But IRD is explicit that even where the application is approved, surcharges are still imposed on tax remaining unpaid after the due date. An instalment arrangement buys time and heads off recovery action; it is not a waiver. Conditional waiver schemes have been offered in particular years as a relief measure, but they are exceptional and year-specific — never assume one applies.

Keep the two regimes apart — this is the distinction to have straight

| Surcharge, s.71 | Penalty, ss.80 / 82A / 82
Triggered by | Paying late | Failing to file or notify, filing an incorrect return, or evading tax
Fault required | None — automatic on the date | Absence of reasonable excuse; for s.82, wilful intent
Amount | 5%, then a further 10% on the total | Up to treble the tax undercharged, plus a fine and, under s.82, imprisonment
Who imposes it | The Commissioner, administratively | The Commissioner (s.82A) or a court (ss.80, 82)
A taxpayer who files a correct return on time but pays late faces the surcharge only. One who files late and pays late faces both.

Source: IRD, Pay Tax On Time to Avoid Penalty and Recovery Actions, and GovHK Consequences of Not Paying Tax On Time and Recovering Tax in Default.

sections.heading: 7. Penalties IRO ss.80, 82, 82A
sections.text:
7. Penalties IRO ss.80, 82, 82A

Contravention | Consequence
Failure to file a return, or filing late, without reasonable excuse | Summary conviction fine and/or additional tax (s.80)
Making an incorrect return, or omitting income, without reasonable excuse | Additional tax up to treble the tax undercharged (s.82A) — an administrative penalty assessed by the Commissioner, distinct from criminal prosecution
Wilfully with intent to evade, or assisting another to evade, tax | Criminal prosecution (s.82) — fine up to treble the tax undercharged plus imprisonment up to 3 years
Additional tax under s.82A is an administrative sanction (no need to prove criminal intent) and can be settled by way of a compound penalty offer from the Commissioner in less serious cases — this is the mechanism most commonly encountered in routine tax computation corrections and voluntary disclosures.

sections.heading: 8. Double Taxation Relief & Tax Clearance IRO ss.49, 50, 51D
sections.text:
8. Double Taxation Relief & Tax Clearance IRO ss.49, 50, 51D

Where Hong Kong has a comprehensive double taxation agreement (CDTA) with another jurisdiction, s.50 provides a tax credit for foreign tax paid on income also taxed in Hong Kong (interacting with the s.16(1)(c)/(2J) deduction restriction on the Profits Tax page). Employers must comply with tax clearance obligations (s.51D) before an employee who is about to leave Hong Kong permanently, or for a substantial period, ceases employment — including withholding final payments until IRD confirms clearance or a specified period has elapsed.

CDTA network (as at 24 September 2026): Hong Kong signed its 60th comprehensive double taxation agreement with Slovenia on 4 September 2026, following Nigeria (13 July 2026) and Cyprus (12 June 2026). Each enters into force only after both sides complete ratification — check the IRD CDTA list for the in-force date before claiming treaty relief.

sections.heading: 9. Automatic Exchange of Information & Crypto-Asset Reporting IRO Part 8A
sections.text:
9. Automatic Exchange of Information & Crypto-Asset Reporting IRO Part 8A

Two separate 2026 measures extend Hong Kong's information-exchange obligations, and both change what a reporting financial institution has to collect:

- Amended CRS — enacted. The Inland Revenue (Amendment) (Automatic Exchange of Information) Bill 2026 passed on 17 June 2026, implementing the OECD's amended Common Reporting Standard.

- CARF — bill stage. The Inland Revenue (Amendment) (Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework and Amended Common Reporting Standard) Bill 2026 was introduced into LegCo on 1 June 2026, and IRD published its Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework page on 22 June 2026. CARF brings crypto-asset service providers into the reporting net — a genuinely new population of reporting entities, not just a new field on an existing return.

Policy watch
The Advisory Committee on Tax Policy held its first meeting on 29 June 2026 — the standing forum now shaping medium-term HK tax policy. IRD also responded to an Ombudsman direct investigation report on 31 August 2026, and published its Annual Report on Performance Pledge 2025-26 on 9 July 2026 (useful for expected turnaround times on objections and refunds).

Fraud alerts — tell clients
IRD issued fraudulent-email alerts on 6 July, 22 July, 4 September and 15 September 2026 (fake prosecution notices, fake tax audit notices, and phishing for email passwords), plus a 25 August 2026 warning not to download the eTAX Mobile Application from unofficial channels. IRD does not request passwords or payment by email link.

sections.heading: 1. How to use this page
sections.text:
1. How to use this page

The Study Hub's tax pages state the law as it stands. This page is the audit trail behind them: what IRD announced, whether it is enacted or still proposed, and which page was edited as a result.

Marker | Meaning
Enacted | In force, or an ordinance already gazetted. Safe to apply, subject to its own commencement date.
Gazetted / bill | Published or before LegCo but not yet law. Know it is coming; do not apply it.
Proposed | Policy announcement only, needs an amendment ordinance. Do not apply it to a live filing or transaction.
The trap this page exists to stop
A Policy Address measure is not law on the day it is announced. Both 2026 Policy Address measures below are drafted into this Hub as proposed, alongside the enacted figure. Quote the enacted figure in any computation until the amendment ordinance is gazetted.

sections.heading: 3. Salaries tax & individuals
sections.text:
3. Salaries tax & individuals

2026 Policy Address — child allowance 16 September 2026 · proposed

Child allowance rises from HKD 140,000 to HKD 160,000 for a taxpayer's second and subsequent children born on or after 16 September 2026, claimable until age 25 on the usual conditions. The additional child allowance for the year of birth and the following year rises to HKD 160,000 on the same basis — so HKD 320,000 per qualifying child in each of those two years.

Child | Born before 16 Sep 2026 | Born on/after 16 Sep 2026
First child | 140,000 | 140,000 (unchanged)
Second and subsequent | 140,000 | 160,000 (proposed)
Intended effect from YA 2026/27, but it requires an amendment ordinance. Two traps: the increase does not reach first-born children, and it is keyed to the child's date of birth, not the year of assessment — an existing second child born in 2024 stays at HKD 140,000 indefinitely. IRD source.

sections.heading: 4. Stamp duty
sections.text:
4. Stamp duty

2026 Policy Address — newborn-family concession 16 September 2026 · proposed

A family with a child born in Hong Kong on or after 16 September 2026, at least one parent being a Hong Kong permanent resident, would receive a stamp duty waiver capped at HKD 20,000 on a residential property bought in the window from one year before to two years after the birth. Effective on enactment of the amendment ordinance. It is a capped waiver, not a rate change — on any purchase where AVD exceeds HKD 20,000 the benefit is a flat HKD 20,000. IRD source.

Stamp Duty (Amendment) (No. 3) Bill 2026 — intra-group relief Announced 29 Sep 2026, gazetted 2 Oct 2026 · bill

Relaxes the s.45 associated bodies corporate relief on intra-group transfers in three ways: the association test drops from 90% to 75%; "association" may be established through direct or indirect beneficial interests or voting rights, not only issued share capital; and relief is extended to entities with no share capital to measure, such as limited liability partnerships and companies limited by guarantee. First reading is set for 14 October 2026, and the Bill proposes to apply retrospectively to instruments executed on or after 25 February 2026.

Not law yet. The Stamp Duty page continues to state the enacted 90% test as its primary figure, with the proposed 75% carried as a marked note. The retrospective date matters: if the Bill passes as drafted, instruments already executed since 25 February 2026 that failed the 90% test but meet 75% would become relievable — worth flagging on any live transaction, but not a basis for stamping today. Press release.

Stamp Duty (Amendment) (No. 2) Ordinance 2026 Passed 8 Jul 2026, gazetted 17 Jul 2026 · enacted

Stamp duty on a transfer of dual-counter stock traded at the RMB counter may be calculated and paid in Renminbi, letting an investor settle trade and duty in one currency at one counter. The 0.2% rate is unchanged. Commencement is on a day to be appointed by the Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury, pending HKEX system readiness — so it is gazetted but not yet operative. Press release.

sections.heading: 8. Fraud alerts

8. Fraud alerts

IRD issued fraudulent-email alerts on 6 July (fake legal prosecution notices), 22 July (phishing for email passwords), 4 September (fake tax audit notices) and 15 September 2026 (fake compliance notices and suspicious links), and warned on 25 August 2026 against downloading the eTAX Mobile Application from any unofficial channel.

Rule of thumb for clients

9. Noted — no content change

Read and deliberately not acted on, so a later reviewer need not re-read them: the five "Full text of The Chief Executive's 2026 Policy Address" transcripts (16 Sep 2026, the underlying speech text for the two measures above); LCQ19 on regulating charitable organisations (8 Jul 2026); LCQ21 on e-commerce tax policy and LCQ16 on fertility measures (17 Jun 2026); and the 15 Jun 2026 notice that LegCo would consider the AEOI Bill. Refresh discipline
Re-read IRD What's New monthly, and always before finalising a filing position. When you do, update the "read on" date in the banner at the top of this page and add a row to §2 — an undated freshness claim is worse than none.

sections.heading: 1. Profits Tax - Trading, Source, Deductions
sections.text:
1. Profits Tax - Trading, Source, Deductions

Illustration PT-1 Badges of trade

Question. A company buys a shop unit with short-term bank finance, renovates it lightly, advertises it for resale within three months, and sells at a gain. Is the gain likely capital or trading?

中文題目：一間公司以短期銀行貸款購入商舖，簡單裝修後三個月內放售並賺取收益。該收益較可能屬資本性質，還是營業買賣收益？

Answer. It is likely trading. Short holding period, financing arranged for quick turnover, resale activity, and commercial organization all point toward an adventure in the nature of trade. The label in board minutes is useful evidence, but the whole fact pattern matters more.

中文答案：較可能屬營業買賣收益。持有期短、以短期融資支持快速轉售、有主動放售行為及商業組織安排，都指向「屬貿易性質的一次性交易」。董事會紀錄的說法有參考價值，但最終仍要整體看事實。

Illustration PT-2 Capital asset disposal

Question. A retailer buys a warehouse for storage, uses it for several years, then sells it after receiving an unsolicited offer. Is the gain automatically taxable because the seller is a business?

中文題目：零售商購入倉庫作儲貨用途，使用數年後因收到買家主動出價而出售。是否因賣方是商業機構，收益便自動須課利得稅？

Answer. No. A business can hold capital assets. If the warehouse was acquired and used as a fixed capital facility rather than trading stock, the gain is more likely capital and outside profits tax, subject to the facts.

中文答案：不是。商業機構也可以持有資本資產。如果倉庫購入及使用目的均屬固定資本設施，而非買賣存貨，出售收益較可能屬資本性質，不屬利得稅課稅範圍；但仍須視乎全部事實。

Illustration PT-3 Source of service income

Question. A Hong Kong company signs contracts in Hong Kong but its staff perform all consultancy fieldwork in Japan. Where should the source analysis focus?

中文題目：香港公司在香港簽約，但員工全部顧問實地工作均在日本進行。判斷利潤來源地時應集中看甚麼？

Answer. Focus on what the taxpayer did to earn the fee and where those profit-producing operations took place. For service income, performance of the services usually carries strong weight; contract signing alone is not always decisive.

中文答案：重點是納稅人做了甚麼來賺取該收入，以及產生利潤的實際操作在何處進行。服務收入通常很重視服務履行地；單靠簽約地點未必具決定性。

Illustration PT-4 Bad debt deduction

Question. A trading debt of HK$90,000 was previously booked as taxable sales income and is later written off as irrecoverable. A separate staff loan of HK$40,000 is also written off. Which write-off is deductible?

中文題目：一筆 HK$90,000 貿易應收款曾計入應課稅銷售收入，後來證實不能收回並撇銷；另有 HK$40,000 員工貸款亦撇銷。哪一項可扣稅？

Answer. The trading debt is deductible because it arose from taxable trading receipts already brought into account. The staff loan is normally not deductible for an ordinary trader because making staff loans is not its money-lending business and the loan principal was not taxable income.

中文答案：貿易壞帳可扣稅，因為它源自已入帳的應課稅營業收入。員工貸款一般不可扣稅，因普通貿易公司並非經營放債業務，而貸款本金亦從未作為應課稅收入入帳。

Question PT-5 Quick MCQ

Question. Which expense is most clearly deductible for profits tax?

中文題目：以下哪項開支最明顯可作利得稅扣除？

A. Private rent of the managing director. B. Capital cost of acquiring a liquor licence. C. Interest on a commercial loan used to buy trading stock, assuming the interest rules are met. D. Cost recovered from an insurer.

Answer. C. The borrowing is for trading stock and can satisfy the production-of-profits test, but interest must still pass the specific interest deduction conditions.

中文答案：C。借款用於購買營業存貨，較能符合「產生應課稅利潤」的要求；但利息仍須通過利息扣除的特定條件。

sections.heading: 2. Salaries Tax - Employment Income and Benefits
sections.text:
2. Salaries Tax - Employment Income and Benefits

Question ST-1 Employment vs self-employment

Question. A marketing worker has fixed office hours, uses the company's equipment, reports to a director, and receives a monthly salary plus commission. Salaries tax or profits tax?

中文題目：市場推廣人員有固定辦公時間，使用公司設備，向董事匯報，並收取月薪加佣金。應較可能屬薪俸稅還是利得稅？

Answer. Salaries tax is more likely. Control, integration into the employer's organization, and lack of entrepreneurial risk point to employment rather than an independent profession or business.

中文答案：較可能屬薪俸稅。受僱主控制、融入僱主組織、缺乏自行承擔營商風險，均指向僱傭關係而非獨立專業或業務。

Question ST-2 Contract for services

Question. A consultant serves several clients, rents her own office, hires assistants, bears overheads, and invoices fixed project fees. What tax head is more likely?

中文題目：一名顧問服務多名客戶，自租辦公室、聘請助理、自行承擔營運開支，並按項目收費。較可能屬哪一稅種？

Answer. Profits tax is more likely. She appears to be carrying on a profession or business on her own account rather than holding an employment.

中文答案：較可能屬利得稅。她看似以自己名義經營專業或業務，而非受僱於單一僱主。

Question ST-3 Share option timing

Question. An employee receives an employment-related share option and later exercises it at a discount. When is the benefit normally measured?

中文題目：僱員因受僱關係取得股份期權，其後以折讓價行使。通常何時計算應課稅利益？

Answer. The taxable benefit is generally measured when the option is exercised, released, or assigned, depending on the event, with the gain computed by reference to the relevant market value and exercise price rules.

中文答案：一般在期權被行使、放棄或轉讓時，按相關事件計算應課稅利益，通常會參考市值與行使價等規則計算收益。

sections.heading: 3. Property Tax - Rental Income and Corporate Owners
sections.text:
3. Property Tax - Rental Income and Corporate Owners

Illustration PrT-1 Tenant-paid expenses

Question. A tenant pays HK$20,000 repair costs that the landlord was obliged to bear under the lease. Is the payment ignored for property tax?

中文題目：租客支付 HK$20,000 修葺費，而根據租約該費用本應由業主承擔。物業稅是否可忽略該款項？

Answer. No. Where the tenant discharges an obligation of the owner, the amount can be treated as consideration for use of the property. The statutory 20% allowance then applies in computing net assessable value.

中文答案：不可忽略。若租客代業主履行責任，該款項可被視為使用物業的代價，然後在計算應評稅淨值時扣除 20% 法定修葺免稅額。

Illustration PrT-2 Simple NAV computation

Question. Annual rent is HK$360,000. Rates of HK$12,000 are paid by the owner. No irrecoverable rent. Compute net assessable value.

中文題目：全年租金 HK$360,000，差餉 HK$12,000 由業主支付，沒有不能追回租金。計算應評稅淨值。

Assessable value before allowance: 360,000 - 12,000 = 348,000
Less statutory repairs allowance: 348,000 x 20% = 69,600
Net assessable value: 278,400
Answer. NAV is HK$278,400.

中文答案：應評稅淨值為 HK$278,400。

Question PrT-3 Corporate property owner

Question. A Hong Kong company lets out an office and the rental income is already included in profits tax. Can it avoid double tax under property tax?

中文題目：香港公司出租辦公室，租金收入已納入利得稅課稅。可否避免再繳物業稅？

Answer. A corporation can usually seek exemption from property tax where the property income is chargeable to profits tax. The rental stream is then dealt with under profits tax rather than being taxed twice.

中文答案：公司如相關物業收入已須繳利得稅，通常可申請豁免物業稅，避免同一租金收入被重複課稅。

sections.heading: 4. Personal Assessment - Election and Loss Set-off
sections.text:
4. Personal Assessment - Election and Loss Set-off

Illustration PA-1 Mortgage interest limit

Question. Under personal assessment, an individual has property NAV of HK$60,000 and interest of HK$75,000 on the loan used to buy that income-producing property. How much interest can be deducted against that property income?

中文題目：在個人入息課稅下，某人有物業應評稅淨值 HK$60,000，購買該收租物業的貸款利息為 HK$75,000。可扣除多少利息？

Answer. HK$60,000. The property-loan interest deduction is limited by the net assessable value of the relevant property included in personal assessment.

中文答案：HK$60,000。可扣除的物業貸款利息以納入個人入息課稅的相關物業應評稅淨值為上限。

Illustration PA-2 Business loss limit

Question. Total income after allowable deductions becomes negative because of concessionary deductions and a business loss. How much personal assessment loss can be carried forward?

中文題目：扣除特惠扣除及業務虧損後，總入息變成負數。可結轉的個人入息課稅虧損是多少？

Answer. The carry-forward personal assessment loss is limited to the business loss element. A deficit caused by personal allowances or non-business concessionary deductions is not carried forward as a business loss.

中文答案：可結轉的個人入息課稅虧損以業務虧損部分為限。由個人免稅額或非業務性特惠扣除造成的不足額，不會作為業務虧損結轉。

Question PA-3 Married couple election

Question. A married person wants personal assessment, but the spouse also has income chargeable to tax. Can one spouse elect alone?

中文題目：已婚人士想選擇個人入息課稅，但配偶亦有應課稅收入。一方可否單獨選擇？

Answer. Generally no. Where both spouses have income within the personal assessment framework, joint election is required. This is important when modelling whether personal assessment is beneficial.

中文答案：一般不可以。若夫婦雙方均有屬個人入息課稅框架內的收入，通常需要共同選擇。判斷個人入息課稅是否有利時必須留意這點。

sections.heading: 5. Stamp Duty - Instruments, Property, Shares, Relief
sections.text:
5. Stamp Duty - Instruments, Property, Shares, Relief

Question SD-1 Instrument-based tax

Question. Why is it imprecise to say that stamp duty taxes "transactions"?

中文題目：為何說印花稅是對「交易」課稅並不精確？

Answer. Stamp duty is charged on instruments. A transaction matters because it produces or explains the instrument, but the charge is imposed by reference to the stampable document and the relevant charging head.

中文答案：印花稅是對文書課稅。交易本身重要，是因為它產生或解釋該文書；但真正課稅基礎是可予徵收印花稅的文件及相關課稅項目。

Illustration SD-2 Hong Kong stock transfer

Question. Hong Kong shares are sold for HK$100,000 but market value is HK$120,000. Which amount is used for ad valorem stamp duty?

中文題目：香港股票以 HK$100,000 出售，但市值為 HK$120,000。從價印花稅應以哪個金額計算？

Answer. HK$120,000. For Hong Kong stock transfers, duty is generally computed on the higher of consideration and value. Check the current stock duty rate before filing, as rates have changed over time.

中文答案：HK$120,000。香港股票轉讓一般按代價及價值兩者中較高者計算印花稅。由於股票印花稅率曾有變動，實際申報前應查核現行稅率。

Question SD-3 Associated company relief

Question. ParentCo transfers Hong Kong immovable property to a 100%-owned subsidiary. What relief may be relevant?

中文題目：母公司把香港不動產轉讓予其 100% 擁有的附屬公司。可能涉及哪項印花稅寬免？

Answer. Associated-company relief under SDO s.45 may be relevant if the ownership threshold and continuity conditions are satisfied. The parties must monitor the post-transfer association period because relief can be clawed back if the conditions break.

中文答案：如符合持股比例及持續關聯條件，可能適用《印花稅條例》第 45 條關聯公司寬免。轉讓後仍須監察關聯關係維持期，否則寬免可能被撤回。

sections.heading: 6. Cross-border Profits Tax - Withholding and Non-residents
sections.text:
6. Cross-border Profits Tax - Withholding and Non-residents

Question CB-1 Non-resident entertainer

Question. A Hong Kong event organizer pays a non-resident performer's company for a Hong Kong performance. Why might Hong Kong tax be withheld even if the performer is paid through a company?

中文題目：香港活動主辦方向非居民表演者的公司支付香港演出費。即使款項經公司支付，為何仍可能需要在香港預扣稅？

Answer. The IRO contains deeming and collection rules for non-resident entertainers and sportspeople. Interposing a company does not necessarily remove the Hong Kong charge where the performance activity is in Hong Kong.

中文答案：《稅務條例》對非居民演藝人員及運動員有視作收入及徵收規則。即使中間有公司收款，只要演出活動在香港進行，未必能避免香港稅務責任。

Illustration CB-2 Deemed profit method

Question. If the law taxes a non-resident entertainer on a deemed profit basis, what are the two moving parts in the computation?

中文題目：若法例以視作利潤方法向非居民表演者課稅，計算時主要有哪兩個變動部分？

Answer. First identify the gross payment that falls within the deeming rule. Then apply the statutory deemed-profit fraction and the applicable tax rate. If the actual-profit method is claimed, only properly connected deductible expenses should be used.

中文答案：第一，確定受視作規則涵蓋的總付款；第二，套用法定視作利潤比例及適用稅率。如改用實際利潤方法，只應扣除與香港演出適當相關的可扣稅開支。

sections.heading: 1. What Personal Assessment is IRO s.41
sections.text:
1. What Personal Assessment is IRO s.41

Hong Kong levies direct tax under three separate heads — Salaries Tax, Profits Tax and Property Tax. Personal Assessment (PA) is not a fourth head of charge. It is a relief: an individual may elect to have all three sources aggregated into one computation, taxed at salaries-tax progressive rates after personal allowances, instead of being taxed separately at the standard rate on each source.

The one-line test for whether PA can possibly help
Property Tax and Profits Tax are charged at the standard rate with no personal allowances. Salaries Tax already gets progressive rates and allowances. So PA can only help someone with property income or unincorporated-business profits. A taxpayer whose only income is employment income cannot benefit from electing — there is nothing for the election to unlock.

The election is annual, must be made in writing, and is not automatic. IRD will not apply it for you, though where an election has been made and turns out to be disadvantageous, the assessor will raise the separate assessments instead and note on the demand that PA was not to your benefit.

Distinguish from Joint Assessment
Joint assessment (s.10(2)) is a Salaries Tax mechanism for married couples — it pools employment income only. Personal Assessment (s.41) pools all three heads of charge. They are different elections under different sections, and the exam trap is treating them as the same thing. See Salaries Tax §6.

sections.heading: 2. Who may elect IRO s.41(1), s.41(4)
sections.text:
2. Who may elect IRO s.41(1), s.41(4)

The conditions changed from YA 2018/19. Both are set out because the older rule still governs any earlier year still under assessment or objection.

Year of assessment | Conditions
2018/19 onwards
current
The individual is 18 or over (or under 18 if both parents are dead); and the elector is personally either ordinarily resident in Hong Kong or a temporary resident.
Up to 2017/18
Same age test; but the residence test could be satisfied by the spouse — the elector, or if married their spouse, had to be ordinarily resident or a temporary resident.
The substantive change is that from 2018/19 the elector must qualify on their own residence. Piggy-backing on a spouse's residence status no longer works.

Term | Meaning
Ordinarily resident
s.41(4)
Resides in Hong Kong voluntarily and for a settled purpose (education, business, employment, family) with a sufficient degree of continuity — habitually and normally resident apart from temporary or occasional absences, living here as an ordinary member of the community for all the purposes of daily life. Ultimately a question of fact. The Ordinance does not define it further; the case law is Lysaght v CIR (regular visits of substantial duration year to year) and Cooper v Cadwalader (maintaining a place of abode).
Temporary resident
Stays in Hong Kong for more than 180 days during the year of assessment for which the election is made, or more than 300 days in two consecutive years of assessment, one of which is the year of election.
Not the same as a permanent identity card
"Ordinarily resident" is a factual test about how and where someone actually lives. Holding a Hong Kong permanent identity card is evidence, not the test, and someone can hold one while no longer ordinarily residing here. Conversely a non-permanent resident who is physically here for enough days qualifies as a temporary resident and may elect.

Deceased taxpayers. Where a person who was eligible to elect dies, the executor has the same right of election over the deceased's total income as the deceased would have had.

sections.heading: 3. Married couples IRO s.41(1A), s.42(2)
sections.text:
3. Married couples IRO s.41(1A), s.42(2)

Separate election has been available since YA 2018/19
The Inland Revenue (Amendment) (No. 9) Ordinance 2018 relaxed what had been a hard joint-election requirement. From YA 2018/19, a married person may elect for Personal Assessment separately from, or jointly with, their spouse.

Situation | Who elects
2018/19 onwards, general rule | Either spouse may elect on their own. A joint election remains available where either or both are eligible and both have income assessable under the Ordinance.
Already jointly assessed under Salaries Tax | The PA election must be made jointly. A couple who elected joint assessment under s.10(2) cannot then split for PA.
Up to 2017/18 | Where both spouses had assessable income and were not living apart, the election had to be made by both. If one refused, neither could elect.
Where a joint election is made, each spouse's total income as appropriately reduced is aggregated into a joint reduced total income, the married person's allowance and other allowances are deducted from the joint figure, and the tax is computed once. The total tax is then apportioned between the spouses in the ratio of their respective reduced total incomes, and each receives their own notice of assessment and demand for payment.

Why the 2018/19 change matters in practice
Under the old joint-election rule, electing meant each spouse necessarily learned the other's income and business losses. A spouse who wanted to keep that private could simply refuse, and the couple lost the relief entirely. Separate election removes that veto.

sections.heading: 4. Time limits — election and withdrawal IRO s.41(2), s.41(3)
sections.text:
4. Time limits — election and withdrawal IRO s.41(2), s.41(3)

Action | Deadline
Election
The later of:

- 2 years after the end of the year of assessment concerned — so for YA 2026/27, not later than 31 March 2029; or

- 2 months after the issue of a notice of assessment or additional assessment for that year.

Withdrawal
Within 6 months of the date the Personal Assessment is issued, or such longer period as the Commissioner considers reasonable. Where the election was made jointly, the withdrawal must also be joint.
An election is made in writing — in practice by completing the relevant section of the Tax Return (BIR60), or on Form IR76C.

Withdrawal is close to one-way
Once an election is withdrawn, the taxpayer may not elect again for that same year unless the Commissioner considers a re-election appropriate. Because the two-year election window is generous but the six-month withdrawal window is short, the safer sequence is to compute both outcomes before electing rather than electing speculatively and unwinding it later.

sections.heading: 5. The computation, step by step IRO s.42, s.42A, s.43
sections.text:
5. The computation, step by step IRO s.42, s.42A, s.43

Three steps: aggregate, deduct, then compare against the standard rate.

Step | What happens
1 | Aggregate income chargeable to Property Tax, Salaries Tax and Profits Tax into total income.
2 | Deduct, in order: interest on money borrowed to produce property income → concessionary deductions → business losses of the year → PA losses brought forward. This gives reduced total income. Then deduct personal allowances to give net chargeable income.
3 | Compute tax as the lower of: progressive rates on net chargeable income, or the standard rate on reduced total income.
The standard-rate cap applies to PA too — and on the right base
The cap compares progressive tax on net chargeable income (after allowances) against standard rate on reduced total income (before allowances). Applying the standard rate to the post-allowance figure is a classic error: it uses the wrong base and understates the cap.

What goes into "total income"

Source | Figure brought in
Property
Net assessable value
Rental income + recovered bad rent − irrecoverable rent = assessable value; less rates agreed and paid by the landlord; less the 20% statutory deduction. See Property Tax §NAV.
Employment
Net assessable income
Assessable income less s.12(1)(a) outgoings, s.12(1)(b) depreciation allowances and s.12(1)(e) self-education, plus any s.12(5) balancing charge. Note this is after self-education but before concessionary deductions — those are taken later, at step 2. See Salaries Tax §4.
Business
Net assessable profits
Profits of every sole proprietorship, plus the individual's share from each partnership — after offsetting losses brought forward and after approved charitable donations already allowed in the profits tax computation. See Profits Tax §5.
Only Hong Kong-source income enters
PA aggregates income chargeable under the three heads. Offshore profits that were never chargeable to Profits Tax do not become chargeable by electing PA — and correspondingly an offshore business loss cannot be brought in to shelter Hong Kong income.

sections.heading: 6. What is deductible under Personal Assessment
sections.text:
6. What is deductible under Personal Assessment

Status | Item | Basis / cap (2026/27)
Deductible | Interest on money borrowed to produce property income — the deduction PA exists for | Capped at the net assessable value of that individual property; no excess relief and no carry-forward (Board of Review D51/04)
Deductible | Approved charitable donations | s.26C — aggregate min. HKD 100, capped at 35% of income after other deductions
Deductible | Elderly residential care expenses | s.26D — HKD 110,000 per parent/grandparent; mutually exclusive with the dependent parent allowance
Deductible | Home loan interest | ss.26E/26F — HKD 100,000 (120,000 with a qualifying child); up to 20 years of assessment
Deductible | VHIS qualifying premiums | ss.26H–26M — HKD 8,000 per insured person
Deductible | Qualifying annuity premiums + MPF voluntary contributions | ss.26N–26U — combined cap HKD 60,000
Deductible | Domestic rents | HKD 100,000 (120,000 with a qualifying child)
Deductible | Assisted reproductive service expenses | HKD 100,000
Deductible | Business losses of the year, and PA losses brought forward | The other reason to elect — a sole-proprietorship loss can shelter salary and property income in the same year
Deductible | Personal allowances | Basic 145,000 / married 290,000 for YA 2026/27 (132,000 / 264,000 on the D26 exam basis) — the full table is on Salaries Tax §5
Non-deductible | Private and domestic expenses generally | PA does not open up deductions that no head of charge allows. It only lets you take, against aggregated income, the reliefs the Ordinance already grants.
Non-deductible | Offshore business losses | Never chargeable, so never available for set-off
Non-deductible | Mortgage interest exceeding that property's NAV | The excess lapses — it cannot create or increase a loss
Don't confuse the two interest deductions
Interest to produce property income (this section, capped at that property's NAV) is a different relief from home loan interest under ss.26E/26F (capped at HKD 100,000, for a dwelling the taxpayer occupies). A let property that is also mortgaged attracts the first; an owner-occupied home attracts the second. They are not interchangeable and a single property will not normally attract both.

sections.heading: 7. When it helps — and when it does not
sections.text:
7. When it helps — and when it does not

PA is likely to help where

- Property is mortgaged — Property Tax gives no relief at all for loan interest.

- There is a business loss to set against salary or property income in the same year.

- Total income is low enough that the progressive rates average out below the standard rate.

- Personal allowances are unused because the income is property or business income rather than salary.

- Concessionary deductions (donations, elderly care) are being wasted against income that gets no relief for them.

PA is unlikely to help where

- The only income is employment income — Salaries Tax already applies progressive rates and allowances, so there is nothing to gain.

- Total income is high: the 17% marginal rate exceeds the 15% standard rate, so aggregating drags property or business income up to 17%.

- The property is unmortgaged and allowances are already fully absorbed elsewhere.

Because the marginal progressive rate (17%) is above the standard rate (15%), PA is a relief that reverses into a cost once income is large enough. It must be computed both ways, not assumed.

sections.heading: 8. Worked illustrations
sections.text:
8. Worked illustrations

Adapted from IRD's own worked examples in A Brief Guide to Personal Assessment (pam37e). IRD's leaflet computes them at YA 2025/26 allowances; every figure below has been recomputed at YA 2026/27 rates (basic allowance 145,000, married person's allowance 290,000), so the answers deliberately differ from the leaflet's.

One-off Budget reductions excluded
IRD's examples net off a 100% tax reduction capped at HKD 3,000 for 2025/26. No equivalent has been assumed here for 2026/27 — check the current Budget before treating any figure below as the final net tax payable.

Illustration 1 — Mortgaged property, no other income IRD pam37e Example 1, recomputed at 2026/27

Miss Chan, single, receives monthly rent of $40,000 from a mortgaged property and paid $42,000 of loan interest during the year.

Without election — Property Tax | HKD
Net assessable value ($40,000 × 12 × 80%) | 384,000
Property tax at the standard rate, 15% | 57,600
With election — Personal Assessment | HKD
Net assessable value | 384,000
Less: mortgage interest (within NAV, so allowed in full) | (42,000)
Reduced total income | 342,000
Less: basic allowance D26 exam (YA 2025/26): $132,000 | (145,000)
Net chargeable income | 197,000
Progressive rates: 2%/6%/10% on the first three $50,000 bands, 14% on the remaining $47,000 | 15,580
Standard-rate comparison: 15% × 342,000 reduced total income | 51,300
Tax payable — the lower of the two | 15,580
Electing saves $42,020 ($57,600 − $15,580). Both reliefs are doing work: Property Tax gives no deduction for mortgage interest and no personal allowance, and PA supplies both. IRD's own 2025/26 version of this example, with a $132,000 basic allowance and the $3,000 one-off reduction, gives tax of $14,700 and a saving of $42,900.

Illustration 2 — Business loss set against salary IRD pam37e Example 2, recomputed at 2026/27

Mr Lee has salary income of $400,000 and incurred a business loss of $100,000 in the same year.

Without election | HKD
Salaries tax: ($400,000 − $145,000) = $255,000 at progressive rates | 25,350
Profits tax: a loss, so nil — the loss is carried forward, unused this year | 0
Total | 25,350
With election — Personal Assessment | HKD
Salary income | 400,000
Less: business loss of the year | (100,000)
Reduced total income | 300,000
Less: basic allowance D26 exam (YA 2025/26): $132,000 | (145,000)
Net chargeable income | 155,000
Tax at progressive rates (standard-rate cap of 15% × 300,000 = 45,000 is higher, so not binding) | 9,700
Electing saves $15,650. The mechanism here is different from Illustration 1: without PA the loss is stranded in the profits tax computation and merely carried forward; PA lets it shelter current-year salary. IRD's 2025/26 version gives $8,520 against $24,560, a saving of $16,040.

Illustration 3 — The same property, but with a good salary: electing now costs money IRD pam37e Example 3, recomputed at 2026/27

As Illustration 1, but Miss Chan also earns $500,000 from employment.

Without election | HKD
Salaries tax on ($500,000 − $145,000) = $355,000 | 42,350
Property tax (as Illustration 1) | 57,600
Total | 99,950
With election — Personal Assessment | HKD
Salary income | 500,000
Net assessable value | 384,000
Total income | 884,000
Less: mortgage interest | (42,000)
Reduced total income | 842,000
Less: basic allowance D26 exam (YA 2025/26): $132,000 | (145,000)
Net chargeable income | 697,000
Tax at progressive rates (standard-rate cap 15% × 842,000 = 126,300, not binding) | 100,490
Electing costs $540 more ($100,490 against $99,950). Miss Chan is already at the 17% marginal rate on salary, so aggregating the property income taxes it at 17% rather than the 15% standard rate — and that outweighs the mortgage-interest deduction the election unlocks. This is the illustration to remember: the same taxpayer, the same property, the same mortgage, opposite answer, purely because of the other income. Under IRD's 2025/26 figures the election was similarly disadvantageous.

Illustration 4 — Married couple electing jointly, and how the tax is split IRD pam37e Example 4, recomputed at 2026/27

Mr Cheung's sole-proprietorship profit is assessed at $480,000. Mrs Cheung receives monthly rent of $20,000 from a mortgaged property and paid $72,000 of loan interest.

Business profits (Mr Cheung) | 480,000
Property, net assessable value (Mrs Cheung) ($20,000 × 12 × 80%) | 192,000
Less: mortgage interest | (72,000)
Mrs Cheung's reduced total income | 120,000
Joint reduced total income | 600,000
Less: married person's allowance D26 exam (YA 2025/26): $264,000 | (290,000)
Net chargeable income | 310,000
Tax at progressive rates (standard-rate cap 15% × 600,000 = 90,000, not binding) | 34,700
Apportionment — in the ratio of each spouse's reduced total income

Mr Cheung: $34,700 × 480,000 / 600,000 | 27,760
Mrs Cheung: $34,700 × 120,000 / 600,000 | 6,940
Each spouse receives their own notice of assessment and demand for the apportioned amount. Note the apportionment base is reduced total income — Mrs Cheung's share is computed on $120,000 after her mortgage interest, not on the $192,000 NAV before it. IRD's 2025/26 version, using a $264,000 married person's allowance and the $3,000 reduction, gives $36,120 split $28,896 / $7,224.

Three further Personal Assessment election scenarios from Module 9 →

sections.heading: 9. Common pitfalls
sections.text:
9. Common pitfalls

Trap | What is actually right
Treating PA as a fourth head of charge | It is a relief and an election. It changes how existing chargeable income is taxed; it never makes non-chargeable income chargeable.
Assuming PA always saves tax | Above roughly the point where the 17% marginal rate bites, it costs money — Illustration 3. Always compute both ways.
Recommending PA to a salary-only taxpayer | There is nothing to gain: progressive rates and allowances already apply.
Applying the standard-rate cap to net chargeable income | The cap is the standard rate on reduced total income, before personal allowances.
Deducting mortgage interest above the property's NAV | Capped at that property's NAV. The excess lapses; it cannot create a loss.
Bringing in an offshore business loss | Offshore profits were never chargeable, so the loss is not available.
Citing the mandatory joint election | Out of date. Separate election has been available since YA 2018/19. It remains mandatory to elect jointly only where the couple is already jointly assessed for Salaries Tax.
Relying on a spouse's residence to qualify | Only for years up to 2017/18. From 2018/19 the elector must satisfy the residence test personally.
Apportioning joint tax by gross income | The ratio is each spouse's reduced total income.
Missing the withdrawal window | Election runs to 2 years after the year end; withdrawal is only 6 months from the assessment, and re-election afterwards needs the Commissioner's agreement.

sections.heading: 1. Why the entity changes the computation
sections.text:
1. Why the entity changes the computation

Profits tax has one charging section for all three. What differs is the rate, what counts as a deductible payment to the owner, and what happens after the assessable profit is struck.

The idea underneath all of it
An unincorporated business is not separate from its owner. A sole proprietor cannot employ himself, and a partner cannot be an employee of his own partnership — so a "salary" to them is an appropriation of profit, not an expense. A company is a separate person, so it genuinely can employ its director and genuinely does pay them a salary.

Nearly every difference below follows from that one point. Once you see it, you do not have to memorise the table — you can derive it.

The second consequence is who bears the tax. A company pays its own profits tax and the director separately pays salaries tax on the salary. A sole proprietor's profit is taxed once, in the business — but the proprietor may then elect personal assessment to have it re-taxed at progressive rates after allowances. A company cannot elect at all.

sections.heading: 2. The three side by side
sections.text:
2. The three side by side

Point | Sole proprietorship | Partnership | Corporation
Two-tiered rates
7.5% on the first $2m, 15% above
7.5% / 15% — but see §2b where a partner is a company
8.25% on the first $2m, 16.5% above
Salary to the owner
Not deductible s.17(2) — an appropriation
Not deductible s.17(2)
Deductible — a director is an employee
Salary to the owner's spouse
Not deductible s.17(2), even if genuinely employed
Not deductible s.17(2)
Deductible if genuine employment at a commercial rate
Owner's own mandatory MPF
Deductible s.16AA, capped at $18,000 — self-employed contributions
Deductible s.16AA for each partner
n/a — the company's contributions for the director are ordinary staff costs
Interest on a loan from the owner
Not deductible s.17(2)
Not deductible s.17(2)
Conditional — deductible only if s.16(2) is satisfied
Allocation between owners
n/a
Required — see §2
n/a
Personal assessment
Available — the assessable profit enters the proprietor's PA
Available to individual partners on their allocated share
Not available — companies cannot elect
Losses
Carried forward indefinitely, or set against other income under PA
Allocated to partners; a corporate partner's share can shelter its own other profits
Carried forward indefinitely against the company's own profits only
Return form
BIR60 (individual), with the business schedule
BIR52
BIR51
s.17(2) reaches the spouse, and that surprises people
A salary to a sole proprietor's or partner's spouse is not deductible even where the spouse works full time for a commercial wage. Worse, the spouse is still chargeable to salaries tax on what they receive — so the same money is taxed in the business and again in the spouse's hands. The equivalent payment in a company is deductible. This is one of the sharper practical differences between the forms.

sections.heading: 3. Sole proprietorship
sections.text:
3. Sole proprietorship

One computation, one taxpayer. The whole assessable profit belongs to the proprietor, and the only question after that is whether personal assessment improves on it.

Illustration

Fiona carries on a design studio as a sole proprietor. The accounts for the year ended 31 March 2027 show a profit of $960,000, after charging a salary of $360,000 to Fiona, a salary of $180,000 to her husband (who works full time in the business at a commercial wage), and Fiona's own mandatory MPF contributions of $18,000. Depreciation allowances are $80,000.

Fiona — Profits Tax Computation · YA 2026/27

Profit per accounts | 960,000
Add: salary to the proprietor — s.17(2) | 360,000
Add: salary to the proprietor's spouse — s.17(2) | 180,000
Proprietor's own mandatory MPF — deductible, s.16AA | 0
| 1,500,000
Less: depreciation allowances | (80,000)
Assessable profit | 1,420,000
Profits tax, unincorporated: $1,420,000 × 7.5% (within the first $2,000,000) | 106,500
Then two further consequences that are easy to forget:

The husband is still taxed
His $180,000 is disallowed to the business but remains his employment income. Salaries tax: $180,000 − $145,000 basic allowance = $35,000 net chargeable income, at 2% = $700. The money is taxed twice.
Personal assessment is available — but here it is worse
Fiona could elect PA on the $1,420,000. Net chargeable income would be $1,275,000, giving $198,750 at progressive rates (the standard-rate comparison on $1,420,000 gives $213,000, so progressive wins). That is well above the $106,500 profits tax she already pays. Do not elect.
The general shape
Personal assessment helps a sole proprietor whose profit is low — where allowances and progressive rates beat a flat 7.5% — or who has property income or a loss to bring in. At $1.4m of profit the 17% marginal rate is already above 7.5%, so it costs money. Compute both; never assume.

sections.heading: 4. Partnership
sections.text:
4. Partnership

One assessment is raised on the partnership, not on the partners. But the profit must still be allocated partner by partner — because the allocation drives loss relief, personal assessment, and (where a partner is a company) the rate itself.

Step | What happens
1 | Compute the partnership's assessable profit or adjusted loss in the ordinary way, adding back salaries and interest to partners and to partners' spouses under s.17(2).
2 | Allocate prior allocations first — the salaries and interest just added back go to the partner they relate to, not into the profit-sharing ratio.
3 | Share the balance in the profit-sharing ratio. The balance is often negative once the prior allocations are taken out.
4 | Reallocate so that no partner is left on the wrong side of zero: where the partnership has assessable profits, a partner cannot keep a loss share, and vice versa.
5 | Apply the rates — by partner if their natures differ (§2b).
Step 4 is the one candidates miss
If the partnership's bottom line is a profit, no partner may be allocated a loss: any negative share is reallocated to the profit-making partners in proportion. If the partnership's bottom line is a loss, the mirror applies — any partner allocated a profit has it reallocated to the loss-making partners. The June 2025 examiner's report names this explicitly.

A full worked partnership allocation, with a loss per the accounts that adjusts to a profit, is Question 9 on the ACCA TX-HKG page →

sections.heading: 5. Partnerships with a corporate partner
sections.text:
5. Partnerships with a corporate partner

A company can be a partner. When it is, the partnership contains partners taxed at different rates, and the two-tiered threshold has to be shared out.

The rule
Each partner's share of the assessable profits is taxed at that partner's own rate — 8.25%/16.5% for a corporate partner, 7.5%/15% for an individual. And the $2,000,000 first-tier band is itself apportioned between the partners in their profit-sharing ratio. The partnership does not get one $2,000,000 band at a single rate.

Illustration

Novena Trading is a partnership with assessable profits of $3,000,000 for YA 2026/27. The partners share profits equally: Carol, an individual, and Elm Holdings Limited, a company.

Novena Trading — profits tax by partner · YA 2026/27

| Carol (individual) | Elm Holdings Ltd | Total
Share of assessable profits, 50 : 50 | 1,500,000 | 1,500,000 | 3,000,000
Share of the $2,000,000 first-tier band
apportioned in the profit-sharing ratio | 1,000,000 | 1,000,000 | 2,000,000
First tier, at the partner's own rate | 1,000,000 × 7.5%
= 75,000 | 1,000,000 × 8.25%
= 82,500 | 157,500
Balance, at the partner's own rate | 500,000 × 15%
= 75,000 | 500,000 × 16.5%
= 82,500 | 157,500
Profits tax | 150,000 | 165,000 | 315,000
What the answer would have been in a uniform partnership

Composition | Profits tax on $3,000,000
All partners individuals | 300,000
Mixed, 50 : 50 as above | 315,000
All partners corporate | 330,000
The mixed partnership lands exactly between the two — which is the point. A single blended rate applied to the whole $3,000,000 would not produce $315,000, and computing the first tier once at either rate would be wrong for one of the partners.

Loss relief for a corporate partner
Where the partnership makes a loss, a corporate partner's allocated share can be set against that company's own other assessable profits — the loss is not trapped in the partnership. An individual partner's share goes into their personal assessment or is carried forward against future shares of the same partnership. The examining team noted that candidates were "not familiar with the loss relief for corporate partners".

sections.heading: 6. How a partner's share flows into personal assessment
sections.text:
6. How a partner's share flows into personal assessment

This is the link between this page and Personal Assessment, and it only exists for individual partners.

Partnership — assessable profits computed and allocated | →
Individual partner's allocated share enters their personal assessment as net assessable profits, alongside their salary and property income | ✓
Corporate partner's allocated share — no personal assessment; the company is assessed on its share at corporate rates and that is the end of it | ✗
Carol's position, continuing §5. Her $1,500,000 share has already borne $150,000 of profits tax within the partnership assessment. If she elects personal assessment, that $1,500,000 becomes part of her total income:

Share of partnership assessable profits | 1,500,000
Less: basic allowance D26 exam (YA 2025/26): $132,000 | (145,000)
Net chargeable income | 1,355,000
Progressive rates | 212,350
Standard-rate comparison: $1,500,000 × 15% | 225,000
Tax under personal assessment | 212,350
Against her share of the partnership profits tax already charged | 150,000
Electing would cost her | 62,350
The pattern, across both illustrations on this page
Fiona at $1.42m and Carol at $1.5m both find personal assessment worse. That is not a coincidence. Business profits are taxed at 7.5% in an unincorporated business, and the progressive marginal rate reaches 17% once net chargeable income passes $200,000. For a profitable business with no other reliefs to unlock, PA is usually a cost.

It turns beneficial when there is something for it to unlock: mortgage interest on a let property, a business loss to set against salary, or allowances going unused because the income is not employment income. Those are the cases to look for — not size of profit.

sections.heading: 7. Corporation
sections.text:
7. Corporation

The standard case, and the one the general profits tax format is written for. The company is a separate person, so payments to its directors are real expenses.

Illustration — the same business as §3, incorporated

Fiona Ltd carries on the same design studio. The accounts show the same profit of $960,000 after the same salary of $360,000 to Fiona, now a director, and $180,000 to her husband, a genuine employee. Depreciation allowances are $80,000.

Fiona Ltd — Profits Tax Computation · YA 2026/27

Profit per accounts | 960,000
Director's salary — deductible, no add-back | 0
Salary to the director's spouse, genuinely employed — deductible | 0
Less: depreciation allowances | (80,000)
Assessable profit | 880,000
Profits tax, corporation: $880,000 × 8.25% | 72,600
The salaries are then taxed in the recipients' hands, which the sole-proprietorship version largely avoided for Fiona:

Fiona — salaries tax on $360,000 ($215,000 net chargeable income) | 18,550
Husband — salaries tax on $180,000 ($35,000 net chargeable income) | 700

sections.heading: 8. Same business, three forms — the figures side by side
sections.text:
8. Same business, three forms — the figures side by side

The identical trade, earning $1,500,000 before remunerating the owner and spouse

| Sole proprietorship | Corporation
Profit per accounts | 960,000 | 960,000
Add back: owner's and spouse's salaries — s.17(2) | 540,000 | —
Less: depreciation allowances | (80,000) | (80,000)
Assessable profit | 1,420,000 | 880,000
Profits tax | 106,500 @ 7.5% | 72,600 @ 8.25%
Owner's salaries tax | — no salary in law | 18,550
Spouse's salaries tax | 700 | 700
Total tax borne | 107,200 | 91,850
The company pays tax at the higher headline rate and still comes out $15,350 lighter, because $540,000 of remuneration moves out of the 7.5%-plus-nothing charge and into the progressive salaries tax bands, where the first $145,000 is covered by an allowance and the next slices are taxed at 2%–14%.

Read that as a structural point, not as advice
The comparison isolates one variable to show how s.17(2) drives the difference. A real incorporation decision turns on much more — limited liability, audit and filing costs, business registration, stamp duty on any transfer of the business, how profits are actually extracted, and what happens on a later sale. The figures above are an illustration of a mechanism, not a recommendation. And the answer reverses at other profit levels: push the profit high enough and the 17% salaries tax band overtakes the 8.25% corporate rate.

sections.heading: 9. Exam checklist
sections.text:
9. Exam checklist

Before you start | Ask
Which entity is it? | Sole proprietorship, partnership or company. This sets the rate before anything else. Answering an unincorporated question at 8.25% loses the rate marks and every figure after them.
Is anyone paid who is the owner, or married to one? | In an unincorporated business both are disallowed under s.17(2). In a company both are deductible if genuine.
Whose MPF is it? | The proprietor's or partner's own mandatory contributions are deductible under s.16AA, capped at $18,000. Their spouse's are not.
Is there a corporate partner? | Then the rates differ by partner and the $2,000,000 band is apportioned in the profit-sharing ratio.
Does anyone have a share on the wrong side of zero? | Reallocate. No loss share when the partnership is in profit; no profit share when it is in loss.
Has the question asked about personal assessment? | Only an individual can elect. Compute it both ways and say which is better — the answer is often "do not elect", and saying so with figures is the mark.
Is the spouse's disallowed salary still taxed? | Yes, on the spouse. If the question gives their personal circumstances, it wants that computation too.

sections.heading: A. From IRD DIPNs
sections.text:
A. From IRD DIPNs

Illustration — Lease premium: Profits Tax vs Property Tax interaction DIPN 4

Company H grants a 6-year lease of its property for a premium of $1,200,000, paid up front. As a person carrying on a property-dealing/letting business, the premium is a revenue receipt taxable under Profits Tax — s.15C spreads it evenly over the lease term, so 1/6 = $200,000 is assessed each year for 6 years. Separately, s.5B(4) deems the premium payable in equal monthly instalments for Property Tax purposes but capped at 3 years, so 1/3 = $400,000 is assessed for Property Tax in each of Years 1–3 only.

Year | Property Tax paid
($400,000 × 80% × 16%) | Profits Tax
($200,000 × 17.5%) | Net position
1–3 (each) | $51,200 | $35,000 | Refund of $16,200 (Property Tax set off against Profits Tax under s.25)
4–6 (each) | — | $35,000 | $35,000 payable
Grand total tax over 6 years = $210,000, i.e. exactly 17.5% of the $1,200,000 premium (the historical standard rate used in the DIPN's example year) — the set-off mechanism ensures the premium is not taxed twice under both heads.

Illustration — Interest deduction restricted by a tax-free secured deposit DIPN 13A

Taxpayer F borrows $1,000,000 at 5% interest, secured by a $1,000,000 deposit earning tax-exempt interest at 4%. Because the loan is secured on a deposit generating tax-free income, s.16(2A)/(2B) restrict the deduction: the $40,000 tax-free interest earned reduces the otherwise-deductible $50,000 loan interest, leaving only $10,000 deductible.

Illustration — Service company "Type II" management fee cap DIPN 24

A professional firm pays $4,000,000 in management fees to a related service company whose actual attributable cost of providing those services is $3,000,000. The deduction is capped at cost plus a 12.5% mark-up: $3,000,000 × 112.5% = $3,375,000. The $625,000 excess is added back, increasing assessable profits from $1,000,000 (per accounts) to $1,625,000.

Illustration — Foreign tax deductible only where no DTA credit is available DIPN 28

Bank-HK pays income tax on interest income in Jurisdiction F. If Hong Kong has no double tax agreement with Jurisdiction F, the foreign tax is deductible under s.16(1)(c). If Hong Kong does have a DTA with Jurisdiction F, s.16(2J) denies the deduction — Bank-HK must instead claim a tax credit under s.50, since double relief (deduction plus credit) is not permitted.

Illustration — Hong Kong bank deposit interest exemption straddling the exemption date DIPN 34

A taxpayer has $10,000,000 trading profits plus $4,000,000 of local bank deposit interest, of which $1,000,000 accrued before 22 June 1998 (the exemption's effective date) and $3,000,000 accrued after. Only the pre-exemption $1,000,000 is taxable; total 1998/99 assessable profits = $11,000,000 rather than $14,000,000.

Illustration — Prepaid expenses follow accounting treatment, not cash timing DIPN 40, following CIR v Secan

Following the Secan case, a full cash prepayment (e.g. 3 years' rent or insurance paid up front) is no longer deductible in full in the year of payment if the applicable accounting standard requires it to be amortised over the period it relates to — the tax deduction now follows the accounting/matching treatment, reversing the Department's older cash-basis practice.

sections.heading: B. From Module 9: Principles of Taxation (4th ed.)
sections.text:
B. From Module 9: Principles of Taxation (4th ed.)

Adapted from a professional taxation qualification manual. Facts are paraphrased, not reproduced verbatim; every figure has been checked against current Hong Kong tax law and corrected where the textbook is outdated (noted per illustration).

Illustration — Basis period on commencement: first accounts cover 18 months Module 9, Ch.3 §3.9.2 — s.18C(1)(b)

A company commences business on 1 July 2018 and adopts a 31 December accounting date, but its first set of accounts is not closed until 31 December 2019 — an 18-month period. Adjusted profits: $90,000 for the 18 months to 31 Dec 2019, then $68,000 for the 12 months to 31 Dec 2020.

Where the first accounting period exceeds 12 months, s.18C(1)(b) gives the Commissioner discretion to take the second year of assessment as the 12 months counted back from the end of the first accounting period, with the commencement year taking the remaining stub — both by time-apportioning the 18-month profit.

Year of assessment | Basis period | Assessable profits | Basis
Commencement year | 1/7/2018 – 31/12/2018 (6 mo.) | $30,000 (= $90,000 × 6/18) | s.18C(1)(b)
Following year | 1/1/2019 – 31/12/2019 (12 mo.) | $60,000 (= $90,000 × 12/18) | s.18B(2)
Third year | 1/1/2020 – 31/12/2020 (12 mo.) | $68,000 | s.18B(2)
Check: $30,000 + $60,000 = $90,000 — the full 18-month profit is accounted for exactly once. No tax rate is involved in this mechanic, so no currency correction was needed.

Illustration — Retirement scheme contribution cap (s.17(1)(h)) Module 9, Ch.3 §3.5.4

An employee earns an annual salary of $100,000. The employer makes an ordinary annual contribution to a recognised retirement scheme equal to 20% of salary, i.e. $20,000.

s.17(1)(h) disallows the deduction of ordinary retirement-scheme contributions to the extent they exceed 15% of the employee's total emoluments: cap = 15% × $100,000 = $15,000 deductible; the remaining $5,000 is non-deductible.

The 15% cap is unchanged in current law — no correction needed.

Illustration — Loss relief: carry-forward vs. surrender on change of trade Module 9, Ch.3 §3.11 — s.19C

Part A — corporation, multi-year carry-forward: a company realises losses of $25M (2016/17) and $75M (2017/18), giving $100M carried forward. It then realises a profit of $80M in 2018/19.

Accumulated losses available | $100,000,000
Less: set off against 2018/19 profit | ($80,000,000)
Assessable profit after set-off | Nil
Unrelieved loss carried forward | $20,000,000
Part B — sole proprietor, same trade vs. changed trade: a sole proprietor has an unrelieved loss of $1,000,000 brought forward from a wine-distribution trade.

Scenario | Result
Continues the same wine trade, earning $1,200,000 in the current year | $1,200,000 − $1,000,000 loss b/f = $200,000 taxable
Ceases the wine trade and starts an unrelated fruit-trading business, earning $500,000 | Loss is tied to the ceased trade and is surrendered — full $500,000 taxable, no relief
Losses only carry forward against future profits of the same source (s.19C) — changing to an unrelated trade forfeits the loss. No tax rate is involved in either part, so no correction was needed.

Illustration — Secured loan test: interest deduction restricted by a tax-free deposit Module 9, Ch.3 §3.5.3.8 — s.16(2A), adapted from DIPN 13A

A taxpayer borrows $1,000,000 from a bank at 5% p.a. ($50,000 interest) for general business use, secured by an overseas deposit earning tax-free interest. The allowable deduction depends on how the security is structured:

Case | Security | Tax-free interest earned | Deduction reduced by | Interest allowed
1 | Deposit $1,000,000 only | $40,000 | $40,000 (full match) | $10,000
2 | Deposit $500,000 + shares $500,000 | $20,000 (deposit only) | $20,000 (shares ignored — not a deposit) | $30,000
3 | Deposit $2,000,000 (exceeds loan) | $80,000 | Pro-rated: $1,000,000/$2,000,000 × $80,000 = $40,000 | $10,000
4 | Deposit $1,000,000 + shares $500,000 | $40,000 (deposit only) | Pro-rated by security mix: $1,000,000/$1,500,000 × $40,000 = $26,667 | $23,333
Only deposits/loans generating tax-free interest trigger this restriction — other security (shares, property, guarantees) is ignored for this test. No profits tax rate is involved, so no correction was needed.

Illustration — Interest flow-back test: debenture interest paid to an untaxed associate Module 9, Ch.3 §3.5.3.8 — s.16(2C), adapted from DIPN 13A

A Hong Kong company issues $10,000,000 of debentures to fund its HK trading business, paying $1,000,000 total interest for the year. $8,000,000 of the debentures is held all year by its overseas subsidiary, an associate not taxed in Hong Kong on the interest it receives.

Proportion held by the untaxed associate | $8,000,000 / $10,000,000 = 8/10
Interest disallowed (flows back untaxed) | $1,000,000 × 8/10 = $800,000
Allowable interest deduction | $200,000
If the associate held the debentures for only 6 of the 12 months, the disallowance is further time-apportioned: $800,000 × 6/12 = $400,000 disallowed instead.

Exception: no restriction applies if the associate is a market maker holding the debentures in the ordinary course of its business (s.16(2G)). No profits tax rate is involved, so no correction was needed.

Note
A plant & machinery pooling illustration and a full two-tier-rate computation exercise were also reviewed from this chapter but are presented on the Depreciation & Allowances illustrations page instead, where they fit topically.

sections.heading: 1. Which Form Applies
sections.text:
1. Which Form Applies

Form | Who files it
BIR51 | Corporations — the primary form for HK incorporated companies, and the focus of this guide.
BIR52 | Persons other than corporations — sole proprietorships, partnerships, limited partnership funds, bodies of persons. See §9 below for how it differs from BIR51.
BIR54 | Not a second "persons other than corporations" form — filed by a Hong Kong resident payer/agent to report a non-resident's HK-sourced profits under ss.20A/20B. See §10 below.
All three are issued annually and must be filed within the deadline stated on the Notice to File (IRC1952 for corporations, IRC1953 for others) — typically extended under the Block Extension Scheme where a tax representative is on record. Since 1 April 2023, all supplementary forms (S1–S22) must be filed electronically via www.ird.gov.hk/e_pfr.

sections.heading: 2. Part 1 — Statement of Assessable Profits or Adjusted Loss
sections.text:

Box | Label | Maps to

2 | Adjusted Loss (before loss brought forward) | Fill instead of box 1 if the year produced a loss.

sections.heading: 3. Parts 2–3 — Tax Liability, Rate Election & Specified Matters
sections.text:
3. Parts 2–3 — Tax Liability, Rate Election & Specified Matters

Part 2 computes Tax Payable/Repayable (IRD-computed, no entry box) and asks:

Box 4 | Chargeable at two-tiered rates? — the two-tiered rate election. If Yes, upload Form S1 (Part 9, box 42).
Part 3 is a run of Yes/No disclosure questions (boxes 5–15) covering non-resident IP payments (s.15(1)), fund/carried-interest deeming provisions, short/medium-term debt instruments, DTA relief claims, advance rulings, alternative bond schemes, regulatory capital securities, permanent-establishment status, and the s.51AAB e-filing mandate. None of these require a computed figure — they flag which supplementary forms and disclosures apply.

sections.heading: 4. Parts 4–8 — Company Details & General Matters
sections.text:
4. Parts 4–8 — Company Details & General Matters

Parts 4–6 are administrative: principal business activity + HSIC code (box 16), return-language preference, and an optional authorized representative section.

Part 7 (General Matters, boxes 17–36) is the section most likely to interact with your tax computation:

Box | What it asks
17–19 | Whether accounts are audited by law, by a HK practice unit, and the signing CPA's practising certificate number.
20 | Basis period From/To — feeds the basis-period rules (s.18/18C).
21–24 | Commencement/cessation of business, and what happened to the business/assets on cessation.
25 | Election to align financial-instrument tax treatment with accounting treatment (ss.18I–18L) — see the DIPN 42 illustration.
26–27 | Foreign-currency financial statements; private company status.
28 | Change in shareholders during the basis period — relevant to loss-carry-forward anti-avoidance (DIPN 15).
29 | Party to a court-free amalgamation (s.680/681 Companies Ordinance) — see DIPN 63.
30 | Contract/import processing arrangement in the Chinese Mainland — the 50:50 apportionment convention (DIPN 21).
31–36 | Insurance RBC-regime transition, family-owned SPE/single-family-office status.
Part 8 (Transactions For/With Non-Residents, boxes 37–41) covers acting as an agent for a non-resident, IP value-creation contributions, and HK$ amounts for hire charges/professional fees paid to non-residents.

Box | Deduction

Category | Initial | Annual | Balancing Allowance | Balancing Charge

sections.heading: 8. Parts 12–13 — Financial Data & Declaration
sections.text:
8. Parts 12–13 — Financial Data & Declaration

Part 12 (boxes 105–127) asks for headline financial-statement figures — gross income, turnover, inventories, gross profit/loss, dividend/interest income and expense, remuneration, commission, IP payments, management/consultancy fees, bad debts, net profit/loss per account, receivables/payables, issued share capital, and total assets. This is IRD cross-checking your return against the shape of your accounts, not a separate computation.

Part 13 (boxes 128–129) is the declaration — tick exactly one: box 128 for a Secretary/Manager/Director/Investment Manager/Provisional Liquidator/Liquidator declaring the return is complete and accurate, or box 129 for a Service Provider declaring it was prepared per the taxpayer's confirmed instructions (IR1476).

sections.heading: 9. BIR52 — How It Differs from BIR51
sections.text:
9. BIR52 — How It Differs from BIR51

Structurally parallel but shorter (129 boxes → ~111) and reorganized. The headline differences:

- Part 1 extras (boxes 4–5): whether the proprietor/spouse/partner received emoluments or interest on capital from the business — such payments are non-deductible under s.17(2), and box 5 confirms the tax computation adjusts for it. The two-tiered rate election is box 6 here, not box 4.

- Part 6 is entirely new: "Personal Particulars of Proprietor or Partners and Allocation of Profits/Loss and Claim for Deduction of Mandatory Contributions" (boxes 18–37) — per-partner HKID/BR number, profit/loss sharing ratio, a Personal Assessment election flag (the actual election is made on the individual's own BIR60, not here), allocated Assessable Profits/Adjusted Loss, and MPF contributions claimed. The allocation total must equal Part 1's box 1/2. See the Personal Assessment section.

- Part 7 drops the corporation-only items (RBC regime, Companies Ordinance amalgamation, private-company/shareholder-change questions) and adds business-specific ones: cessation by death of the proprietor, and property purchase for building allowance purposes.

- Part 9 lists only 10 supplementary forms (the corporation-only concessions S6–S14, S16–S18 don't apply).

- Part 10 swaps BIR51's "interest to non-HK associated corporations" box for a "mandatory MPF contributions for proprietor/partners" deduction.

- No separate depreciation-allowances Part — Financial Data shifts one part earlier, and the corporation-only "share-based payments"/"issued share capital" fields are dropped.

- Declaration title varies by entity type: sole proprietorship → "person"; partnership → "precedent partner"; limited partnership fund → "general partner" / "investment manager"; body of persons → "principal officer"; no resident proprietor/partner → "agent"/"manager"; deceased estate → "executor."

sections.heading: 10. BIR54 — What It Actually Is
sections.text:
10. BIR54 — What It Actually Is

Common misconception, corrected
BIR54 is not a second "persons other than corporations" return. Its actual title is "Profits Tax Return — In Respect of Non-Resident Persons." It is filed under ss.20A/20B by the Hong Kong resident payer or agent, in the non-resident's own name, to report that non-resident's Hong Kong-sourced trade/business profits — most commonly royalty/IP payments, or income received via a Hong Kong agent. It's bilingual (Chinese/English) and far shorter than BIR51/52 (~22 boxes).

Key sections: a two-tiered rate election made on behalf of the non-resident (box 3, with the same connected-entity disclosure logic as BIR51/S1); an IP use/assignment block (boxes 11–17) determining whether the deemed-profit computation under s.21A(1)(a) applies 100% or 30% of the royalty receipt as assessable profit; a section on the agent's role in Hong Kong; and a reciprocal shipowner exemption block (boxes 18–20, s.23B(4A)) for non-resident shipowners.
