sections.heading: 1. Overview & Charging Basis IRO s.14
sections.text:
1. Overview & Charging Basis IRO s.14

Hong Kong taxes profits on a territorial source basis, not on residence. Section 14(1) charges profits tax on every person (including a corporation) carrying on a trade, profession or business in Hong Kong, on assessable profits arising in or derived from Hong Kong for that trade/profession/business — profits from the sale of capital assets are expressly excluded from the charge.

Statutory text — s.14(1)
"...profits tax shall be charged for each year of assessment on every person carrying on a trade, profession or business in Hong Kong in respect of his assessable profits arising in or derived from Hong Kong for that year from such trade, profession or business (excluding profits arising from the sale of capital assets) as ascertained in accordance with this Part."

Three conditions must all be met for a charge to arise: (1) the person carries on a trade, profession or business in Hong Kong; (2) the trade/profession/business produces profits other than from the sale of capital assets; (3) the profits are sourced in Hong Kong. Locality of profits is a question of fact determined by what the taxpayer did to earn the profit and where — see DIPN 21 (Locality of Profits) for the "broad guiding principle" drawn from Hang Seng Bank, HK-TVB International, Kwong Mile, and other leading cases.

sections.heading: 2. Rates & Recent Changes Schedule 8B
sections.text:
2. Rates & Recent Changes Schedule 8B

Two-tiered profits tax rates (from YA 2018/19, current)

Taxpayer type | First HKD 2,000,000 of assessable profits | Remainder
Corporations | 8.25% | 16.5%
Unincorporated businesses (sole proprietors / partnerships) | 7.5% | 15%
Legislated via s.14(2)/(3) referring out to Schedule 8B (two-tiered rates) — Schedule 8 sets the flat standard/corporate rate that continues to apply where a group of connected entities has more than one entity in Hong Kong (only one connected entity per group may be nominated each year to access the discounted first-tier rate; s.14AAC deals with connected entities generally).

Recent changes to watch

- Refined FSIE regime — effective 1 January 2023 (Division 3A of Part 4, added by 17 of 2022) — see §6 below.

- Patent Box concession — 5% concessionary rate on qualifying IP income from YA 2023/24 (Inland Revenue (Amendment) (Tax Concessions for Intellectual Property Income) Ordinance 2023).

- Pillar Two — Income Inclusion Rule + Hong Kong Minimum Top-up Tax for in-scope MNE groups, effective for fiscal years beginning on/after 1 January 2025.

- One-off relief — Inland Revenue (Amendment) Ordinance 2026 (gazetted 22 May 2026): 100% profits tax reduction for YA 2025/26, capped at HKD 3,000 per taxpayer. (Source: PwC Tax Summaries, reviewed 22 Jul 2026 — verify against the gazetted ordinance before relying on this for a filing.)

Bills in progress — not yet law (as at 24 September 2026)

- Funds / FIHV / carried interest — Inland Revenue (Amendment) (Preferential Tax Regimes for Funds, Family-owned Investment Holding Vehicles and Carried Interest) Bill 2026, gazetted 12 June 2026, first reading 24 June 2026. Widens the definition of "fund", broadens the schedule of qualifying assets (notably to support private credit), removes the 5% cap on incidental transactions, relaxes the exemption conditions for special purpose entities and family-owned SPEs, and enhances the carried interest regime — but adds a tax reporting mechanism and economic substance requirements modelled on the FIHV regime. (Gazettal press release, 12 Jun 2026; FSTB response on carried interest, 12 Aug 2026.)

- Shipping & physical commodity trading — Inland Revenue (Amendment) (Tax Concessions for Shipping-related Activities and Physical Commodity Trading) Bill 2026, gazetted 12 June 2026. Offers shipping-related companies an elective 15% concessionary rate (elected annually) as a BEPS 2.0-aware alternative to the existing 0%/8.25% concessions, and creates a new half-rate (8.25%) concession for physical commodity trading. (Press release, 10 Jun 2026.)

- Corporate treasury centres — the Government published an Action Plan to Promote Development of Corporate Treasury Centres (9 Jun 2026) and launched a consultation on enhancing the CTC tax concession regime (27 Jul 2026). Expect the qualifying-activity and safe-harbour conditions for the 8.25% CTC rate to change — check before advising a group treasury structure.

- Qualifying debt instruments — the list of debt instruments and sovereign bonds eligible for profits tax concession or exemption was refreshed on 30 June 2026. The list is the operative test — do not rely on an older copy.

- Pillar Two filing — IRD published the GIR XML schema and user guides for the GloBE Information Return on 8 June 2026. In-scope MNE groups now have the machine-readable filing format. (IRD BEPS 2.0 page.)

sections.heading: 3. Taxable / Non-Taxable Receipts IRO s.15
sections.text:
3. Taxable / Non-Taxable Receipts IRO s.15

Section 15(1) deems certain sums to be Hong Kong-source trading receipts even though they might not otherwise be so regarded — this closes gaps the general s.14 source test would otherwise leave open (e.g. royalties, hire charges). Combine this with the general case-law source principle (DIPN 21) and the FSIE deeming rule (§6) to classify any receipt.

Status | Receipt | Basis
Taxable | Royalties / sums for the use of, or right to use in Hong Kong, any patent, trade mark, copyright, design, secret process/formula or similar IP | s.15(1)(b)
Taxable | Sums for use outside Hong Kong of IP where the payer claimed a Hong Kong deduction for the payment | s.15(1)(ba)
Taxable | Grants, subsidies or similar financial assistance connected with carrying on the HK trade/business (other than towards capital expenditure) | s.15(1)(c)
Taxable | Hire, rental or similar charges for use of movable property in Hong Kong | s.15(1)(d)
Taxable | Interest derived from Hong Kong received by a corporation carrying on a HK trade/business | s.15(1)(f)
Taxable | Sums from exhibition/use in HK of film, tape, sound recording or related advertising material | s.15(1)(a)
Non-taxable | Profits from the sale of capital assets | s.14(1) (excluded from the charge)
Non-taxable | Interest on a Hong Kong bank deposit earned by a person other than a financial institution | Exemption from Profits Tax (Interest Income) Order 1998 — see DIPN 34; lost if the deposit secures a loan whose interest is tax-deductible (no partial exemption)
Non-taxable | Specified foreign-sourced income that satisfies the FSIE economic substance / nexus / participation conditions | Division 3A, Part 4 (s.15H onward) — see §6
Taxable (deemed) | Specified foreign-sourced income (interest, dividends, IP income, disposal gains on equity interests) that fails the FSIE conditions | s.15I — deemed to arise in/derive from Hong Kong

sections.heading: 4. Deductible / Non-Deductible Expenses IRO ss.16–17
sections.text:
4. Deductible / Non-Deductible Expenses IRO ss.16–17

The general test (s.16(1)) is that outgoings and expenses are deductible to the extent incurred in the basis period in the production of chargeable profits (the "Ronpibon Tin" apportionment principle — see DIPN 3 for apportioning mixed-purpose expenses). Section 17 then carves out specific exclusions even where the general test would otherwise be met.

Status | Item | Basis / conditions
Deductible | Interest on money borrowed for producing chargeable profits, plus related legal/procuration fees and stamp duty | s.16(1)(a), subject to the anti-avoidance conditions in s.16(2)–(2C) (see DIPN 13A)
Deductible | Rent paid for land/buildings used to produce chargeable profits (capped at assessable value if paid to a related party) | s.16(1)(b)
Deductible | Foreign tax of substantially the same nature as HK tax, paid on income also chargeable under s.15(1)(f)/(g)/(i)–(lb) | s.16(1)(c)/(ca), restricted by s.16(2J) where a DTA already gives s.50 credit relief (see DIPN 28)
Deductible | Bad debts written off, and doubtful debts to the extent estimated bad, if previously included as a trading receipt | s.16(1)(d)
Deductible | R&D expenditure — 100% for Type A, enhanced 300%/200% for Type B (see §4A) | s.16B
Deductible | Capital expenditure on patents / know-how rights (one-off, no spreading) | s.16E — see DIPN 49
Deductible | Capital expenditure on "Specified IP Rights" (copyright, registered trade marks/designs, plant variety rights) — spread over 5 years | ss.16EA–16EC — see DIPN 49
Deductible | Capital expenditure on "prescribed fixed assets" (manufacturing plant, computer hardware/software) — 100% one-off | s.16G — see DIPN 5
Non-deductible | Domestic or private expenses (incl. home-to-office travel; MPF contributions in the person's own capacity as scheme member) | s.17(1)(a)
Non-deductible | Any disbursement or expense not incurred for the purpose of producing the chargeable profits | s.17(1)(b)
Non-deductible | Capital expenditure, or any loss or withdrawal of capital | s.17(1)(c)
Non-deductible | Cost of improvements (as opposed to repairs) | s.17(1)(d)
Non-deductible | Sums recoverable under insurance or an indemnity contract | s.17(1)(e)
Non-deductible | Rent/expenses for premises not occupied or used to produce the chargeable profits | s.17(1)(f)
Non-deductible | Tax paid under the IRO itself (property tax not set off, profits tax) — except salaries tax paid on employees' remuneration | s.17(1)(g)
Non-deductible | Employer retirement-scheme contributions (ORSO/MPF) in excess of 15% of the employee's total emoluments for the period | s.17(1)(h)/(i)
Non-deductible | Management fee paid to a related "Type II" service company in excess of cost plus a 12.5% mark-up | DIPN 24 minimum-requirements test (administrative practice, not a numbered section)

sections.heading: 4A. Research and Development — the enhanced deduction IRO s.16B, Schedule 45
sections.text:
4A. Research and Development — the enhanced deduction IRO s.16B, Schedule 45

Qualifying R&D expenditure splits into two types with very different treatment. Getting the split wrong, or applying the enhanced rate to the whole of Type B, is the error the June 2026 examining team reported on the question fewest candidates answered correctly.

Type | What falls in it | Deduction
Type A
Qualifying R&D expenditure that is not Type B — including plant and machinery bought for R&D, fees paid to an outside expert or consultant, and testing fees
100% — a normal full deduction, no uplift
Type B
Staffing costs of employees directly and actively engaged in qualifying R&D, and consumable items used up in it. Also payments to a designated local research institution.
300% on the first $2,000,000, then 200% on the remainder — no cap on the 200% tier
Three ways to get this wrong
1. Applying 300% to all Type B expenditure instead of only the first $2,000,000.

2. Treating everything as Type B — plant and machinery, consultancy fees and testing fees are Type A and get 100% only.

3. Leaving plant and machinery out altogether because it is capital. Under s.16B it is deductible at 100%; it does not go into the depreciation allowance pools.

Worked example Original; mechanics verified against the June 2026 examiner's report worked answer

Delta Ltd incurred the following on qualifying R&D in the year: plant and machinery $0.6m, a consultancy fee to an independent expert $0.4m, staffing costs of the research team $1.5m, and consumable items $0.9m.

Type A — plant and machinery $0.6m + consultancy $0.4m = $1.0m, at 100% | 1.0m
Type B — staffing $1.5m + consumables $0.9m = $2.4m
First $2.0m at 300% | 6.0m
Remaining $0.4m at 200% | 0.8m
Total deduction | 7.8m
$3.4m was actually spent and $7.8m is deducted. Common wrong answers on these facts: $8.2m (300% on all $2.4m of Type B), $7.2m (plant and machinery omitted as capital), and $3.4m (no enhancement at all).

sections.heading: 5. Basis Period & Loss Relief IRO ss.18, 18C, 19C
sections.text:
5. Basis Period & Loss Relief IRO ss.18, 18C, 19C

Assessable profits are normally computed on the accounting year ending within the year preceding the year of assessment (s.18(1)). Where a business commences or ceases partway through a year, ss.18C–18H set special opening/closing basis periods. Trading losses are carried forward indefinitely and set off against future assessable profits from the same source (s.19C) — there is no time limit, but no carry-back and no group relief between separate legal entities in Hong Kong (each company is assessed on its own profits).

Where a taxpayer has both "normal" and "concessionary rate" trading receipts (e.g. under a qualifying debt instrument or reinsurance concession), s.19CA/19CB impose a cross-set-off formula using a statutory adjustment factor rather than a straight one-for-one offset — see DIPN 8.

sections.heading: 6. Foreign-Sourced Income Exemption (FSIE) Part 4, Division 3A
sections.text:
6. Foreign-Sourced Income Exemption (FSIE) Part 4, Division 3A

Division 3A (ss.15H onward, added by the Inland Revenue (Amendment) (Taxation on Specified Foreign-sourced Income) Ordinance 2022, effective 1 January 2023) deems specified categories of foreign-sourced income — interest, dividends, disposal gains on equity interests, and IP income — received in Hong Kong by an MNE entity to be Hong Kong-sourced unless the entity meets an economic substance requirement (for interest/dividends/disposal gains) or complies with the nexus approach (for IP income), or qualifies for the participation exemption (for dividends/disposal gains on substantial equity interests).

Practical effect
A Hong Kong holding or treasury company receiving offshore dividends, interest, or IP royalties that would otherwise be treated as offshore (non-taxable) under the ordinary source principle may now be taxed on that income unless it can document adequate economic substance in Hong Kong or a qualifying participation/nexus position. This is a common trap in tax computations for group treasury/holding entities — always check FSIE before treating offshore passive income as automatically non-taxable.

sections.heading: A. From IRD DIPNs
sections.text:
A. From IRD DIPNs

Illustration — Premium spread over the statutory 3-year cap DIPN 14

A $60,000 premium is paid for a 5-year lease running from 1 June 2006 to 31 May 2011 (60 months). Because s.5B(4) caps the spreading period at 3 years (36 months) even though the lease itself runs 5 years, the premium is spread over 36 months only:

Year of assessment | Months falling in year | Assessable value included
2006/07 | 10 of 36 | $16,667
2007/08 | 12 of 36 | $20,000
2008/09 | 12 of 36 | $20,000
2009/10 | 2 of 36 | $3,333
Nothing is assessed for 2010/11 or 2011/12 even though the lease itself continues — the 3-year statutory cap has already fully absorbed the premium.

Illustration — Net assessable value computation chain DIPN 14

The DIPN sets out the standard computation chain: Consideration receivable, plus rent recovered previously written off, less irrecoverable rent, gives Assessable Value; deduct rates paid by the owner (if any); deduct the flat 20% statutory allowance on the balance, to arrive at Net Assessable Value — the figure to which the 15% standard rate is applied.

Illustration — Premium taxed twice under two different spreading rules DIPN 4 (see also Profits Tax page)

Where the property owner is also carrying on a property-dealing/letting trade, the same premium is spread differently for the two taxes: over the full lease term (no cap) for Profits Tax purposes as a trading receipt, but capped at 3 years for Property Tax purposes under s.5B(4). The s.25 set-off then reconciles the two — see the full worked example on the Profits Tax illustrations page.

sections.heading: B. From Module 9: Principles of Taxation (4th ed.)
sections.text:
B. From Module 9: Principles of Taxation (4th ed.)

Adapted from a professional taxation qualification manual, following its running "Tong family" case study. Facts are paraphrased, not reproduced verbatim. The 15% standard rate and 20% statutory allowance used throughout already match current law — no correction was needed for this topic.

Illustration — Premium spreading: lease term shorter than, equal to, and longer than the 3-year cap Module 9, Ch.5 §5.2 — s.5B(3)/(4)

Three properties are let on different lease terms, each with a lump-sum premium spread evenly over the lease period or 3 years, whichever is shorter:

Property | Lease term | Premium | Spreading
A | 5 years (60 months) | $360,000 | Capped at 36 months → $10,000/month for 3 years, then nil for the remaining 2 years
B | 3 years (36 months, exactly) | $240,000 | Full term used (36 = cap) → $6,667/month throughout
C | 2 years (24 months) | $144,000 | No cap needed → $6,000/month throughout
Property A shows the cap actually biting: the $360,000 premium is fully exhausted at month 36, and nothing further is assessed for the lease's remaining 24 months even though the tenancy continues.

Illustration — Full net assessable value computation, three properties Module 9, Ch.5 §5.3 — DIPN 14 template

Three commonly-tested variations on the NAV computation chain (all at the current 15%/20% rates):

| Property A (jointly owned) | Property B | Property C
Rent for the year | $600,000 | $240,000 | $120,000
Add: premium instalment | $80,000 | $80,000 | $60,000
Add: other consideration (furniture/repairs borne by tenant/rent recovered/management fee, as applicable) | — | $37,000 | $14,000
Assessable value | $680,000 | $357,000 | $194,000
Less: rates paid by owner | ($16,000) | — (tenant pays rates) | —
Less: 20% statutory allowance | ($132,800) | ($71,400) | ($38,800)
Net assessable value | $531,200 | $285,600 | $155,200
Tax @ 15% | $79,680 (split 50/50: $39,840 each) | $42,840 | $23,280
Key traps illustrated: (1) rates are only deductible if the owner agreed to bear them — Property B's tenant pays rates, so no deduction; (2) government rent, management fees, mortgage interest, and repair costs actually paid by the owner are never separately deductible — the flat 20% allowance is deemed to cover all of them regardless of actual spend.

Illustration — Irrecoverable rent exceeding the year's own rent, carried back Module 9, Ch.5 §5.4 — s.7C

A 2-year tenancy at $10,000/month runs from 1 July 2016; the tenant stops paying from 1 January 2017 and disappears on 1 May 2017, with the assessor accepting the outstanding rent as bad.

| Original YA1 (filed before default known, 9 months' rent) | YA2 (year debt confirmed bad)
Rent / assessable value | $90,000 | $10,000
Less: bad debt confirmed irrecoverable (4 months, Jan–Apr) | — | ($40,000)
Result for YA2 | — | ($30,000) — a loss
Since the $40,000 bad debt exceeds YA2's own $10,000 rent, the $30,000 excess is carried back under s.7C(3) to amend YA1:

YA1 revised: $90,000 rent − $30,000 carried-back loss | $60,000
Less: 20% statutory allowance | ($12,000)
Revised NAV | $48,000
Revised tax @15% ($7,200) vs. originally paid ($10,800) | Refund of $3,600
Mere non-payment (without the debt being proved bad) gives no deduction at all — this only applies once the assessor accepts the rent as genuinely irrecoverable.

Illustration — Property tax set off against profits tax for a corporation Module 9, Ch.5 §5.6 — s.25

A company's rental income is already included in its accounts and taxed under profits tax. It did not apply for the s.5(2)(a) upfront exemption, and separately paid $3,000 property tax on the same property.

Profits tax payable for the year | $10,000
Less: property tax already paid on the same property | ($3,000)
Net profits tax payable | $7,000
A straight set-off, unaffected by rate levels — if property tax paid had exceeded the profits tax bill, the excess would be refundable instead.

sections.heading: 1. Overview & Charging Basis IRO s.5
sections.text:
1. Overview & Charging Basis IRO s.5

Property tax is charged for each year of assessment on every person who owns land or buildings in Hong Kong, computed at the standard rate on the net assessable value — regardless of whether the owner carries on any trade or business. It is a tax on ownership + letting, not on trading profit as such.

Statutory text — s.5(1)
"Property tax shall...be charged for each year of assessment on every person being the owner of any land or buildings or land and buildings wherever situate in Hong Kong and shall be computed at the standard rate on the net assessable value of such land or buildings..."

Current rate

Standard rate applied to net assessable value | 15%
Owner-occupied property generates no rental consideration and therefore has no assessable value — no property tax arises. Where the owner of the land is not the owner of the buildings on it, separate assessments are made for each (s.5(1)(b)).

sections.heading: Traps in the property tax computation
sections.text:
Traps in the property tax computation

Three points the June 2026 examining team reported as weak
1. Compute each property separately. Where a taxpayer owns more than one let property, property tax is computed property by property, not on the aggregate. Each gets its own assessable value, its own rates deduction and its own 20% allowance.

2. Repairs and replacements get no separate deduction. Actual spending on repairs, redecoration or replacing fittings is deemed to be covered by the 20% statutory allowance — however much was really spent. Candidates could say the cost was not deductible but could not explain why.

3. There are no depreciation allowances under property tax. Replacing air-conditioners or other plant in a let property attracts no depreciation allowance, because Part 6 does not apply to the property tax charge. If the owner is a company carrying on business the position differs — the income is then within profits tax, where allowances are available.

The rental deposit — two different things
A deposit taken at the start of a lease is not assessable income; it is security held for the tenant. A deposit later forfeited and retained is set off against irrecoverable rent. The June 2026 report names both including the deposit as income and failing to set off a forfeited deposit as common errors.

sections.heading: 2. Net Assessable Value IRO s.5(1A), s.5B, s.7C
sections.text:
2. Net Assessable Value IRO s.5(1A), s.5B, s.7C

Assessable value (s.5B(2)) is the consideration in money or money's worth payable for the right to use the land/buildings during the year — i.e. rent and other consideration receivable, not merely received. Net assessable value (s.5(1A)) then deducts:

Assessable value (rent/consideration receivable for the year) | X
Less: irrecoverable consideration proved bad during the year (s.7C) | (X)
Less: rates paid by the owner, if the owner agreed to bear them | (X)
Less: statutory 20% allowance for repairs and outgoings (on the balance after rates) | (X)
Net assessable value | X
The 20% repairs/outgoings allowance is flat and statutory — it applies regardless of the owner's actual repair costs, and cannot be varied by claiming higher actual expenditure. Consideration recovered in a later year, having previously been written off as irrecoverable under s.7C, is brought back into that later year's assessable value (s.7C(2)).

Lease premiums paid up front are deemed under s.5B(3)/(4) to be payable in equal monthly instalments spread over the period of the right of use, capped at a maximum of 3 years — even if the actual lease term is longer. See the DIPN 4/DIPN 14 illustrations below.

sections.heading: 3. Taxable / Non-Taxable Items
sections.text:
3. Taxable / Non-Taxable Items

Status | Item | Basis
Taxable | Rent receivable for the year (whether or not actually received) | s.5B(2)
Taxable | Lease premiums / non-returnable deposits / key money, spread over up to 3 years | s.5B(3)/(4); DIPN 4, DIPN 14
Taxable | Consideration for services/benefits connected with the right of use (e.g. furniture, management services bundled into rent) | s.5B(6)
Non-taxable | Owner-occupied property (no rent receivable) | No assessable value arises — s.5(1)
Non-taxable | Rent/consideration proved to have become irrecoverable during the year | s.7C(1)
Deduction (fixed) | Rates paid by owner + flat 20% repairs/outgoings allowance | s.5(1A)(b)

sections.heading: 4. Corporate Interaction with Profits Tax IRO s.25, s.5(2)(a)
sections.text:
4. Corporate Interaction with Profits Tax IRO s.25, s.5(2)(a)

For a corporation carrying on a trade, profession or business in Hong Kong, property tax and profits tax can otherwise double-tax the same rental income. Two relief mechanisms apply:

- Set-off (s.25): where the rental profits form part of the corporation's trading profits (or the property is used to produce chargeable profits), profits tax payable is reduced by the property tax already paid on that property. If property tax paid exceeds the profits tax payable, the excess is refunded (s.25, proviso (b), via s.79).

- Upfront exemption (s.5(2)(a)): instead of paying property tax and later claiming the set-off, a corporation entitled to the s.25 set-off may apply in writing to the Commissioner for the property to be exempted from property tax altogether. The corporation must notify the Commissioner within 30 days of any change in ownership/use affecting the exemption (s.5(2)(c)).

Practical note
Non-corporate owners (individuals, partnerships) do not get the s.25 set-off/exemption against profits tax in the same way — they may instead elect Personal Assessment (IRO s.41) to have property tax effectively absorbed into a single personal-assessment computation where advantageous. See the Salaries Tax page for Personal Assessment.

What this is

Section C mirrors the exam's constructed-response questions: no multiple choice here — each question gives a scenario and asks you to prepare an actual computation or a written explanation, the same way you would in the exam itself. Attempt each part on paper first, then open the model answer to mark your own work.

Same computation engine as Sections A and B
Every figure in all eight model answers was generated from and checked against scripts/qbank_tax.py, the same module behind Section A's and Section B's answers — nothing here was worked out by hand and left unchecked.

sections.heading: Question 1 — Mr Ivan Ho (15 marks)
sections.text:
Question 1 — Mr Ivan Ho (15 marks)

Scenario15 marks

Ivan Ho is employed on an annual salary of $1,020,000 for the year of assessment 2026/27. During the year he incurred $60,000 on a job-related course, qualifying as a deductible self-education expense, and made the mandatory MPF contribution of $18,000. He is married; his wife has no income of her own.

Ivan also wholly owns a separate residential flat, which he lets out unconnected with his employment. Its net assessable value for the year (after rates and the 20% statutory allowance) is $200,000. He pays mortgage interest of $150,000 a year on the loan used to acquire that flat.

(a) Compute Ivan's salaries tax liability for the year, ignoring any election for personal assessment. (10 marks)

(b) Advise, with supporting calculations, whether Ivan should elect personal assessment for the year. (5 marks)

Show model answer

(a) Ivan Ho — Salaries Tax Computation, YA 2026/27

Salary | 1,020,000
Less: self-education expenses (1 mark) | (60,000)
Less: mandatory MPF contribution (1 mark) | (18,000)
Net income | 942,000
Less: married person's allowance (1 mark) | (290,000)
Net chargeable income | 652,000
Tax payable — lower of two methods

Progressive rates on $652,000 (3 marks)
2%/6%/10%/14% on four $50,000 bands ($16,000) + 17% on the $452,000 remainder ($76,840) | 92,840
Standard rate on net income before allowances: $942,000 × 15% (2 marks) | 141,300
Salaries tax payable (the lower of the two) (2 marks) | 92,840
Total for part (a): 10 marks. Using the standard rate on net income after allowances ($652,000 × 15% = $97,800) instead of before them, is the single commonest way to lose the 2 marks on the comparison.

(b) Without electing personal assessment

Salaries tax (from part (a)) | 92,840
Property tax: $200,000 × 15% (1 mark) | 30,000
Total tax | 122,840
Electing personal assessment

Total income (net income $942,000 + property NAV $200,000) | 1,142,000
Less: mortgage interest, capped at that property's own NAV of $200,000 (2 marks) | (150,000)
Reduced total income | 992,000
Less: married person's allowance | (290,000)
Net chargeable income | 702,000
Progressive rates: $16,000 + ($502,000 × 17%) | 101,340
Standard rate on reduced total income: $992,000 × 15% | 148,800
Tax payable under personal assessment (the lower) (1 mark) | 101,340
Advice (1 mark): Ivan should elect personal assessment. It saves $122,840 − $101,340 = $21,500, because the election lets his mortgage interest on the let property (which property tax alone cannot deduct) shelter his aggregated income. Total for part (b): 5 marks.

sections.heading: Question 2 — XYZ Trading Ltd (25 marks)
sections.text:
Question 2 — XYZ Trading Ltd (25 marks)

Scenario25 marks

XYZ Trading Ltd, a Hong Kong company with no connected entities, reports a net profit per accounts of $8,000,000 for the year ended 31 March 2027. The accounts include depreciation of $450,000, approved charitable donations of $200,000, and legal fees of $60,000 for acquiring a new five-year retail lease.

The company's plant and machinery pool (20% pool) had a written-down value brought forward of $600,000; during the year it bought qualifying plant for $800,000 and sold plant for $100,000. Separately, it incurred $1,500,000 of qualifying Type B R&D expenditure, already charged as an expense (and so already included) in the $8,000,000 net profit above. The company also has an unrelieved trading loss of $500,000 brought forward from an earlier year.

(a) Compute XYZ Trading Ltd's profits tax payable for the year. (20 marks)

(b) XYZ Trading Ltd is considering whether the $500,000 loss could instead be surrendered to a profitable fellow group company. Advise, with reasons. (5 marks)

Show model answer

(a) XYZ Trading Ltd — Profits Tax Computation, YA 2026/27

Net profit per accounts | 8,000,000
Add: non-allowable items |
Depreciation (1 mark) | 450,000
Charitable donations (1 mark) | 200,000
Legal fees — capital, acquiring a new lease (2 marks) | 60,000
| 8,710,000
Less: additional R&D deduction (4 marks)
Type B enhanced deduction: min($1,500,000, $2,000,000) × 300% = $4,500,000 total, less the $1,500,000 already expensed = $3,000,000 additional | (3,000,000)
Less: depreciation allowances (4 marks)
IA: $800,000 × 60% = $480,000. Pool: $600,000 + $800,000 − $480,000 − $100,000 disposal = $820,000. AA: $820,000 × 20% = $164,000. Total $480,000 + $164,000 | (644,000)
Profit before loss brought forward | 5,066,000
Less: loss brought forward (1 mark) | (500,000)
Profit before donations (Z) | 4,566,000
Less: approved charitable donations (2 marks)
lower of $200,000 actual and 35% × $4,566,000 = $1,598,100 — fully allowable | (200,000)
Assessable profit | 4,366,000
Tax payable

First $2,000,000 at 8.25% (2 marks) | 165,000
Remaining $2,366,000 at 16.5% (2 marks) | 390,390
Profits tax payable | 555,390
Total for part (a): 20 marks. Stating the total enhanced R&D deduction ($4,500,000) instead of the additional amount still to be deducted ($3,000,000), and computing the annual allowance on the pool before deducting the initial allowance, are the two errors this question is designed to catch.

(b) (5 marks): Hong Kong has no group loss relief of any kind. Each company, including XYZ Trading Ltd and any fellow group company, is a separate person chargeable to profits tax in its own right (2 marks). The $500,000 loss cannot be surrendered to, or set off against, a fellow group company's profits, however profitable that company is or however closely the two are connected (2 marks). The loss simply remains within XYZ Trading Ltd itself, carried forward indefinitely with no time limit, to be set off only against XYZ's own future assessable profits from the same trade (1 mark).

sections.heading: Question 3 — Mr Anthony Cheung (15 marks)
sections.text:
Question 3 — Mr Anthony Cheung (15 marks)

Scenario15 marks

Anthony Cheung owns two properties in Hong Kong, both let in his own name during the year of assessment 2026/27.

The shop was let for the whole year at $45,000 a month. Anthony paid rates of $20,000 on it. The tenant fell into difficulty and three months' rent was proved irrecoverable during the year.

The flat was let for the whole year at $22,000 a month, and Anthony also received a premium of $540,000 on granting that five-year lease at the start of the year. The flat's tenant pays the rates direct to the Government.

(a) Compute Anthony's property tax liability for the year. (11 marks)

(b) Anthony is considering transferring both properties into a Hong Kong company he owns, which carries on a trading business here. Explain the property tax consequences. (4 marks)

Show model answer

(a) Anthony Cheung — Property Tax Computation, YA 2026/27 — the shop

Rent receivable ($45,000 × 12) | 540,000
Less: irrecoverable rent ($45,000 × 3) (2 marks) | (135,000)
Assessable value | 405,000
Less: rates paid by the owner (1 mark) | (20,000)
| 385,000
Less: 20% statutory allowance (1 mark) | (77,000)
Net assessable value | 308,000
Property tax at 15% (1 mark) | 46,200
(a) continued — the flat

Rent receivable ($22,000 × 12) | 264,000
Add: premium spread (3 marks)
$540,000 over the lease term or 36 months, whichever is shorter — the lease runs 60 months, so the cap bites: $540,000 ÷ 36 × 12 | 180,000
Assessable value | 444,000
Less: rates (1 mark)
nil — the tenant pays them direct, so there is nothing for the owner to deduct | —
Less: 20% statutory allowance | (88,800)
Net assessable value | 355,200
Property tax at 15% (1 mark) | 53,280
Total

Shop | 46,200
Flat | 53,280
Total property tax payable (1 mark) | 99,480
Total for part (a): 11 marks. Each property is computed separately, with its own rates deduction and its own 20% allowance — aggregating the two into one computation loses marks. Spreading the premium over the full 60 months (giving $108,000) instead of applying the 36-month cap is the other error this question tests.

(b) (4 marks): A corporation carrying on a trade or business in Hong Kong may apply under s.5(2)(a) for exemption from property tax, on the basis that the rental income is instead brought into its profits tax computation (2 marks). If no such application is made, property tax is charged on the company in the ordinary way, but s.25 then sets that property tax off against the profits tax payable, so the same rent is not taxed twice either way (1 mark). Note the rate difference this creates: the rental profit would move from the flat 15% property tax charge to the corporate two-tier profits tax rates of 8.25%/16.5%, and the company could then deduct actual outgoings such as mortgage interest and repairs rather than being confined to the fixed 20% statutory allowance (1 mark).

sections.heading: Question 4 — Summit & Vale Partners (25 marks)
sections.text:
Question 4 — Summit & Vale Partners (25 marks)

Scenario25 marks

Summit & Vale Partners is a Hong Kong partnership with two partners: Mr Vale, an individual, holding a 70% profit share, and Summit Holdings Ltd, a Hong Kong company, holding the remaining 30%.

The partnership's accounts for the year ended 31 March 2027 show a net profit of $6,400,000, after charging: a partner's salary of $900,000 paid to Mr Vale, a salary of $300,000 paid to Mr Vale's spouse (who works in the business), depreciation of $350,000, and approved charitable donations of $120,000.

The partnership's 30% plant and machinery pool had a written-down value brought forward of $500,000. During the year it bought qualifying plant for $900,000 and sold plant for $400,000.

(a) Compute the partnership's assessable profit for the year. (14 marks)

(b) Compute the profits tax payable by each partner, and in total. (8 marks)

(c) Mr Vale asks whether Summit Holdings Ltd could elect personal assessment on its share. Advise. (3 marks)

Show model answer

(a) Summit & Vale Partners — Assessable Profit, YA 2026/27

Net profit per accounts | 6,400,000
Add: non-allowable items |
Partner's salary — Mr Vale (2 marks) | 900,000
Salary to the partner's spouse (2 marks) | 300,000
Depreciation (1 mark) | 350,000
Charitable donations (1 mark) | 120,000
| 8,070,000
Less: depreciation allowances (5 marks)
IA: $900,000 × 60% = $540,000. Pool: $500,000 + $900,000 − $540,000 − $400,000 disposal = $460,000. AA: $460,000 × 30% = $138,000. Total $540,000 + $138,000 | (678,000)
Profit before donations | 7,392,000
Less: approved charitable donations (2 marks)
lower of $120,000 actual and 35% × $7,392,000 = $2,587,200 — fully allowable | (120,000)
Assessable profit | 7,272,000
Total for part (a): 14 marks. Both the partner's own salary and the salary to his spouse are added back under s.17(2) — a partnership cannot deduct either, and forgetting the spouse's salary is the commonest omission. Computing the annual allowance on the pool before deducting the initial allowance is the other error tested here.

(b) Profits tax payable — each partner's own share and rate

Mr Vale — individual, 70% |
Share of assessable profit ($7,272,000 × 70%) | 5,090,400
Apportioned first-tier band ($2,000,000 × 70%) at 7.5% (2 marks) | 105,000
Balance ($5,090,400 − $1,400,000 = $3,690,400) at 15% (2 marks) | 553,560
Mr Vale's profits tax | 658,560
Summit Holdings Ltd — corporate, 30% |
Share of assessable profit ($7,272,000 × 30%) | 2,181,600
Apportioned first-tier band ($2,000,000 × 30%) at 8.25% (2 marks) | 49,500
Balance ($2,181,600 − $600,000 = $1,581,600) at 16.5% (1 mark) | 260,964
Summit Holdings Ltd's profits tax | 310,464
Total profits tax payable (1 mark) | 969,024
Total for part (b): 8 marks. The $2,000,000 two-tier band is apportioned between the partners in the profit-sharing ratio, and each partner's slice is then taxed at their own rates — 7.5%/15% for the individual, 8.25%/16.5% for the corporate partner. Applying one flat set of rates to the whole $7,272,000, as if the partnership were a single taxpayer, is the error a mixed partnership is set to catch.

(c) (3 marks): No. Personal assessment is available to individuals only (1 mark). Summit Holdings Ltd is a company, so its share of the partnership's assessable profit simply stays in its own profits tax computation at the corporate rates, with no personal assessment route available to it (1 mark). Mr Vale, being an individual, could elect on his own share — but on these figures it would not help him: his share alone far exceeds the level at which the 17% marginal progressive rate overtakes the 15% standard rate, and there is no loss or interest here for the election to unlock (1 mark).

sections.heading: Question 5 — Mr Daniel Lau (15 marks)
sections.text:
Question 5 — Mr Daniel Lau (15 marks)

Scenario15 marks

Daniel Lau is an individual resident in Hong Kong. In May 2026 he bought three adjacent mini-storage units in Kwun Tong for $3,200,000. He paid stamp duty and legal costs of $120,000 and spent $280,000 partitioning, repainting and installing access controls. He borrowed to fund the purchase and paid $180,000 interest during the holding period.

The units were never used by Daniel or let to tenants. He placed online advertisements for a resale before the renovation works were completed and sold all three units in February 2027 for $4,350,000, paying selling agency and legal costs of $90,000. Daniel says the gain is capital because he originally described the units as a "long-term store of value".

(a) Explain whether the gain is more likely to be taxable as profits from trade or non-taxable as capital. (10 marks)

(b) Assuming the gain is taxable as trading profits, compute Daniel's assessable profit and profits tax payable for YA 2026/27. (5 marks)

Show model answer
(a) (10 marks): The issue is whether Daniel was carrying on an adventure in the nature of trade, so that the profit arises from a trade, profession or business carried on in Hong Kong and is chargeable under s.14 (1 mark). Intention is relevant but is judged objectively from the facts, not merely from Daniel's label (1 mark). The subject matter points towards trade: three adjacent units are more consistent with a resale package than a personal long-term investment (1 mark). The short period of ownership, from May 2026 to February 2027, is a strong badge of trade (1 mark). The renovation and access-control works improved the units for onward sale rather than for own use or rental yield (1 mark). The early online advertisements, before completion of the works, show a pre-existing resale plan (1 mark). Borrowing and interest exposure support a need for quick realisation rather than passive holding (1 mark). There was no rental income or own use during the holding period, so there is little evidence of investment exploitation (1 mark). The buying, improving and selling activity was carried out in Hong Kong, so the source of any trading profit is Hong Kong (1 mark). On balance, the gain is more likely a taxable trading profit, and Daniel bears the practical burden of supporting any capital-gain claim if challenged (1 mark).

(b) Daniel Lau — Trading Profit and Profits Tax, YA 2026/27

Sale proceeds (1 mark) | 4,350,000
Less: purchase cost (1 mark) | (3,200,000)
Less: stamp duty and legal costs (1 mark) | (120,000)
Less: renovation and access controls | (280,000)
Less: interest and selling costs | (270,000)
Assessable profits (1 mark) | 480,000
Profits tax at the individual first-tier rate, $480,000 × 7.5% (1 mark) | 36,000
Total for part (b): 5 marks. This question is designed to catch the error of treating a self-serving "capital intention" statement as decisive, instead of weighing the badges of trade objectively.

sections.heading: Question 6 — JadeTech Manufacturing Ltd (25 marks)
sections.text:
Question 6 — JadeTech Manufacturing Ltd (25 marks)

Scenario25 marks

JadeTech Manufacturing Ltd is a Hong Kong manufacturing company with no connected entities. Its net profit per accounts for the year ended 31 March 2027 is $7,850,000, after charging depreciation of $740,000 and approved charitable donations of $260,000, and after crediting an accounting gain of $450,000 on the sale of its old factory.

The old factory had qualifying construction cost of $2,400,000. Before the sale, total industrial building allowances granted were $1,152,000 and the residue of expenditure was $1,248,000. The sale proceeds attributable to the building, excluding land, were $1,560,000.

The 30% plant and machinery pool had written-down value brought forward of $520,000. During the year JadeTech bought qualifying plant for cash of $900,000 and sold pooled plant for $180,000. It also acquired a machine on hire purchase: deposit paid $240,000, eight instalments paid in the year, and the capital element of each instalment was $55,000.

During the year JadeTech completed and first used a new factory. The purchase price included land of $2,100,000 and qualifying construction cost of $4,200,000.

(a) Compute JadeTech's assessable profits and profits tax payable for YA 2026/27. (22 marks)

(b) State three depreciation-allowance errors this question is designed to catch. (3 marks)

Show model answer

(a) JadeTech Manufacturing Ltd — Profits Tax Computation, YA 2026/27

Net profit per accounts (1 mark) | 7,850,000
Add back / deduct accounting and tax adjustments |
Depreciation, non-deductible under s.17(1)(c) (1 mark) | 740,000
Approved charitable donations added back first (1 mark) | 260,000
Less: accounting gain on factory sale, capital receipt | (450,000)
Add: industrial building balancing charge (3 marks)
Proceeds $1,560,000 less residue $1,248,000 = $312,000, capped by prior allowances of $1,152,000 | 312,000
Adjusted profit before depreciation allowances | 8,712,000
Less: depreciation allowances |
30% plant pool (4 marks)
IA: $900,000 × 60% = $540,000. Pool: $520,000 + $900,000 − $540,000 − $180,000 = $700,000. AA: $700,000 × 30% = $210,000 | (750,000)
Hire-purchase machine (3 marks)
Qualifying capital paid: $240,000 + (8 × $55,000) = $680,000. IA $408,000 and AA $81,600 | (489,600)
New factory industrial building allowance (3 marks)
Land $2,100,000 excluded. Construction cost $4,200,000: IA 20% = $840,000; AA 4% = $168,000 | (1,008,000)
Profit before donations (1 mark) | 6,464,400
Less: approved charitable donations (2 marks)
Actual $260,000 is below the 35% cap of $2,262,540 | (260,000)
Assessable profits (1 mark) | 6,204,400
Profits tax: first $2,000,000 at 8.25%, balance $4,204,400 at 16.5% (1 mark) | 858,726
Total for part (a): 22 marks. The tax payable is $165,000 + $693,726 = $858,726.

(b) (3 marks): The first error is giving building allowances on land: only qualifying construction cost is used (1 mark). The second is computing initial allowance on the full hire-purchase cash price instead of the capital sums actually paid in the year (1 mark). The third is omitting the balancing charge on the old factory sale and taxing the accounting gain instead (1 mark).

sections.heading: Question 7 — Harbor Link Sourcing Ltd (15 marks)
sections.text:
Question 7 — Harbor Link Sourcing Ltd (15 marks)

Scenario15 marks

Harbor Link Sourcing Ltd is incorporated and managed in Hong Kong. During the year ended 31 March 2027 it earned net sourcing commission profit of $3,200,000 from overseas customers who bought electronic components from factories in Mainland China.

Harbor Link's Hong Kong staff found suppliers, negotiated prices and specifications, arranged purchase orders and dealt with quality complaints from its office in Hong Kong. Factory visits and shipment inspections in Mainland China were carried out by independent contractors engaged job by job. Customers signed their master supply agreements outside Hong Kong and paid Harbor Link into an overseas bank account.

(a) Advise whether Harbor Link's offshore claim is likely to succeed. (10 marks)

(b) If the whole profit is taxable in Hong Kong, compute the profits tax payable. (5 marks)

Show model answer
(a) (10 marks): The charge under s.14 is on profits arising in or derived from Hong Kong from a trade, profession or business carried on here (1 mark). The company carries on business in Hong Kong: it is incorporated and managed here and its staff conduct the sourcing business from the Hong Kong office (1 mark). Source is decided by identifying the profit-producing operations and where those operations take place, not by asking where the customer is resident or where money is banked (1 mark). For a sourcing commission business, the relevant operations are finding suppliers, negotiating price and specifications, arranging purchase orders and handling performance problems (2 marks). Those core operations were performed by Harbor Link's own staff in Hong Kong (1 mark). The Mainland factory visits and inspections were ancillary execution work, and they were performed by independent contractors rather than by Harbor Link's own profit-producing team (1 mark). Signing master agreements outside Hong Kong is not decisive if the commercial work that earned the commission was done in Hong Kong (1 mark). The overseas bank account is administrative evidence, not a source rule (1 mark). Harbor Link bears the burden of proving the facts supporting an offshore claim under s.68(4); on these facts the claim is unlikely to succeed (1 mark).

(b) Harbor Link Sourcing Ltd — Profits Tax if the Offshore Claim Fails, YA 2026/27

Assessable profits | 3,200,000
First $2,000,000 at 8.25% (2 marks) | 165,000
Balance $1,200,000 at 16.5% (2 marks) | 198,000
Profits tax payable (1 mark) | 363,000
Total for part (b): 5 marks. This question is designed to catch the error of treating overseas customers, overseas signing or an overseas bank account as decisive, instead of applying the operations test to the profit-producing activities.

sections.heading: Question 8 — East Point Design Ltd (25 marks)
sections.text:
Question 8 — East Point Design Ltd (25 marks)

Scenario25 marks

East Point Design Ltd filed its profits tax return late after omitting a major service invoice. The Inland Revenue Department later issued an additional assessment on 15 August 2027, showing tax undercharged of $420,000, and requiring payment on 15 September 2027. East Point accepts that the invoice was taxable but says the omission was caused by a bookkeeper's spreadsheet error.

The directors are considering an objection because they also believe a separate deduction has been refused wrongly. They cannot pay the full assessment by the due date and expect cash will not be available until eight months after the due date.

(a) Explain the objection procedure and what East Point must do if it wants collection held over. (10 marks)

(b) Compute the maximum penalty under s.80 and the late-payment amount if the tax remains unpaid for eight months. (8 marks)

(c) Advise on the penalty exposure and the practical steps East Point should take now. (7 marks)

Show model answer
(a) (10 marks): A valid objection must be made in writing to the Commissioner within one month after the notice of assessment, stating precisely the grounds of objection (2 marks). Filing an objection does not by itself suspend collection: the tax remains payable unless the Commissioner orders holdover (2 marks). East Point should therefore request holdover at the same time, explaining the disputed deduction and providing supporting documents (2 marks). Holdover may be conditional, including requiring the taxpayer to purchase a tax reserve certificate or provide security (1 mark). If the objection is determined against East Point, the company may appeal to the Board of Review within one month after the determination (1 mark). The accepted omitted invoice should not be included in the objection grounds: East Point should separate the conceded undercharge from the genuinely disputed deduction (1 mark). Missing the payment date without holdover exposes the company to late-payment surcharges even while correspondence continues (1 mark).

(b) East Point Design Ltd — Penalty and Late-Payment Exposure

Tax undercharged / additional tax assessed | 420,000
Maximum s.80 penalty: $10,000 plus treble the tax undercharged (3 marks) | 1,270,000
First surcharge for late payment: 5% of $420,000 (1 mark) | 21,000
Further surcharge after six months: 10% of $441,000 (2 marks) | 44,100
Total surcharges after eight months | 65,100
Amount payable after eight months (2 marks) | 485,100
Total for part (b): 8 marks. The late-payment computation applies the second 10% surcharge to the tax plus the first surcharge, not to the original tax alone.

(c) (7 marks): The omission of taxable income creates penalty exposure even if the bookkeeper made the spreadsheet error: the company remains responsible for the correctness of its return (1 mark). A maximum s.80 penalty is not automatically imposed; IRD will consider culpability, cooperation, voluntary disclosure, previous compliance and whether prosecution or additional tax procedures are used (2 marks). East Point should make a full written disclosure of the omitted invoice, correct the computation, explain the control failure and provide evidence that the error was not deliberate (1 mark). It should pay the undisputed part as soon as possible, or at least seek instalment arrangements, because cash difficulty does not remove statutory surcharges (1 mark). It should support the disputed deduction with invoices, contracts, board approvals and accounting records, and keep the objection focused on that point (1 mark). Finally, it should improve controls over sales cut-off and return review before the next filing, since repeated errors aggravate penalties (1 mark).

sections.heading: A. From IRD DIPNs
sections.text:
A. From IRD DIPNs

Illustration — Joint assessment saves tax vs separate taxation DIPN 18

Mr A earns $680,000, Mrs A earns $100,000. Taxed separately, their combined liability is $23,030. Electing joint assessment under s.10(2) — pooling income and allowances — reduces the combined liability to $17,505, because Mrs A's unabsorbed allowances/deductions offset Mr A's higher-rate income.

Illustration — Home loan interest apportionment by ownership type DIPN 35

Mr C is sole owner, pays $120,000 interest — allowable deduction capped at $100,000. Mr & Mrs D are joint tenants, pay $100,000 total interest between them — each gets $50,000. Mr E (1/4 share) and Mr F (3/4 share) are tenants in common on a $100,000 interest bill — Mr E gets $25,000, Mr F gets $75,000 (apportioned strictly by ownership share, not by who actually paid).

Illustration — VHIS premium cap applied per insured person DIPN 56

Mr J pays VHIS premiums for himself ($5,000), spouse ($4,000), grandmother ($16,000), father ($12,000), mother ($11,000), son ($3,000) — total $51,000 paid. Because the cap is HKD 8,000 per insured person, the grandmother/father/mother claims are each capped at $8,000: allowable deduction = $5,000 + $4,000 + ($8,000 × 3) + $3,000 = $36,000. The $15,000 excess simply lapses — no carry-forward.

Illustration — Charitable donation cap at 35% of reduced assessable income DIPN 37

Mr A has salary $500,000, deductible expenses $10,000 (reduced assessable income $490,000), and made donations of $210,000. Since $210,000 exceeds 35% of $490,000, the deduction is capped at $490,000 × 35% = $171,500 — the remaining $38,500 of donations gives no further tax benefit.

Illustration — Share option gain apportioned by vesting days in Hong Kong DIPN 38

An employee's share option has a 730-day vesting period, of which 292 days were spent working in Hong Kong. At exercise, only 292/730 = 40% of the gain is assessable to Hong Kong salaries tax — the remainder relates to non-Hong Kong employment and falls outside the charge.

sections.text:
B. From Module 9: Principles of Taxation (4th ed.)

Adapted from a professional taxation qualification manual. Facts are paraphrased, not reproduced verbatim; every allowance/rate figure has been checked against current Hong Kong tax law and corrected where the textbook was using a stale amount (noted per illustration).

Illustration — The 60-day rule: two early departures tip the count over the line Module 9, Ch.4 §4.1 — s.8(1B)

An employee holds a Hong Kong employment contract but works full-time in Mainland China, returning to Hong Kong only periodically. His visits (quarterly meetings plus connecting travel) total 59 "ordinary" days for the year. On two occasions, however, he leaves Hong Kong very early in the morning to connect onward (once via Osaka, once via London) rather than flying straight back to China. Under the counting convention, both the day of arrival and the day of departure count as a full day each — even for a same-day transit.

Days in HK from ordinary visits | 59
Extra day — early departure via Osaka | +1
Extra day — early departure via London | +1
Total days in Hong Kong | 61
61 > 60, so the s.8(1B) exemption fails entirely — his full Hong Kong-employment income becomes chargeable, even though he worked in China almost all year. It's a hard cliff-edge test on days present, not days worked, and transit days count in full. No allowance/rate figures involved, so no correction was needed.

Illustration — Rent-free housing benefit: the "rental value" method Module 9, Ch.4 §4.2 — s.9(2)

An employee on a $600,000 salary gets a company-leased apartment rent-free; the employer also reimburses $16,800 of medical insurance (a taxable perquisite). Rental value = 10% of (salary + taxable perquisites) for a self-contained flat/house.

Salary + taxable perquisite | $616,800
Rental value (10% × $616,800) | $61,680
Contrast — two staff sharing one room in a company flat (boarding-house-type arrangement, not a self-contained flat) use the lower 4% rate instead of 10%:

Employee | Income | Rental value (4%)
Staff A | $150,000 | $6,000
Staff B | $120,000 | $4,800
Rate scale (s.9(2)): flat/house = 10% of net employment income; hotel/hostel/boarding-house of ≤2 rooms = 8%; ≤1 room / shared-room = 4%. These percentages sit in the Ordinance itself (not an annually-adjusted allowance) — no update needed, but worth a one-line confirmation against IRD's current housing-benefit guide before relying on it for a filing.

Illustration — Share option gain: OMV at exercise, less strike price and option cost Module 9, Ch.4 §4.3 — s.9(1)(d)/(4)

An employee is granted an option (by virtue of employment) to buy 5,000 shares at a strike price of $12/share, paying $6,000 for the option itself. Open market value (OMV) at grant was $24/share; two years later he exercises when OMV has risen to $30/share.

OMV at exercise (5,000 × $30) | $150,000
Less: consideration paid on exercise (5,000 × $12) | ($60,000)
Less: cost of the option itself | ($6,000)
Chargeable gain, assessed in year of exercise | $84,000
The gain is taxed at exercise, not at eventual sale — any share-price movement after exercise is a capital (non-taxable) matter. No allowance/rate figures involved, so no correction was needed.

Illustration — Termination gratuity "related back" over a 36-month window Module 9, Ch.4 §4.6 — s.11D(b)(i)

An employee made redundant after 7 years 11 months of service receives a $140,400 contract-end gratuity and elects to have it "related back" under s.11D(b)(i). Because total service exceeded 3 years, the law spreads the gratuity evenly over the 36 months ending on the earlier of the payment date or last day of employment — not over the full 7-year service period.

Year of assessment | Months in the 36-month window | Gratuity allocated
Year 1 (partial) | 8 | $31,200
Year 2 | 12 | $46,800
Year 3 | 12 | $46,800
Year 4 (partial) | 4 | $15,600
Total | 36 | $140,400
Contrast: for service of 3 years or less, the gratuity spreads only over the actual contract/service period, not artificially capped at 36 months. Pure time-apportionment mechanic — no correction needed.

Illustration — Child allowance depends on "full-time education," not just age Module 9, Ch.4 §4.9 — s.31

Twins both turn 19 partway through a year and finish secondary school that same year — the allowance still applies for that year since both were in full-time education for part of it (age >18 doesn't disqualify a student). The following year, one twin enrols in a full-time vocational diploma (still qualifies); the other instead starts a technician apprenticeship structured as an employment contract — drawing a wage as an employee rather than being a student — which fails the "full-time education" condition.

Year | Children qualifying | Child allowance claimable (YA 2026/27: $140,000/child; D26 exam basis YA 2025/26: $130,000)
Year twins turn 19 | Both twins | 2 × $140,000 = $280,000
Following year | Diploma student only | 1 × $140,000 = $140,000
Original book figure used $100,000/child (correct for YA 2018/19, now stale); updated above to the current YA 2026/27 rate of $140,000/child. Mechanic: no age cap while a child remains in full-time education; a paid apprenticeship/employment contract breaks eligibility even though the person is still "training." Watch: the 2026 Policy Address (16 Sep 2026) proposes HKD 160,000 for a second or subsequent child born on or after 16 September 2026 — twins born years earlier stay at HKD 140,000, so this illustration is unaffected even once the amendment ordinance passes.

Illustration — Full computation: salary, housing benefit, share option gain, deductions, allowances, tax payable Module 9, Ch.4 §4.11 — the "master" illustration

A bank compliance director receives salary $1,500,000, bonus $200,000, a rent-free company flat (taxed via the 10% rental-value method), and a gain on exercising vested overseas stock options. He deducts a professional subscription, self-education fees, a charitable donation, and mandatory MPF, and claims the basic and child allowances (married, assessed as an individual).

Salary + bonus | $1,700,000
Add: rental value = 10% × (salary+bonus − professional subscription) | $169,882
Add: share option exercise gain (FX-converted) | $25,476
Assessable income | $1,895,358
Less: professional subscription | ($1,179)
Less: self-education expenses | ($77,100)
Net assessable income | $1,817,079
Less: approved charitable donation | ($50,000)
Less: mandatory MPF contribution (capped) | ($18,000)
Net income | $1,749,079
Less: basic allowance (YA 2026/27; D26 exam: $132,000) | ($145,000)
Less: child allowance × 1 (YA 2026/27; D26 exam: $130,000) | ($140,000)
Net chargeable income | $1,464,079
Tax at progressive rates vs. standard rate — pay the lower

Progressive rates on $1,464,079 net chargeable income (2%/6%/10%/14% on the first four $50,000 bands, 17% on the $1,264,079 remainder) | $230,893
Standard rate: 15% × $1,749,079 net income (well under the $5,000,000 cap) | $262,362
Tax payable = lower of the two | $230,893
Original book figures used a basic allowance of $132,000 (YA 2019/20 rate) and child allowance of $120,000 — both stale; updated above to the current YA 2026/27 rates of $145,000 and $140,000, which cascades through to a different net chargeable income and tax payable than the book's original answer. Note: a one-off percentage tax reduction (capped at a fixed HKD amount) is announced in most Budgets and would further reduce this figure for the specific year being computed — check the current year's Budget measure before treating $230,893 as the final "net tax payable" (see the one-off relief callout on the main Salaries Tax page).

sections.heading: C. Personal Assessment — from Module 9 (Textbook)
sections.text:
C. Personal Assessment — from Module 9 (Textbook)

Personal Assessment (§6 of the main page) aggregates salaries, property, and unincorporated-business income into one computation. These three illustrations, adapted from Module 9's running "Chan/Lip family" case study, are recomputed against current allowances/rate bands throughout.

Illustration — Should a sole proprietor with rental property elect Personal Assessment? Module 9, Ch.6 §6.3 — s.41

A taxpayer runs a sole-proprietorship business (profit $800,000, of which he donates $400,000 to charity) and separately owns a rental property (rental income $400,000), while paying $400,000 mortgage interest on his own home. Without election, profits tax and property tax are assessed separately with no relief for the home loan interest at all, and the charitable donation is capped at 35% of the business profit alone.

Item | Without election | With Personal Assessment
Business profit, after donation capped at 35% of $800,000 ($280,000 used, $120,000 of the $400,000 paid gets no relief) | Profits tax @15% on $520,000 = $78,000 | Combined income $840,000, less a recomputed donation ceiling (35% of grossed-up income — $112,000 more becomes usable), less home loan interest (capped at $100,000/yr), less married allowance ($290,000) → net chargeable income $338,000 → tax at progressive rates = $39,460
Rental property, NAV after 20% allowance | Property tax @15% on $320,000 = $48,000
Total | $126,000
Tax saved by electing | $86,540
Original book figures used the 2017/18 married allowance ($264,000) and old 4-band rates; updated above to current allowances/bands. Key trap: under Personal Assessment, the charitable donation ceiling is recomputed as 35% of the grossed-up combined income, not simply 35% of the post-donation business profit — this typically unlocks extra donation relief. Home loan interest also becomes claimable for the first time once there is a combined computation to set it against, even though the taxpayer has no salaries income. Figures exclude any one-off Budget tax reduction for the specific year being computed — check the current year's measure before treating either total as final.

Illustration — Married couple, joint election: salaries + property + business + partnership loss Module 9, Ch.6 §6.4 — s.41(1A)

Husband has salaries income $520,000 plus a $120,000 share of a partnership loss. Wife owns a rental property (NAV $192,000, mortgage interest ≥ $192,000) and runs a business (net profit $400,000 after an approved donation already used at business level). One 15-year-old child.

Husband's income − partnership loss share | $520,000 − $120,000 = $400,000
Wife's income − mortgage interest (capped at NAV) − extra donation relief | $692,000 − $192,000 − $160,000 = $340,000
Combined reduced total income | $740,000
Less: married allowance (current rate) | ($290,000)
Less: child allowance × 1 (current rate) | ($140,000)
Net chargeable income | $310,000
Tax at progressive rates | $34,700
Tax is then apportioned back to each spouse in proportion to their own net contribution to the combined income: husband $400,000/$740,000 × $34,700 ≈ $18,757; wife $340,000/$740,000 × $34,700 ≈ $15,943.

Original book figures used the 2017/18 married allowance ($264,000) and child allowance ($100,000); updated above to current rates ($290,000 / $140,000). Mechanic: aggregating income across both spouses, capping loan interest at the property's own NAV (not the higher amount actually paid), and apportioning the joint tax bill back to each spouse by their share of net income — not a 50/50 split.

Illustration — Dependent parent allowance, elderly care deduction, and a business loss driving one spouse's share to zero Module 9, Ch.6 §6.5 — ss.26D, 31

Husband has employment income (incl. a share option gain), pays for his elderly mother's support (not living with him) and his elderly father's residential care home fees. Wife has no employment, runs a business at a loss for the year, and owns a rental property with mortgage interest exceeding its NAV.

Husband's net assessable income + Wife's NAV | $1,368,000 + $105,600 = $1,473,600
Less: mortgage interest (capped at wife's NAV) | ($105,600)
Less: approved donation, MPF (capped) | ($10,000 + $18,000)
Less: elderly residential care expenses (current cap $120,000/parent) | ($120,000)
Less: wife's business loss for the year | ($450,000)
Reduced total income | $770,000
Less: married allowance (current rate) | ($290,000)
Less: dependent parent allowance (60+, not co-residing — current rate) | ($55,000)
Net chargeable income | $425,000
Tax at progressive rates | $54,250
Original book figures used 2017/18 rates throughout (married allowance $264,000, dependent parent allowance $46,000, elderly care cap $92,000); all updated above to current rates. Because the wife's own income is more than wiped out by her mortgage interest, donation, and business loss, her apportioned share of the joint tax floors at nil — the husband bears the entire $54,250. Note the dependent parent allowance (mother, not co-residing) and the elderly care deduction (father, in a care home) apply to different dependants — you cannot double-claim both reliefs for the same parent, but can use different reliefs for different parents in the same year.

Figures to re-verify before publishing
The elderly residential care expenses cap and any one-off percentage tax reduction (with its HKD cap) are announced fresh in most annual Budgets — confirm both against the current year's Budget measure before treating any "final tax payable" figure above as authoritative. The MPF mandatory-contribution cap ($18,000) and 35%-of-income donation ceiling are carried through from established practice; a quick check against current IRD guidance is still worthwhile before publishing.

sections.heading: 1. Overview & Charging Basis IRO s.8
sections.text:
1. Overview & Charging Basis IRO s.8

Salaries tax is charged on income arising in or derived from Hong Kong from an office, employment of profit, or pension (s.8(1)) — again a territorial-source tax, not a residence-based one. Whether employment income is "Hong Kong employment" or "non-Hong Kong employment" is decided on the "totality of facts" test from Goepfert — the three key factors are: (1) where the employment contract was negotiated and is enforceable, (2) the residence of the employer, and (3) where the employee's remuneration is paid (see DIPN 10).

The 60-day rule — s.8(1A)(b)/(1B)
Income from services rendered wholly outside Hong Kong by a person not employed by the Government (and not ship/aircraft crew) is excluded from the charge — unless the person visited Hong Kong for more than 60 days in the basis period, in which case services rendered during those visits are brought back into charge.

Directors' fees from a Hong Kong resident company are always Hong Kong-sourced regardless of where the director renders services. Income taxed in a DTA territory that gives a s.50 credit is excluded from the s.8(1A)(c) exemption route (must use the credit mechanism instead, not double relief).

sections.heading: 2. Rates & Standard Rate Cap IRO s.13, Schedule 2
sections.text:
2. Rates & Standard Rate Cap IRO s.13, Schedule 2

Progressive rates on net chargeable income (2025/26 and continuing into 2026/27 basis) — Schedule 2

Band | Rate
First HKD 50,000 | 2%
Next HKD 50,000 (50,001–100,000) | 6%
Next HKD 50,000 (100,001–150,000) | 10%
Next HKD 50,000 (150,001–200,000) | 14%
Remainder (above 200,000) | 17%
Under s.13, tax computed progressively on net chargeable income (i.e. after allowances) is capped at a standard-rate calculation applied to net total income (i.e. before personal allowances, but after concessionary deductions): 15% on the first HKD 5,000,000, 16% on the remainder. The taxpayer pays whichever of the two computations is lower — this matters most for higher earners with large personal allowances.

One-off relief
Inland Revenue (Amendment) Ordinance 2026 (gazetted 22 May 2026): 100% reduction of salaries tax/personal assessment tax for YA 2025/26, capped at HKD 3,000. (Source: PwC, reviewed 22 Jul 2026 — verify against the gazetted ordinance.)

sections.text:
3. Taxable / Non-Taxable Income

Status | Item | Basis
Taxable | Salary, wages, bonus, commission, leave pay for services rendered in Hong Kong | s.8(1)(a), s.8(1A)(a)
Taxable | Director's fee from a Hong Kong resident company | s.8(1)(a) — sourced to the company's residence, not where services are performed
Taxable | Pension attributable to Hong Kong employment/office | s.8(1)(b)
Taxable | Employer-provided holiday journey benefits — actual cost to employer, regardless of convertibility, apportioned for business-cum-holiday trips | s.9(2A)(c); DIPN 41
Taxable | Share option gains at exercise (HK-employment portion) and share award vesting benefits | s.9(1)(d)/(4)/(5); DIPN 38
Taxable | Fringe benefits convertible into money, or specifically deemed by s.9(1)(a)(iv) "liability test" (e.g. employer settling the employee's personal debt/liability) | DIPN 16
Non-taxable | Income from services rendered wholly outside Hong Kong (non-Government employee, ≤60 days HK visits) | s.8(1A)(b), s.8(1B)
Non-taxable | Income already taxed in a non-DTA territory of substantially the same nature, tax actually paid | s.8(1A)(c)
Non-taxable | Genuine reimbursement of business expenses (no personal benefit) | General principle — not "income from employment"

sections.heading: 4. Deductible / Non-Deductible Items IRO s.12
sections.text:
4. Deductible / Non-Deductible Items IRO s.12

The general test (s.12(1)(a)) is stricter than the profits tax test — expenses must be "wholly, exclusively and necessarily" incurred in producing the assessable income (not merely "to the extent"), and domestic/private expenses and capital expenditure are excluded outright. In practice very few ordinary employment expenses pass this test (see DIPN 9).

Status | Item | Basis / cap (2026/27)
Deductible | Outgoings/expenses wholly, exclusively and necessarily incurred in producing the income (rare in practice for employees) | s.12(1)(a)
Deductible | Self-education expenses | s.12(1)(e) — capped at HKD 100,000
Deductible | Mandatory MPF contributions | Capped at HKD 18,000
Deductible | Home loan interest (ss.26E/26F) | HKD 100,000 (120,000 if a qualifying child born after 25 Oct 2023); up to 20 years of assessment; apportioned among joint owners/tenants in common (DIPN 35)
Deductible | Domestic rent (new, non-owner-occupiers) | HKD 100,000 (120,000 with qualifying child)
Deductible | Elderly residential care expenses (s.26D) | HKD 110,000 per parent/grandparent; mutually exclusive with the dependent parent/grandparent allowance (DIPN 36)
Deductible | Approved charitable donations (s.26C) | Min. HKD 100 aggregate; capped at 35% of income after other deductions (DIPN 37)
Deductible | Health insurance premiums under VHIS Certified Plans (ss.26H–26M) | HKD 8,000 per insured person (DIPN 56)
Deductible | Qualifying annuity premiums + MPF voluntary contributions (ss.26N–26U) | Combined cap HKD 60,000/year, TVC deducted first (DIPN 57)
Deductible | Assisted reproductive services expenses | HKD 100,000 (from 2024/25)
Non-deductible | Cost of travel between home and workplace | s.12(1)(a) excludes domestic/private expenses (DIPN 9)
Non-deductible | Clothing, entertainment expenses of a personal nature | DIPN 9
Non-deductible | Excess deductions beyond each item's statutory cap (e.g. donations above 35%, VHIS above HKD 8,000/insured) | Excess simply lapses — no carry-forward for salaries tax deductions (unlike profits tax losses)

Allowance | YA 2026/27 — current | YA 2024/25 & 2025/26 — D26 exam
Basic allowance | 145,000 | 132,000
Married person's allowance | 290,000 | 264,000

Child allowance — 2nd and subsequent child born on/after 16 Sep 2026 proposed | 160,000 each (320,000 in year of birth + following year)
Single parent allowance | 145,000 | 132,000
Dependent parent/grandparent allowance (60+, not residing with taxpayer) | 55,000 | 50,000
Dependent parent/grandparent allowance (60+, residing with taxpayer) | 110,000 | 100,000
Dependent parent/grandparent allowance (55–59) | 27,500 / 55,000 (not residing / residing) | 25,000 / 50,000

Disabled dependant allowance | 75,000 per dependant | 75,000
Child allowance claim period for the enhanced "year of birth" rate was extended from 1 to 2 years effective YA 2026/27 — check whether this affects the year you're computing.

Proposed — 2026 Policy Address, 16 September 2026
The Chief Executive announced that child allowance will rise from HKD 140,000 to HKD 160,000 for a taxpayer's second and subsequent children born on or after 16 September 2026 (claimable until age 25, on the usual full-time education / disability conditions). The enhanced additional child allowance for the year of birth and the following year rises to HKD 160,000 on the same basis, so those two years give HKD 320,000 per qualifying child. Intended to take effect from YA 2026/27, but it requires an amendment ordinance — until that is enacted, the enacted figure for every child remains HKD 140,000. First-born children are not covered by the increase.
Source: IRD — 2026 Policy Address, Tax-related Policy Measures (on Individuals), published 16 Sep 2026.

sections.heading: 6. Personal Assessment IRO s.41
sections.text:
6. Personal Assessment IRO s.41

Personal Assessment is an election (not automatic) available to individuals (and, if both elect, jointly for married couples under s.41(1A)) that aggregates all sources of income — including property tax and profits tax from an unincorporated business — into one computation, deducting personal allowances and applying salaries-tax-style progressive rates. It is beneficial mainly where the taxpayer has property tax or unincorporated-business profits tax that would otherwise get no benefit from personal allowances, or has losses in one source that can offset income in another.

Joint assessment (s.10(2), distinct from Personal Assessment) lets a married couple be taxed as one for salaries tax where beneficial — typically where one spouse has income below the value of their own allowances (DIPN 18).

Personal Assessment has its own page
This summary is here because Personal Assessment is where Salaries Tax meets the other two heads of charge. The full treatment — eligibility and the residence tests, the 2018/19 change letting married persons elect separately, election and withdrawal time limits, the three-step computation and the standard-rate cap, what is deductible, and four worked illustrations including one where electing costs money — is on the Personal Assessment page.

Full Personal Assessment page → · 3 further election illustrations from Module 9 →

sections.heading: 7. Illustrations
sections.text:
7. Illustrations

14 worked illustrations back this page — DIPN-sourced (joint assessment, home loan interest apportionment, VHIS/donation caps, share option vesting) plus Module 9 textbook examples (the 60-day rule, housing benefit valuation, termination gratuities, child allowance eligibility, a full computation, and 3 Personal Assessment election scenarios), all cross-checked against current YA 2026/27 rates and allowances.

Illustration — Joint assessment saves tax vs separate taxation DIPN 18

Mr A earns $680,000, Mrs A earns $100,000. Taxed separately, their combined liability is $23,030. Electing joint assessment under s.10(2) — pooling income and allowances — reduces the combined liability to $17,505, because Mrs A's unabsorbed allowances/deductions offset Mr A's higher-rate income.
