sections.heading: A. From SOIPNs
sections.text:
A. From SOIPNs

Illustration — Provisional vs formal agreement timing SOIPN 1

Provisional agreement signed 1 March 2014, formal agreement signed 8 March 2014 (within 14 days) → only the formal agreement needs stamping, by 7 April 2014; the provisional agreement is duty-free. If the formal agreement instead follows more than 14 days later (e.g. 17 March), the provisional agreement itself becomes chargeable at full AVD by 31 March 2014, and the formal agreement is separately chargeable at a fixed $100 by 16 April 2014.

Illustration — AVD on a multi-asset instrument (residential + car parks) SOIPN 8, historical figures — pre-2023 flat-15% Scale 1

An HKPR buyer purchases a $13,000,000 residential property plus two car parking spaces worth $2,000,000 in one instrument. Scale 2 (3.75% at that value band) applies to the residential portion: $487,500. The car parks (non-residential, Scale 3) at the equivalent band: $150,000. Total AVD = $637,500. Historically (SOIPN 8, Nov 2018), a non-HKPR buyer paid a flat 15% Scale 1 on the residential portion instead: $1,950,000 + $150,000 = $2,100,000 — but Scale 1 is no longer flat; see illustration B1 below for how the same fact pattern is taxed today.

Illustration — Current graduated Scale 1 vs. Scale 2 Corrected from Cap. 117 First Schedule, post-2026 amendment

Same $13,000,000 residential property, non-HKPR (or corporate) buyer, no Scale 2 concession available: Scale 1 is graduated exactly like Scale 2 at this value band (3.75%), giving the same $487,500 — not a flat-15% $1,950,000. The two scales only diverge for a single residential property with consideration above $100,000,000: at $150,000,000, Scale 2 (HKPR sole property) still applies its 4.25% top rate = $6,375,000, while Scale 1 hits the new 6.5% flat band = $9,750,000 — a HKD 3.375 million difference driven entirely by the 2026 amendment's new top bands.

Illustration — SSD tiered by holding period SOIPN 5

Under the (now 0%-rated but still operative) post-27-Oct-2012 regime: a $3,000,000 residential property resold within 6 months would attract SSD at 20% ($600,000); resold within 6–12 months, 15% ($450,000); a $4,000,000 property resold within 12–36 months, 10% ($400,000). At the current 0% rate none of this is actually payable, but the tiering logic remains the statutory mechanism.

Illustration — BSD ignores which joint owner actually paid SOIPN 7

A Hong Kong permanent resident buys a $4,000,000 residential property jointly with an unrelated non-HKPR co-buyer. Because one joint owner is a non-HKPR and the two are not close relatives, BSD (at the applicable rate) applies to the full $4,000,000 value — it is not pro-rated to only the non-HKPR's share.

sections.heading: B. From Module 9: Principles of Taxation (4th ed.)
sections.text:
B. From Module 9: Principles of Taxation (4th ed.)

Adapted from a professional taxation qualification manual. Facts are paraphrased, not reproduced verbatim. This textbook predates the 2023 Scale 1 reform and the Feb 2024 BSD/SSD rate cut — every AVD/BSD/SSD figure below has been recomputed against current (2026) law, with the book's original figure shown for contrast.

Illustration B1 — AVD on residential + non-residential property in one purchase Module 9, Ch.7 §7.4

A Hong Kong company (never a HKPR) buys two properties on the same day: a commercial warehouse for $25,000,000, and a residential flat for $20,000,000 (consideration assumed to equal market value in both cases).

Property | Scale | Book figure (flat 15% on residential) | Current law (graduated)
Warehouse (non-residential) | Scale 3, 4.25% band | $1,062,500 | $1,062,500 (unchanged)
Residential flat | Scale 1, "$6.72M–$20M" band, 3.75% | $3,000,000 (flat 15%) | $750,000
Original book figure used $3,000,000 (flat 15% Scale 1, the 2016–2023 rule); current law figure is $750,000 — a 75% reduction. The flat-15% Scale 1 was replaced by the same graduated table Scale 2 uses back in 2023; the 2026 amendment only adds new top bands above $100,000,000, irrelevant to a $20M deal.

Illustration B2 — Full AVD + SSD + BSD stack on a quick resale to a non-HKPR buyer Module 9, Ch.7 §7.6 — ss.24, 27

A residential flat is bought on 1 March 2018 and sold on 1 March 2019 (12 months + 1 day later) to a Mainland Chinese buyer who resides in HK ~183 days/year but holds no HK permanent ID — so he is not a HKPR for stamp duty purposes despite the residence. The stated price is $2,000,000 "subject to" an existing $5,000,000 mortgage, but market value at the (earlier, binding) contract date was $8,000,000. Because the transfer is at an undervalue and the debt is assumed, s.24 and s.27 deem the full $8,000,000 market value as the stampable amount for all three duties — that valuation mechanic is unaffected by any rate change.

Duty | Book figure | Current law (2026) | Why
AVD | $1,200,000 (flat 15%) | $300,000 (3.75% graduated) | Flat-15% Scale 1 superseded 2023
SSD (holding >12mo, ≤36mo tier) | $800,000 (10% tier) | $0 | SSD rate cut to 0% from 28 Feb 2024 (tier logic itself unchanged)
BSD | $1,200,000 (flat 15%) | $0 | BSD rate cut to 0% from 28 Feb 2024
Fixed duty on assignment | $100 | $100 (unchanged) | —
Total | $3,200,100 | $300,100 | Over 90% lower today
Residence alone (183 days/year) does not confer HKPR status — the buyer here is a non-HKPR by ID/citizenship regardless of how much time he spends in Hong Kong.

Illustration B3 — Gift between close relatives: Scale 2 applies regardless of the recipient's residency Module 9, Ch.7 §7.6 — s.27, s.29AJ

A father gifts a residential flat (market value $10,000,000) to his son, a Canadian citizen with no HK permanent ID. Nil consideration is disregarded as a voluntary disposition — full market value is used. Because the transfer is between close relatives (parent–child), Scale 2 applies regardless of the son's residency status, and both BSD and SSD are exempt on the same close-relative basis.

AVD, Scale 2, "$6.72M–$20M" band, 3.75% | $375,000
SSD | Exempt (close relative)
BSD | Exempt (close relative)
No correction needed — Scale 2 rates were not touched by the 2026 amendment, so the book's $375,000 figure is still correct today. Included deliberately as a contrast case: not every textbook figure in this chapter is wrong.

Illustration B4 — Hong Kong share transfer with failed group relief Module 9, Ch.7 §7.2 — s.45

A Hong Kong holding company transfers a 10% stake in an HKSE-listed (but overseas-incorporated) company to its 80%-owned subsidiary for $400,000, though market value is $500,000. Because the shares are HKSE-listed, they are Hong Kong stock for stamp duty purposes regardless of the issuer's place of incorporation. Group relief under s.45 fails — the parent only owns 80% of the subsidiary (below the 90% threshold), and an individual co-owner's personal stake cannot count toward that 90% test. The transfer at an undervalue is a voluntary disposition, so duty is charged on the higher $500,000 market value.

Stamp duty: $500,000 × 0.2% | $1,000
Plus: fixed duty on the instrument of transfer | $5
No correction needed — the 0.2% rate (0.1% buyer / 0.1% seller) matches current law exactly. Flag: elsewhere in the same textbook chapter, a rate of 0.26% is quoted — that was only correct for the temporary uplift period 1 Aug 2021–16 Nov 2023 and is now obsolete; 0.2% (as used in this illustration) is the figure to rely on.

Illustration B5 — Lease duty by term band (constructed — the textbook gives only the rate table, no worked figures) Module 9, Ch.7 §7.5, rate table only

A 5-year shop lease at $50,000/month rent, no premium. Term exceeds 3 years, so the 1% rate applies to average yearly rent.

Average yearly rent ($50,000 × 12) | $600,000
Lease duty (1% of average yearly rent) | $6,000
Rate bands (unchanged, current): 0.25% (≤1yr/undefined), 0.5% (1–3yr), 1% (>3yr) of average annual rent. If the lease is first executed as an "agreement for lease," that instrument bears this duty; a later formal lease on the same terms bears only a nominal $3 fixed duty.

Bottom line for this chapter
Every AVD/BSD/SSD figure quoted in older study material — this textbook included — should be treated as showing the mechanic (which band, which test, which exemption) correctly, but the rate itself needs a fresh check against the Stamp Duty page's corrected tables before use in any real computation.

sections.heading: 1. Overview
sections.text:
1. Overview

Stamp duty is a transaction tax, not an income tax — it is charged on specific categories of instruments (documents), not on profit. The three main heads for a Hong Kong company are: (1) Hong Kong stock transfers, (2) immovable property conveyances/agreements, and (3) leases. Hong Kong has no capital gains tax, estate duty, gift tax, or VAT — stamp duty is the main transaction-based levy filling that gap.

2026 amendment
Stamp Duty (Amendment) Ordinance 2026 (gazetted 29 May 2026, effective retrospectively from 26 February 2026) revised the residential/non-residential AVD rate bands — figures below reflect the post-26-Feb-2026 rates per PwC (reviewed 22 Jul 2026). Verify against the gazetted schedule before relying on a specific banding for a transaction.

sections.heading: 2. Share Transfers SDO s.19 (contract notes), First Schedule Head 2(1)
sections.text:
2. Share Transfers SDO s.19 (contract notes), First Schedule Head 2(1)

Ad valorem duty on transfer of Hong Kong stock | 0.2% of consideration or market value, whichever is higher (split 0.1% buyer / 0.1% seller, plus a small fixed contract note duty)
Contract notes are charged under s.19 (First Schedule Head 2(1)); s.21 prohibits stock being passed through without duty on the intervening step, s.22 covers consideration paid in stock/securities, and s.23 covers periodical-payment consideration. s.20 (formerly a related contract-note provision) has been repealed (33 of 2024 s.5) — do not cite it. Reliefs exist for stock borrowing/lending transactions (s.19(11) excludes a stock borrowing/return from the charge; s.19(12A) sets the borrower's return conditions; registration fee currently $270, must register within 30 days) and for intra-group ("associated companies") transfers under s.45 (§6 covers this in more detail) — see SOIPN 2.

New — RMB settlement of stamp duty on dual-counter stock
The Stamp Duty (Amendment) (No. 2) Ordinance 2026 (Bill passed 8 July 2026, gazetted 17 July 2026) lets stamp duty on a transfer of dual-counter stock traded at the RMB counter be calculated and paid in Renminbi, so an investor settles the trade and the duty in the same currency at the same counter. The 0.2% rate is unchanged — this is a settlement-currency and administration change only. Commencement is on a day to be appointed by the Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury, pending HKEX system readiness, so it is not yet in force.
Source: Government welcomes passage of Stamp Duty (Amendment) (No. 2) Bill 2026, 8 Jul 2026.

sections.heading: 2A. Conveyances & Agreements for Sale — Charging Mechanics SDO s.4, Part IIIA (ss.29A–29DV)
sections.text:
2A. Conveyances & Agreements for Sale — Charging Mechanics SDO s.4, Part IIIA (ss.29A–29DV)

The general charge is s.4 ("Charging of, liability for, and recovery of stamp duty") read together with the First Schedule, which sets out each "Head of charge" and its rate. For immovable property, Part IIIA (originally ss.29A–29I, now expanded to ss.29A–29DV across 7 Divisions covering interpretation, conveyances, agreements for sale, refunds, and the AVD scale machinery) supplies the detailed mechanics — including the provisional/formal agreement stamping rules illustrated in DIPN/SOIPN 1 below.

sections.heading: 3. Property Transfers — Ad Valorem Duty (AVD) First Schedule Head 1(1)/(1A); ss.29AI, 29AJ, 29AK
sections.text:
3. Property Transfers — Ad Valorem Duty (AVD) First Schedule Head 1(1)/(1A); ss.29AI, 29AJ, 29AK

Correction vs. common assumption
AVD Scale 1 is not a flat 15% on residential property. The flat-15% Scale 1 that applied from 5 Nov 2016 was superseded by a 2023 reform that made Scale 1 a graduated table matching Scale 2's bands (top rate 4.25%) — the only remaining difference is a new top band the Stamp Duty (Amendment) Ordinance 2026 added above ~$109.57M (see below). If your prior understanding was "flat 15% for non-HKPR/company buyers," that is now out of date except at the very top of the market.

AVD has three rate tables, all graduated (not flat), all sharing the same lower bands:

Scale | Applies to | Top rate
Scale 1 (First Schedule Head 1(1)/(1A), default table — s.29AI) | Residential property, buyer not qualifying for the Scale 2 concession (incl. companies, non-HKPRs) | 4.25% up to $100,000,000; a transitional band charging $4,250,000 + 30% of the excess from $100,000,000–$109,574,470; 6.5% flat above $109,574,470 (new top bands added by the Stamp Duty (Amendment) Ordinance 2026, s.14)
Scale 2 (s.29AJ concession) | Hong Kong Permanent Resident buying their sole residential property, or a qualifying closely-related-person reassignment | 4.25% — unchanged by the 2026 amendment
Scale 3 (s.29AI(b) default for non-residential; also s.29AK for a car park bought alongside a Scale-2 residential purchase) | Non-residential property | 4.25% — unchanged by the 2026 amendment
All three scales start at a flat $100 for low-value transactions and climb through the same intermediate bands (1.5% / 2.25% / 3% / 3.75%) before reaching their respective top rate. Duty is charged on consideration or market value, whichever is higher. "Closely related persons" (for Scale 2 eligibility and for the close-relative exemptions on BSD/SSD) is defined at s.29AD — broadly parent/spouse/child/sibling. Reliefs: replacement of a sole residential property (refund window), exchange/partition ("equality money" only), court orders, mortgagee sales, associated-company transfers under s.45 (§6) — see SOIPN 8, though note SOIPN 8 (Nov 2018) predates the 2023 Scale 1 reform and the 2026 amendment.

sections.heading: 4. Buyer's Stamp Duty (BSD) & Special Stamp Duty (SSD) First Schedule Head 1(1AAB)/(1C) [BSD]; Head 1(1AA) [SSD]
sections.text:
4. Buyer's Stamp Duty (BSD) & Special Stamp Duty (SSD) First Schedule Head 1(1AAB)/(1C) [BSD]; Head 1(1AA) [SSD]

Correction vs. common assumption
There is no "Part IIIAA" or "Part IVA" for BSD/SSD in the current ordinance structure — Part IVA is actually the unrelated Unit Trusts/Open-ended Fund Companies part (ss.37A–41). BSD and SSD are instead defined as separate Heads of charge in the First Schedule, cross-referenced from Part IIIA.

Duty | Applies to | Rate
Buyer's Stamp Duty (BSD) — Head 1(1AAB) conveyance / Head 1(1C) agreement for sale | Residential property acquired by a non-HKPR (companies are always treated as non-HKPR); subject to ss.29C, 29CB, 29CC | 0% — reduced from 15% in stages (L.N. 148 of 2023; 3 of 2024 s.14; L.N. 26 of 2024; 8 of 2024 s.6)
Special Stamp Duty (SSD) — Head 1(1AA), Part 4 (property disposed of on/after 28 Feb 2024) | Residential property resold within the holding-period window; subject to ss.29D, 29DA | 0% — reduced from up to 20% (L.N. 26 of 2024; 8 of 2024 s.6)
Note
BSD and SSD remain fully defined in the First Schedule with their mechanics unchanged (liable party, timing, holding-period tiers for SSD) — only the rate was reduced to 0% as a market-support measure from 28 February 2024. Head 1(1AA)'s historical Parts 1–3 are preserved verbatim for legacy holding-period windows still being assessed (20 Nov 2010–27 Oct 2012 at 15/10/5%; 27 Oct 2012–25 Oct 2023 and 25 Oct 2023–28 Feb 2024, both at 20/15/10%) — relevant only if assessing an old disposal that hasn't yet been finalised. Both duties could in principle be reactivated at a non-zero rate by future amendment — see SOIPN 5 (SSD) and SOIPN 7 (BSD), noting both predate the current 0% rate and Head numbering nuances above.

sections.heading: 5. Leases SDO Head 1(2)
sections.text:
5. Leases SDO Head 1(2)

Lease term | Duty
Not defined or uncertain / ≤ 1 year | 0.25% of average annual rent (plus any premium, taxed as a sale)
Between 1 and 3 years | 0.5% of average annual rent
Over 3 years | 1% of average annual rent
A premium paid for a lease is chargeable as if it were a sale consideration, separately from the rent-based duty above — see the interaction with Property Tax/Profits Tax premium-spreading rules on the Property Tax page.

sections.heading: 6. Reliefs SDO s.45; s.29AD
sections.text:
6. Reliefs SDO s.45; s.29AD

Associated bodies corporate relief (s.45) — relieves a conveyance from one associated body corporate to another from AVD, SSD, BSD, and HK-stock contract-note duty (it spans Heads 1(1), 1(1AA), 1(1AAB), 2(1) and 2(3)), where a ≥90% common-ownership test is met. A clawback applies under s.45(5A) if the ≥90% association ceases within 2 years of the relieved conveyance.

Bill before LegCo — do not apply yet · 法案仍待立法會審議
The Stamp Duty (Amendment) (No. 3) Bill 2026 (announced 29 Sep 2026, gazetted 2 Oct 2026, first reading 14 Oct 2026) would relax this relief: the association test would fall from 90% to 75%, association could be established through direct or indirect beneficial interests or voting rights rather than issued share capital alone, and the relief would extend to entities with no share capital — limited liability partnerships and companies limited by guarantee. The Bill proposes to apply to instruments executed on or after 25 February 2026.
The enacted test remains ≥90%. Quote 90% for any instrument being stamped now. The retrospective date is the part to watch: if enacted as drafted, transfers already executed since 25 Feb 2026 that met 75% but not 90% would become relievable. See IRD What's New §2.

Closely related persons (s.29AD) — defines the parent/spouse/child/sibling relationships that qualify for the Scale 2 AVD concession (§3) and are also picked up by the close-relative exemption notes applied to the BSD/SSD sub-heads (co-purchasers who are closely related are treated as "the same person" for ownership-counting purposes).

Proposed — newborn-family stamp duty concession, 2026 Policy Address (16 Sep 2026)
A family with a child born in Hong Kong on or after 16 September 2026, where at least one parent is a Hong Kong permanent resident, would get a stamp duty waiver capped at HKD 20,000 on a residential property purchased in the window running from one year before to two years after the birth. To take effect on enactment of the amendment ordinance — not yet law, so do not apply it to a current transaction. Note it is a capped waiver, not a rate change: on any purchase where AVD exceeds HKD 20,000 the relief is a flat HKD 20,000.
Source: IRD — 2026 Policy Address, Tax-related Policy Measures (on Individuals), published 16 Sep 2026.

sections.heading: 7. Partnership Admission & Retirement
sections.text:
7. Partnership Admission & Retirement

Where a partner is admitted to, or retires from, a partnership that holds Hong Kong stock or immovable property, the change in each partner's proportionate interest can itself be a chargeable "sale and purchase" of the underlying property/stock for stamp duty purposes (the incoming/continuing partners are treated as acquiring the outgoing/diluted partners' fractional interest). This is assessed using the same AVD/stock-transfer rules above, applied to the fractional interest that changes hands — always check partnership deeds and capital-account movements for a hidden stamp duty trigger whenever partners change.

sections.heading: 8. Illustrations
sections.text:
8. Illustrations

10 worked illustrations back this page — SOIPN-sourced (agreement timing, AVD/SSD/BSD mechanics) plus Module 9 textbook examples. This is the topic needing the most correction: both source books predate the 2023 AVD Scale 1 reform and/or the 2024 BSD/SSD rate cut, so most headline rates in the older material are wrong — corrected figures are shown alongside the originals throughout.

Illustration — Current graduated Scale 1 vs. Scale 2 Corrected from Cap. 117 First Schedule, post-2026 amendment

A $13,000,000 residential property bought by a non-HKPR (or corporate) buyer with no Scale 2 concession available: Scale 1 is graduated exactly like Scale 2 at this value band (3.75%), giving $487,500 — not a flat-15% $1,950,000 as older material describes. The two scales only diverge for a single residential property with consideration above $100,000,000, where the 2026 amendment gives Scale 1 a new 6.5% flat top band that Scale 2 does not get.

sections.heading: 1. The question type, and what it is really testing
sections.text:
1. The question type, and what it is really testing

You are given a profits tax or personal assessment computation prepared by a bookkeeper, a client, or "the previous accountant". It is internally consistent — the arithmetic adds up — but several treatments are wrong. A set of numbered notes gives you the facts. You must produce the corrected computation.

It is not a computation question. It is a review question.
A blank-page computation tests whether you can build a format. This tests something harder: whether you can look at a plausible-looking answer and find what is wrong with it. That is what tax work actually is — almost nothing arrives as a blank page, and the figure in front of you always looks reasonable.

Three consequences follow, and they drive everything on this page:

Because… | …therefore
The given computation looks plausible | You cannot spot errors by eye. You must work note by note, in order, and decide an adjustment for each — including "no adjustment".
Some notes are distractors | A note that needs no adjustment still earns a mark if you say so and why. Silence earns nothing and looks like an oversight.
Errors can offset each other | The bottom line can look close to right while several treatments are wrong. Never sanity-check by the final figure. Illustration A below is built to show this happening.

sections.heading: 2. The six-step method
sections.text:
2. The six-step method

Step | Do this
1 | Do not edit the given computation. Start a clean one from profit per the accounts (or, for personal assessment, from each source's own correct figure). Editing someone else's layout inherits their structural errors.
2 | Rule up a note-by-note working schedule before touching the computation: note number, treatment, adjustment, amount. Every note gets a row, including the ones needing no adjustment.
3 | Decide each note in isolation. Is the item chargeable / deductible? Was it already in the accounts? Those two questions together give the adjustment — an item can be deductible and still need no adjustment because it was already correctly charged.
4 | Build the revised computation in the standard format, feeding in the schedule's figures. Keep the donation add-back-then-relieve round trip, and keep depreciation allowances before the donation.
5 | Reconcile from the given figure to yours, line by line. This is the step candidates skip, and it is where the marks and the self-check both live.
6 | Reconcile the tax too, not just the profit. Rate errors, set-offs and reliefs live below the net assessable profit line and are easy to leave uncorrected.
Why step 5 is worth the minutes it costs
The reconciliation is self-marking. If it does not arrive at your revised figure, you have made an error somewhere and you still have time to find it. If it does arrive, you have proved your answer and shown the examiner your reasoning in one compact table. It is the cheapest insurance in the paper.

sections.heading: 3. Illustration A — Profits tax: the question
sections.text:
3. Illustration A — Profits tax: the question

Question

Kingsway Trading Limited carries on a trading business in Hong Kong and prepares accounts to 31 December. The profit per the audited accounts for the year ended 31 December 2026 was $3,200,000.

The company's bookkeeper prepared the following profits tax computation for the year of assessment 2026/27.

REQUIRED: Using the notes below, prepare a revised profits tax computation for the year of assessment 2026/27, and reconcile the revised net assessable profit to the figure computed by the bookkeeper.

✗ As prepared by the bookkeeper — Kingsway Trading Limited, YA 2026/27

Profit per accounts | 3,200,000
Add: depreciation | 420,000
| 3,620,000
Less: dividend income | (150,000)
Less: charitable donations | (250,000)
Less: depreciation allowances | (380,000)
Assessable profit | 2,840,000
Less: loss brought forward | (240,000)
Net assessable profit | 2,600,000
Profits tax at 8.25% | 214,500
Notes

Note | Information
1 | The profit is after charging depreciation of $420,000. Depreciation allowances properly computed under Part 6 of the IRO for the year amount to $505,000.
2 | Turnover includes $680,000 of profit on a contract negotiated and concluded entirely in Singapore by the company's Singapore branch. The Assessor has accepted this profit as offshore.
3 | Other income includes dividends of $150,000 from a company listed in Hong Kong.
4 | Other income includes $90,000 of interest on a Hong Kong dollar deposit with a licensed bank in Hong Kong.
5 | Administrative expenses include a fine of $35,000 imposed for a breach of licensing conditions.
6 | Administrative expenses include an increase in the general provision for doubtful debts of $60,000, and a specific bad debt written off of $45,000 in respect of a trade debtor who has been wound up.
7 | Charitable donations of $250,000 to approved charitable institutions were charged in arriving at the profit per the accounts.
8 | Finance costs include $120,000 of interest paid to a director on a loan to the company. The director is not chargeable to profits tax on that interest, so the conditions in s.16(2) are not satisfied.
9 | The company owns an office in Hong Kong which it lets to a tenant. The rental income is included in the profit per the accounts. Property tax of $48,000 for the year was paid and charged in the accounts.
10 | The agreed loss brought forward from the year of assessment 2025/26 is $240,000. Kingsway Trading Limited is the only Hong Kong entity in its group and is entitled to the two-tiered profits tax rates.

sections.heading: 4. Illustration A — note-by-note working
sections.text:
4. Illustration A — note-by-note working

Build this before the computation. Two questions per note: is the item chargeable or deductible? and how was it treated in the accounts? The adjustment is the difference between the two.

Note | Correct treatment | Adjustment | $
1
Accounting depreciation is not deductible; statutory depreciation allowances replace it. Add back $420,000; deduct the correct allowances of $505,000, not the bookkeeper's $380,000.
Add / Deduct | 420,000
(505,000)
2
Offshore profit is outside the s.14 charge. The bookkeeper missed it entirely — the largest single error.
Deduct | (680,000)
3
Dividends from a Hong Kong company are not chargeable (s.26). Correctly deducted by the bookkeeper.
Deduct | (150,000)
4
Interest on a HKD deposit with a licensed bank is exempt under the Exemption from Profits Tax (Interest Income) Order. Missed.
Deduct | (90,000)
5
A fine is not incurred in the production of profits and is not deductible. Missed.
Add back | 35,000
6
General provision is not deductible (s.16(1)(d)) — add back $60,000. The specific write-off of a debt of a wound-up debtor is deductible and was correctly charged — no adjustment.
Add back
no adj. | 60,000
—
7
Add back the $250,000 charged, then relieve it under s.16D restricted to 35% of the profit after depreciation allowances. The bookkeeper simply deducted it a second time.
Add back
then relieve | 250,000
(250,000)
8
Interest failing s.16(2) is not deductible. Missed.
Add back | 120,000
9
Two separate points. Property tax charged in the accounts is not deductible — add back $48,000. Separately, it is set off against the profits tax payable under s.25, below the tax line. Both were missed.
Add back
and set off | 48,000
(48,000)
10
Loss brought forward is set off after the donation. The two-tiered rates apply, so 8.25% on the first $2,000,000 and 16.5% on the remainder — not 8.25% on the whole.
Deduct / rate | (240,000)
Note 6 is the distractor, and Note 9 is the double-barrelled one
Note 6 gives you two figures where only one moves — say explicitly that the specific write-off needs no adjustment. Note 9 carries two marks in two different places: an add-back in the computation and a set-off under the tax. Answering only the add-back loses half of it.

sections.heading: 6. Illustration A — the reconciliation
sections.text:
6. Illustration A — the reconciliation

This is the part the question specifically asked for, and the part most candidates omit. It starts at the bookkeeper's figure and arrives at yours.

Reconciliation of net assessable profit

Net assessable profit per the bookkeeper's computation | 2,600,000
Offshore profit not excluded (2) | (680,000)
Exempt bank deposit interest not excluded (4) | (90,000)
Fine not added back (5) | 35,000
General provision not added back (6) | 60,000
Interest failing s.16(2) not added back (8) | 120,000
Property tax charged not added back (9) | 48,000
Donations deducted without being added back (7) | 250,000
Additional depreciation allowances ($505,000 − $380,000) (1) | (125,000)
Revised net assessable profit | 2,218,000
Reconciliation of tax

Profits tax per the bookkeeper's computation | 214,500
Effect of the reduction in net assessable profit, at the rates properly applicable | (13,530)
Revised profits tax | 200,970
Property tax set off under s.25, omitted (9) | (48,000)
Revised profits tax liability | 152,970
The point of this illustration: two errors pulling in opposite directions
The bookkeeper overstated the profit by $382,000 ($2,600,000 against $2,218,000) — which pushes tax up. But they also applied 8.25% to the whole profit instead of tiering at $2,000,000 — which pulls tax down. On the correct profit of $2,218,000, a flat 8.25% would have given $182,985 against the true $200,970, understating tax by $17,985.

The two errors partly cancel. That is exactly why the bottom line tells you nothing about whether a computation is right, and why the note-by-note schedule is not optional.

sections.heading: 7. Illustration B — Personal assessment
sections.text:
7. Illustration B — Personal assessment

Question

Mr and Mrs Lam have elected jointly for personal assessment for the year of assessment 2026/27. Mr Lam's net assessable income from employment is $600,000. Mrs Lam runs a sole proprietorship whose assessable profit is $180,000, and owns a Hong Kong flat let at $30,000 a month throughout the year. She paid rates of $12,000 and mortgage interest of $200,000 on that flat. Neither has any other income, deduction or dependant.

A friend prepared the computation below. REQUIRED: prepare the revised computation, show the apportionment between the spouses, and reconcile to the friend's figure.

✗ As prepared by a friend — Mr & Mrs Lam, YA 2026/27

Mr Lam — salary | 600,000
Mrs Lam — business profit | 180,000
Mrs Lam — rental income ($30,000 × 12) | 360,000
Total income | 1,140,000
Less: mortgage interest | (200,000)
Less: rates paid | (12,000)
Reduced total income | 928,000
Less: basic allowance D26 exam (YA 2025/26): $132,000 | (145,000)
Net chargeable income | 783,000
Tax at progressive rates | 115,110
Error | What is wrong
1 | Property brought in at gross rent. Personal assessment takes the net assessable value: rates are deducted inside the property computation, and the 20% statutory allowance is then taken. Deducting rates as a separate line below total income skips the 20% entirely.
2 | A basic allowance claimed where a jointly electing married couple is entitled to the married person's allowance of $290,000.
3 | No standard-rate comparison. Tax under personal assessment is the lower of progressive rates on net chargeable income and the standard rate on reduced total income.
4 | No apportionment between the spouses. On a joint election each receives their own assessment for their share.
✓ Mr & Mrs Lam — Personal Assessment Computation, YA 2026/27

Mr Lam — net assessable income | 600,000
Mrs Lam — net assessable profit | 180,000
Mrs Lam — net assessable value: |
Rent ($30,000 × 12) | 360,000
Less: rates paid by owner | (12,000)
Less: 20% statutory allowance ($348,000 × 20%) | (69,600)
Net assessable value | 278,400
Total income | 1,058,400
Less: interest to produce property income
$200,000, within the $278,400 NAV cap, so allowed in full | (200,000)
Reduced total income | 858,400
Less: married person's allowance D26 exam (YA 2025/26): $264,000 | (290,000)
Net chargeable income | 568,400
(b) Progressive: 1,000 + 3,000 + 5,000 + 7,000 + ($368,400 × 17%) | 78,628
(c) Standard rate: $858,400 × 15% | 128,760
Tax payable — the lower | 78,628
Apportionment — in the ratio of each spouse's reduced total income

Mr Lam: $78,628 × 600,000 / 858,400 | 54,959
Mrs Lam: $78,628 × 258,400 / 858,400
her share is $180,000 + $278,400 − $200,000 = $258,400 | 23,669
Total | 78,628
Reconciliation

Net chargeable income per the friend's computation | 783,000
Property taken at gross rent instead of net assessable value (1) | (81,600)
Rates wrongly deducted a second time, below total income (1) | 12,000
Married person's allowance in place of basic allowance (2) | (145,000)
Revised net chargeable income | 568,400
Tax: $115,110 per the friend, against $78,628 revised — overstated by $36,482.
Note how the rates error works
The friend deducted rates of $12,000 — and got a worse answer than ignoring them, because deducting them in the wrong place forfeited the 20% statutory allowance of $69,600. Doing something reasonable in the wrong line of a computation is not half right; it is wrong, and here it is wrong by $57,600.

sections.heading: 8. The errors examiners plant, in rough order of frequency
sections.text:
8. The errors examiners plant, in rough order of frequency

Planted error | How to catch it
Offshore profit left in | Any note mentioning a place outside Hong Kong is a source question. Decide it explicitly.
Donation deducted without being added back | If it was charged in the accounts it must go back in first, or the 35% cap cannot be computed.
Donation cap on the wrong base | 35% of profit after depreciation allowances, not of profit per accounts.
Accounting depreciation left in, or DA figure wrong | Add back the accounts figure and deduct the Part 6 figure. They are never the same number.
General vs specific provision | General is added back, specific is not. The question will give you both.
Flat rate instead of two-tiered | Check the rate line every time, and check whether the entity is the nominated group member.
Property tax: add-back or set-off missed | It is two adjustments in two places, from one note.
Interest failing s.16(2) | Any interest paid to a director, shareholder or associate is a s.16(2) question.
Exempt bank interest left in | HKD deposit interest from a licensed bank is exempt.
Loss brought forward in the wrong place | After the donation, not before.
Personal assessment: gross rent not NAV | Property always enters at net assessable value.
Personal assessment: standard-rate comparison omitted | And when performed, on reduced total income — before allowances.
Wrong allowance for a married couple | Joint election takes the married person's allowance.

sections.heading: 9. Marking technique
sections.text:
9. Marking technique

Earns marks

- A note number against every line of the revised computation — the marker can follow your reasoning without hunting.

- Saying "no adjustment" for a distractor, with one clause of reason.

- Showing the cap working even when the cap does not bite: "lower of $250,000 and 35% × $2,708,000 = $947,800".

- The reconciliation, even a rough one.

- Correct subtotal names: assessable profit, net assessable profit, reduced total income, net chargeable income.

- A one-line heading: taxpayer, tax, year of assessment, basis period.

Loses marks

- Editing the given computation instead of starting clean — you inherit its structure and its errors.

- Silence on a distractor note. Indistinguishable from missing it.

- Netting several adjustments into one unexplained figure.

- Stopping at net assessable profit when the question asked for the liability — rate, set-offs and reliefs are marks.

- Checking your work against the bottom line. Offsetting errors make a wrong answer look right.

- Correct treatment written in the wrong line, as with the rates in Illustration B.

If you run short of time
Produce the note-by-note schedule and stop. It carries most of the technical marks, since it shows the decision on every item. A beautifully formatted computation with three treatments wrong scores less than a rough schedule that gets all ten notes right.

sections.heading: 10. Source documents
sections.text:
10. Source documents

- Both illustrations are original — written for this Hub in the standard exam format, not reproduced from any paper or textbook24 Sep 2026

- Formats follow Hong Kong Taxation and Tax Planning (22nd ed.) Ch.20 and IRD's Personal Assessment guide — see Computation Formats—

- Rates and allowances: IRD Allowances, Deductions and Tax Rate Table (pam61e), YA 2026/27read 24 Sep 2026

Every figure was computed, not estimated
Both illustrations were built arithmetically so that the reconciliations close exactly: Illustration A's eight adjustments take $2,600,000 to $2,218,000, and Illustration B's three take $783,000 to $568,400. If you work them yourself and land elsewhere, the error is worth finding — that is the point of the exercise.

transactions.item: Trading receipts from sale of goods/services in the ordinary course of a HK business
transactions.note: Core charge — profits arising in/derived from Hong Kong.

transactions.item: Royalty for use, or right to use, IP (patent/trade mark/copyright/secret process) in Hong Kong
transactions.note: Deemed HK-source trading receipt.

transactions.item: Royalty for use of IP outside Hong Kong, where payer claimed a HK deduction for the payment
transactions.note: Closes the gap where the payer got a deduction but the recipient claimed offshore.

transactions.item: Grant or subsidy connected with carrying on the HK trade (not towards capital expenditure)
Hire/rental charges for use of movable property in Hong Kong
transactions.note: E.g. equipment leasing income sourced to HK use.

transactions.item: Interest derived from Hong Kong received by a corporation
transactions.note: Corporations are taxed on HK-source interest regardless of trade nexus.

transactions.item: Lease premium / key money received by a person carrying on a property-dealing or letting business
transactions.note: Spread over the lease term as a revenue receipt; interacts with Property Tax — see DIPN 4 illustration.

transactions.item: Profit on sale of a capital asset (e.g. disposal of a long-term investment property, fixed asset)
transactions.note: Expressly excluded from the charge — but badges-of-trade analysis matters; a frequent trader may find the same asset treated as trading stock instead.

transactions.item: Dividend income received from another company (not a share dealer)
transactions.section: General principle — not a s.15 deemed receipt
transactions.note: Hong Kong does not tax dividends as such; if the recipient is a securities dealer, gains on the underlying shares may instead be trading receipts.

transactions.item: Interest on a Hong Kong bank deposit, earned by a person other than a financial institution
transactions.section: Exemption from Profits Tax (Interest Income) Order 1998 / DIPN 34
transactions.note: Exemption is lost (no partial exemption) if the deposit secures a loan whose interest is tax-deductible.

transactions.item: Compensation received for cancellation of a trading contract (revenue in nature)
transactions.section: Case law — follows the character of the right/profit given up
transactions.note: Compensation for loss of a capital asset/structure is instead capital and non-taxable — always check what right was actually surrendered.

transactions.item: Specified foreign-sourced income (interest/dividends/IP income/disposal gains) failing FSIE conditions
transactions.note: Deemed HK-sourced unless economic substance / nexus / participation conditions are met.

transactions.item: Specified foreign-sourced income meeting the FSIE economic substance/nexus/participation conditions
Interest on money borrowed for producing chargeable profits (+ related legal/procuration fees, stamp duty)
transactions.note: Subject to anti-avoidance conditions in s.16(2)–(2C) — see DIPN 13A (e.g. tax-free secured deposits restrict the deduction).

transactions.item: Rent paid for business premises
transactions.note: Capped at assessable value if paid to a related party (spouse/partner).

transactions.item: Bad debts written off / doubtful debts estimated bad (previously included as a trading receipt)
Foreign tax paid, where no DTA credit relief is available under s.50
transactions.note: If a DTA exists and s.50 credit relief applies, the deduction is denied by s.16(2J) instead — see DIPN 28.

transactions.item: R&D expenditure (qualifying Type B)
transactions.note: Enhanced deduction available for qualifying categories.

transactions.item: Capital expenditure on patent/know-how rights
transactions.note: 100% one-off, no spreading — see DIPN 49.

transactions.item: Capital expenditure on prescribed fixed assets (manufacturing plant, computer hardware/software)
transactions.note: 100% one-off; excludes leased assets — see DIPN 5.

transactions.item: Management fee paid to a related "Type II" service company, up to cost + 12.5% mark-up
transactions.note: Excess above cost+12.5% is added back — see DIPN 24 illustration.

transactions.item: Domestic or private expenses (incl. home-to-office travel)
Capital expenditure, or any loss/withdrawal of capital
transactions.note: Distinguish from revenue repairs/outgoings.

transactions.item: Cost of improvements (vs. repairs)
Sums recoverable under insurance or an indemnity contract
Rent/expenses for premises not used to produce chargeable profits
Profits tax / property tax paid under the IRO itself (salaries tax on employees excepted)
transactions.note: Salaries tax paid on employees' remuneration IS deductible — the exception, not the rule.

transactions.item: Employer retirement-scheme (ORSO/MPF) contributions exceeding 15% of the employee's emoluments
transactions.note: Only the excess above 15% is disallowed.

transactions.item: Accounting depreciation charged in the financial statements
transactions.note: Always add back — replace with the statutory allowance instead (see Depreciation & Allowances page).

transactions.item: Prepaid expense required by accounting standards to be amortised over future periods
transactions.note: Only the amortised portion for the current period is deductible — no full deduction on a cash-prepayment basis.

transactions.item: Rent receivable for letting land/buildings in Hong Kong (whether or not actually received)
Lease premium / non-returnable deposit / key money
transactions.note: Deemed payable in equal monthly instalments, capped at 3 years even if the lease term is longer.

transactions.item: Owner-occupied property (no rent receivable)
transactions.note: No assessable value arises.

transactions.item: Rent proved to have become irrecoverable during the year
transactions.note: Recovered amounts are brought back into charge in the year recovered.

transactions.item: Rates paid by the owner + flat 20% repairs/outgoings allowance
transactions.note: Flat statutory allowance — not based on actual repair spend.

transactions.item: Property tax paid by a corporation on business-use property, set off against profits tax
transactions.note: Or apply for upfront exemption under s.5(2)(a) instead of paying and reclaiming.

transactions.item: Salary, wages, bonus, commission for services rendered in Hong Kong
Director's fee from a Hong Kong resident company
transactions.note: Sourced to the company's residence, regardless of where the director actually works.

transactions.item: Holiday journey benefit provided by employer (package tour, flights)
transactions.note: Taxed at employer's actual cost even if not convertible into cash; apportioned for business-cum-holiday trips.

transactions.item: Share option gain at exercise / share award vesting benefit (Hong Kong employment portion)
transactions.note: Apportioned by vesting days spent in Hong Kong if the employment straddles jurisdictions.

transactions.item: Employer settling an employee's personal debt/liability (fringe benefit passing the s.9(1)(a)(iv) liability test)
Income from services rendered wholly outside Hong Kong (non-Government employee, ≤60 HK visit days)
transactions.note: Exceeding 60 days brings those visit-day services back into charge.

transactions.item: Genuine reimbursement of business expenses actually incurred on the employer's behalf
transactions.note: Not "income from employment" if there is no personal benefit to the employee.

transactions.item: Severance / long service payment, to the extent of the statutory entitlement under the Employment Ordinance
transactions.section: General principle — statutory entitlement is capital in nature
transactions.note: Any excess paid above the statutory entitlement is more likely taxable as employment income/gratuity.

transactions.item: Genuine compensation for loss of office (not a reward for past/future services)
transactions.note: Must be genuinely for loss of office, not disguised salary/bonus/gratuity — fact-sensitive.

transactions.item: Cost of travel between home and workplace
transactions.note: Domestic/private expense.

transactions.item: Self-education expenses
transactions.note: Capped at HKD 100,000.

transactions.item: Mandatory MPF contributions
transactions.note: Capped at HKD 18,000.

transactions.item: Home loan interest on the principal place of residence
transactions.note: Capped at HKD 100,000 (120,000 with a qualifying child); apportioned by ownership share for joint owners/tenants in common.

transactions.item: Elderly residential care home expenses for a parent/grandparent
transactions.note: Capped at HKD 110,000/parent; mutually exclusive with the dependent parent/grandparent allowance.

transactions.item: Approved charitable donations
transactions.note: Min. HKD 100 aggregate; capped at 35% of reduced assessable income.

transactions.item: VHIS health insurance premiums (Certified Plan)
transactions.note: Capped at HKD 8,000 per insured person — no carry-forward of excess.

transactions.item: Qualifying annuity premiums (QDAP) + MPF voluntary contributions (TVC)
transactions.note: Combined cap HKD 60,000/year; TVC deducted first.

transactions.item: Donations/deductions claimed above their statutory cap
transactions.note: Excess simply lapses — unlike profits tax losses, there is no carry-forward.

transactions.item: Transfer of Hong Kong stock (shares in a HK company)
transactions.note: 0.2% of consideration/market value (whichever higher), split buyer/seller.

transactions.item: Conveyance/agreement for sale of residential property by a non-HKPR or a company
transactions.note: Graduated, NOT a flat rate — top rate 4.25% up to $100M, then a 2026-amendment transitional band, then flat 6.5% above ~$109.57M.

transactions.item: Conveyance/agreement for sale of residential property by an HKPR buying their only residential property
transactions.note: Graduated rate from $100 up to 4.25% top — unaffected by the 2026 amendment.

transactions.item: Conveyance/agreement for sale of non-residential property
transactions.note: Graduated up to 4.25% top — unaffected by the 2026 amendment.

transactions.item: Lease of land/buildings in Hong Kong
transactions.note: 0.25%/0.5%/1% of average annual rent depending on lease term; premiums taxed separately as a sale.

transactions.item: Residential property acquisition by a non-HKPR (Buyer's Stamp Duty)
transactions.statusLabel: No duty (relief or a 0% rate — read the note; the charging mechanism may still exist)
transactions.note: Mechanism still in force but rate reduced to 0% effective 28 Feb 2024.

transactions.item: Short-term resale of residential property within the holding-period window (Special Stamp Duty)
transactions.statusLabel: No duty (relief or a 0% rate — read the note; the charging mechanism may still exist)
transactions.note: Mechanism still in force but rate reduced to 0% effective 28 Feb 2024.

transactions.item: Transfer between close relatives / associated bodies corporate meeting the relief conditions
transactions.statusLabel: No duty (relief or a 0% rate — read the note; the charging mechanism may still exist)
transactions.section: SDO s.45 (associated bodies corporate); s.29AD (closely related persons)
transactions.note: 90% common-ownership test for s.45, with a 2-year clawback — conditions must be strictly met.

transactions.item: Stock borrowing/lending transaction meeting the relief conditions
transactions.statusLabel: No duty (relief or a 0% rate — read the note; the charging mechanism may still exist)
transactions.note: Registration fee still applies; must register within 30 days.

transactions.item: Change in a partner's fractional interest in a partnership holding HK stock/property (admission/retirement)
transactions.section: General AVD/stock-transfer rules applied to the fractional interest
transactions.note: Easy to miss — check partnership capital account movements whenever partners change.

transactions.item: Industrial building/structure — initial allowance
transactions.note: 20% of cost, year of first use.

transactions.item: Industrial or commercial building/structure — annual allowance
transactions.note: 4% straight-line on cost.

transactions.item: Plant & machinery — initial allowance (pooled)
transactions.note: 60% of cost, given once on acquisition.

transactions.item: Plant & machinery — annual allowance (pooled, reducing balance)
transactions.note: 10% / 20% / 30% by asset class on the pool's reducing value.

transactions.item: Balancing charge on disposal (proceeds exceed reducing value)
transactions.note: Capped at total allowances previously granted for that asset — never more than was originally allowed.

transactions.item: Prescribed fixed assets (manufacturing plant, standalone computer hardware/software)
transactions.note: 100% one-off in year of payment; excludes leased assets.

transactions.item: Environmental protection machinery / vehicles / installations (from 2018/19)
transactions.note: 100% one-off (previously 5-year spread pre-2018/19).

transactions.item: Refurbishment/renovation of a non-domestic building
transactions.note: 5 equal annual instalments (20%/year).

transactions.item: Patent rights / know-how purchase
transactions.note: 100% one-off, no spreading.

transactions.item: Specified IP Rights (copyright, registered trade mark/design, plant variety rights)
transactions.note: 5 equal annual instalments, or shorter to match remaining legal protection.

dipn.summary: ss.16E/16EA–16EC patent/know-how and Specified IP Rights deduction timing, with worked examples.

dipn.title: Taxation of Specified Alternative Bond Schemes
dipn.summary: 2013 amendment giving Sharia-compliant instruments (sukuk — lease/profit-sharing/purchase-sale/agency structures) debt-like tax treatment, with qualifying conditions and disqualification triggers.

dipn.title: Profits Tax Exemption for Offshore Private Equity Funds
dipn.summary: Extends the offshore fund exemption to private equity structures — fund vehicles, 'specified person' regime, excepted private companies, SPVs, anti-abuse deemed-profits rules. Restricted in scope for YAs from 1 April 2019 (see DIPN 61).

dipn.title: Taxation of Corporate Treasury Activity
dipn.summary: Interest deduction conditions for intra-group financing and the Qualifying Corporate Treasury Centre (QCTC) concession, with interest-diversion/loss-shifting anti-avoidance rules — relevant to FSIE-exposed treasury entities (see Profits Tax page §6).

dipn.title: Tax Treatment of Regulatory Capital Securities
dipn.summary: Treats AT1/T2 capital instruments and LAC debt (Basel III/FIRO) as debt for tax purposes under ss.17A–17G, including arm's-length rules for non-arm's-length RCS transactions.

dipn.title: Taxation of Aircraft Leasing Activities
dipn.summary: Qualifying aircraft lessor/leasing manager profits tax concession (20% tax base) under the 2017 Amendment Ordinance — qualifying activity/lease definitions, substantial business presence requirements.

dipn.title: Deduction for Research and Development Expenditure
dipn.summary: s.16B enhanced R&D deduction — Type A/B expenditure, 300%/200% deduction tiers, exclusions, sale-of-rights treatment — 6 worked examples. Closely related to §4 of the Profits Tax page.

dipn.title: Concessionary Deductions: Health Insurance Premiums (ss.26H–26M)
dipn.summary: VHIS Certified Plan premium deduction, HKD 8,000/insured-person cap, with worked example.

dipn.title: Concessionary Deductions: Annuity Premiums and MPF Voluntary Contributions (ss.26N–26U)
dipn.summary: QDAP and TVC combined HKD 60,000 cap and claim-sharing rules.

dipn.title: Transfer Pricing Documentation and Country-by-Country Reports
dipn.summary: Pending detailed review — master file/local file/CbC reporting obligations under Part 9A.

dipn.title: Transfer Pricing between Associated Persons
dipn.summary: Pending detailed review — the general transfer pricing rule and arm's length principle under Part 8AA.

dipn.title: Attribution of Profits to Permanent Establishments in Hong Kong
dipn.summary: Pending detailed review — the authorised OECD approach to attributing profits to a HK PE.

dipn.title: Profits Tax Exemption for Funds
dipn.summary: Pending detailed review — the unified fund exemption regime (successor/complement to DIPN 43/51).

dipn.title: Taxation of Ship Leasing Activities
dipn.summary: Parallel regime to DIPN 54 for ship leasing — profits tax concessions for qualifying ship lessors/leasing managers, operating-vs-funding-lease tax base rules, substantial activities and anti-avoidance (main purpose, interest flow-back) tests.

dipn.title: Qualifying Amalgamation of Companies; Transfer/Succession of Specified Assets without Sale
dipn.summary: Part A: tax treatment of court-free statutory amalgamations (Schedule 17J — business/asset/trading-stock succession, pre-amalgamation losses). Part B: transfer/succession of specified assets without a sale.

dipn.title: Controlled Companies Provisions under the Estate Duty Ordinance (Cap. 111)
dipn.summary: Legacy/obsolete — Estate Duty was abolished in Hong Kong in 2006. Anti-avoidance deeming rules (ss.34–45) for controlled companies, 5 worked examples — kept for historical reference only.

dipn.title: Stamping of Agreements for Sale and Purchase of Immovable Property
dipn.summary: Provisional/formal agreement stamping timing rules, with worked examples.

dipn.title: Relief for Stock Borrowing and Lending Transactions
dipn.summary: s.19(11)/(12A) stock borrowing/lending relief mechanics and registration requirements.

dipn.title: Deemed Consideration under s.24 of the Stamp Duty Ordinance
dipn.summary: Anti-avoidance rule deeming discharged debts/disguised equity as part of chargeable consideration.

dipn.title: Deemed Sale and Purchase under s.19(1E) of the Stamp Duty Ordinance
dipn.summary: Deems certain non-instrument beneficial-interest transfers of HK stock to be a sale and purchase.

dipn.title: Special Stamp Duty
dipn.summary: SSD holding-period tiers and mechanics (rate currently 0% — see the Stamp Duty page for the corrected Head reference).

dipn.title: Alternative Bond Schemes
dipn.summary: Stamp duty relief for Islamic/sukuk bond structures, with a worked example.

dipn.title: Buyer's Stamp Duty
dipn.summary: BSD mechanics and exemptions (rate currently 0% — see the Stamp Duty page for the corrected Head reference).

dipn.title: Ad Valorem Stamp Duty
dipn.summary: AVD Scale 1/2/3 mechanics — note this SOIPN predates the 2023 Scale 1 reform and 2026 amendment; see the Stamp Duty page's correction.

questions.question: Within what period must a taxpayer or employer notify chargeability to profits tax where no return has been issued?
options: 4 months after the end of the basis period
1 month after the end of the basis period
3 months after the end of the basis period
6 months after the end of the basis period
questions.answer: 4 months after the end of the basis period
questions.explain: A person chargeable to tax who has not received a return must notify the Commissioner in writing within 4 months after the end of the basis period for the year of assessment concerned.

questions.question: Within what period must a taxpayer or employer notify the commencement of an employee's employment?
options: 1 month after the date of commencement
3 months after the date of commencement
2 months after the date of commencement
before the employee starts work
questions.answer: 3 months after the date of commencement
questions.explain: An employer must file Form IR56E within 3 months of employing anyone likely to be chargeable to salaries tax.

questions.question: Within what period must a taxpayer or employer notify the cessation of an employee's employment?
options: 3 months after the date of cessation
1 month after the date of cessation
1 month before the date of cessation
within 14 days of the date of cessation
questions.answer: 1 month before the date of cessation
questions.explain: Form IR56F is due not later than 1 month before the employee ceases to be employed.

questions.question: Within what period must a taxpayer or employer notify that an employee is about to leave Hong Kong permanently?
options: 1 month after the date of departure
3 months before the expected date of departure
on the date of departure
1 month before the expected date of departure
questions.answer: 1 month before the expected date of departure
questions.explain: Form IR56G must be filed not later than 1 month before the expected date of departure. This is the obligation the June 2026 examining team reported candidates most often missed.

questions.question: Within what period must a taxpayer or employer notify a change of the taxpayer's postal address?
options: 1 month after the change
3 months after the change
before the change takes effect
at the time the next return is filed
questions.answer: 1 month after the change
questions.explain: Any person chargeable who changes address must inform the Commissioner in writing within 1 month.

questions.question: Within what period must a taxpayer or employer apply for business registration after commencing business?
options: 3 months after commencement
1 month after commencement
before commencement
4 months after the end of the first basis period
questions.answer: 1 month after commencement
questions.explain: Business registration must be applied for within 1 month of commencing business, separately from the s.51(2) notification of chargeability.

questions.question: Within what period must a taxpayer or employer lodge a valid notice of objection against an assessment?
options: 1 month after the end of the year of assessment
2 months after the date of the notice of assessment
1 month after the date of the notice of assessment
6 months after the date of the notice of assessment
questions.answer: 1 month after the date of the notice of assessment
questions.explain: An objection must be lodged in writing within 1 month of the date of the notice of assessment, and must state the precise grounds.

questions.question: Within what period must a taxpayer or employer appeal to the Board of Review against the Commissioner's determination?
options: 14 days after the determination
2 months after the determination
3 months after the determination
1 month after the determination is transmitted
questions.answer: 1 month after the determination is transmitted
questions.explain: An appeal to the Board of Review must be lodged within 1 month of the Commissioner's written determination.

questions.question: For how long must a person carrying on a trade, profession or business in Hong Kong retain sufficient business records?
options: 7 years
5 years
6 years
10 years
questions.answer: 7 years
questions.explain: Section 51C requires records sufficient to enable assessable profits to be readily ascertained to be kept for at least 7 years after the transaction. Failure carries a fine at level 6.

questions.question: From what point does the statutory retention period for business records run?
options: 7 years after the end of the year of assessment
7 years after the transaction to which they relate
6 years after the transaction
Until the assessment for that year becomes final and conclusive
questions.answer: 7 years after the transaction to which they relate
questions.explain: The period runs for 7 years from the completion of the transaction, not from the year end or the date of assessment.

questions.question: A landlord letting a Hong Kong property is obliged to keep rental records. What must those records cover?
options: Only the tenancy agreement
Only bank statements showing rent received
Rent records, and records of rates and any irrecoverable rent
No records are required for property income
questions.answer: Rent records, and records of rates and any irrecoverable rent
questions.explain: Records must be sufficient to establish the assessable value: rent receivable, any premium, rates paid by the owner, and any rent treated as irrecoverable. June 2026 candidates could state the 7-year period but not what had to be kept.

questions.question: Within what period may the Assessor normally raise an additional assessment where income has been under-assessed?
options: 4 years from the end of the year of assessment
7 years from the end of the year of assessment
There is no time limit
6 years from the end of the year of assessment
questions.answer: 6 years from the end of the year of assessment
questions.explain: Six years from the end of the relevant year of assessment, extended to 10 years in a case of fraud or wilful evasion.

questions.question: Where a taxpayer has been guilty of fraud or wilful evasion, within what period may an additional assessment be raised?
options: 10 years
6 years
12 years
No limit applies
questions.answer: 10 years
questions.explain: The ordinary 6-year limit is extended to 10 years.

questions.question: A taxpayer failed to notify chargeability to tax under s.51(2) without reasonable excuse. The tax that would have been undercharged is $11,250. What is the maximum penalty on summary conviction?
questions.explain: Section 80(2) imposes a fine at level 3 ($10,000) plus treble the tax undercharged: $10,000 + (3 × $11,250) = $43,750. Answering $10,000 alone - the fine without the treble-tax element - is the error the examining team reports most often on this question type.

questions.question: A taxpayer failed to notify chargeability to tax under s.51(2) without reasonable excuse. The tax that would have been undercharged is $24,000. What is the maximum penalty on summary conviction?
questions.explain: Section 80(2) imposes a fine at level 3 ($10,000) plus treble the tax undercharged: $10,000 + (3 × $24,000) = $82,000. Answering $10,000 alone - the fine without the treble-tax element - is the error the examining team reports most often on this question type.

questions.question: A taxpayer failed to notify chargeability to tax under s.51(2) without reasonable excuse. The tax that would have been undercharged is $8,400. What is the maximum penalty on summary conviction?
questions.explain: Section 80(2) imposes a fine at level 3 ($10,000) plus treble the tax undercharged: $10,000 + (3 × $8,400) = $35,200. Answering $10,000 alone - the fine without the treble-tax element - is the error the examining team reports most often on this question type.

questions.question: A taxpayer failed to notify chargeability to tax under s.51(2) without reasonable excuse. The tax that would have been undercharged is $46,500. What is the maximum penalty on summary conviction?
questions.explain: Section 80(2) imposes a fine at level 3 ($10,000) plus treble the tax undercharged: $10,000 + (3 × $46,500) = $149,500. Answering $10,000 alone - the fine without the treble-tax element - is the error the examining team reports most often on this question type.

questions.question: What is the maximum additional tax the Commissioner may assess under s.82A for an incorrect return made without reasonable excuse?
options: A fine of $10,000 only
Additional tax not exceeding treble the amount undercharged
Imprisonment for up to 3 years
A surcharge of 5% of the tax undercharged
questions.answer: Additional tax not exceeding treble the amount undercharged
questions.explain: Section 82A is an administrative penalty - no criminal intent need be proved - of up to treble the tax undercharged. It is assessed by the Commissioner, in place of prosecution.

questions.question: What is the maximum penalty for wilfully and with intent evading tax, on conviction on indictment?
options: A fine of $10,000 and imprisonment for 6 months
Additional tax of treble the amount undercharged only
A fine of treble the tax undercharged and imprisonment for 3 years
A surcharge of 15.5% of the tax
questions.answer: A fine of treble the tax undercharged and imprisonment for 3 years
questions.explain: Section 82 is the criminal provision: a fine of treble the tax undercharged plus imprisonment for up to 3 years. Distinguish it from s.82A, which is administrative and carries no imprisonment.

questions.question: Tax of $100,000 remained unpaid more than six months after the due date. What is the total amount now payable, including surcharges?
questions.explain: A 5% surcharge arises on the due date ($5,000), and a further 10% is then charged on the tax plus that surcharge ($10,500), giving $115,500. The total surcharge is 15.5% of the original tax, not 15% - the second surcharge compounds on the first.

questions.question: Tax of $48,000 remained unpaid more than six months after the due date. What is the total amount now payable, including surcharges?
questions.explain: A 5% surcharge arises on the due date ($2,400), and a further 10% is then charged on the tax plus that surcharge ($5,040), giving $55,440. The total surcharge is 15.5% of the original tax, not 15% - the second surcharge compounds on the first.

questions.question: Tax of $250,000 remained unpaid more than six months after the due date. What is the total amount now payable, including surcharges?
questions.explain: A 5% surcharge arises on the due date ($12,500), and a further 10% is then charged on the tax plus that surcharge ($26,250), giving $288,750. The total surcharge is 15.5% of the original tax, not 15% - the second surcharge compounds on the first.

questions.question: A demand note is payable in two instalments and the taxpayer misses the first. What is the consequence?
options: Only the unpaid first instalment attracts the 5% surcharge
The surcharge is deferred until the second instalment falls due
The second instalment becomes immediately due and the 5% surcharge applies to the whole outstanding balance
No surcharge arises until 6 months after the second due date
questions.answer: The second instalment becomes immediately due and the 5% surcharge applies to the whole outstanding balance
questions.explain: Missing the first instalment accelerates the second, and the 5% surcharge is imposed on the entire outstanding balance - not merely on the instalment that was missed.

questions.question: A taxpayer in financial difficulty applies successfully to pay tax by instalments. What is the effect on surcharges?
options: Surcharges are waived once the arrangement is approved
Surcharges are halved
Surcharges are deferred until the final instalment
Surcharges are still imposed on tax unpaid after the due date
questions.answer: Surcharges are still imposed on tax unpaid after the due date
questions.explain: IRD is explicit that an approved instalment arrangement does not stop the surcharge. It buys time and heads off recovery action; it is not a waiver.

questions.question: Under which provision may the Commissioner issue a recovery notice to a third party who owes money to the defaulter?
options: s.82A
questions.explain: A recovery notice under s.76 may be served on an employer, bank, tenant, debtor or customer, requiring them to pay the money to IRD instead.

questions.question: Under which provision may the Commissioner apply to a District Judge to stop a defaulter leaving Hong Kong?
questions.explain: A departure prevention direction under s.77 lasts until the tax is paid or security is given.

questions.question: Under which provision may the Commissioner sue for tax in default as a civil debt in the District Court?
questions.explain: Tax in default is recoverable as a civil debt, with the usual consequences of judgment including costs.

questions.question: Four people own a let property as co-owners in equal shares. How are they liable for the property tax?
options: Severally only - each owner is liable for their own share
Jointly only - all owners must be sued together
Only the owner named first on the demand note is liable
Jointly and severally - any one owner may be pursued for the whole
questions.answer: Jointly and severally - any one owner may be pursued for the whole
questions.explain: Liability is joint and several: IRD may pursue any one co-owner for the whole amount, not merely their quarter share. Once one pays in full, recovery against the others stops and tax is never collected twice.

questions.question: By when must an application to hold over payment of provisional tax be made?
options: Not later than 28 days before the due date, or 14 days after the notice is issued, whichever is later
Not later than 14 days before the due date
At any time before the end of the year of assessment
Within 1 month of the notice being issued
questions.answer: Not later than 28 days before the due date, or 14 days after the notice is issued, whichever is later
questions.explain: The later of 28 days before the due date and 14 days after the notice. The grounds are prescribed - for instance a fall in income of more than 10%, cessation, or an election for personal assessment.

questions.question: Which of the following is a valid statutory ground for holding over provisional salaries tax?
options: The taxpayer expects a lower salary next year
Assessable income for the year is likely to be less than 90% of that of the preceding year
The taxpayer has already paid the first instalment
The taxpayer objects to the amount of the provisional tax
questions.answer: Assessable income for the year is likely to be less than 90% of that of the preceding year
questions.explain: A fall to below 90% of the preceding year's assessable income is one of the prescribed grounds. Mere disagreement with the amount is not.

questions.question: What may the Assessor issue where a taxpayer fails to file a return?
options: No assessment until the return is filed
An automatic penalty of treble the tax
An estimated assessment based on the best information available
A referral to the Board of Review
questions.answer: An estimated assessment based on the best information available
questions.explain: An estimated assessment under s.59(3). It protects the statutory time limit and is superseded once the actual figures are agreed, usually through an objection.

questions.question: What happens to the tax in dispute while an objection is under consideration?
options: It is automatically suspended until the objection is determined
Half the tax must be paid and half is suspended
The Commissioner must always accept security instead
It is not automatically suspended; a separate holdover application is needed
questions.answer: It is not automatically suspended; a separate holdover application is needed
questions.explain: Lodging an objection does not suspend the tax. The taxpayer must separately apply to hold over the disputed portion, and the Commissioner may require security or purchase of a Tax Reserve Certificate.

questions.question: A notice of objection is lodged in time but states no grounds. What is the consequence?
options: It may be rejected as invalid
It is treated as valid but given lower priority
The Assessor must request further particulars before rejecting it
It automatically becomes an appeal to the Board of Review
questions.answer: It may be rejected as invalid
questions.explain: An objection must state the precise grounds. A bare, unparticularised objection can be rejected as invalid even though it was lodged within the month.

questions.question: What is the status of a DIPN?
options: DIPNs have the force of law
Departmental Interpretation and Practice Notes are not binding on taxpayers or the courts
DIPNs bind the taxpayer but not the Commissioner
DIPNs override the Inland Revenue Ordinance where they conflict
questions.answer: Departmental Interpretation and Practice Notes are not binding on taxpayers or the courts
questions.explain: DIPNs explain how IRD interprets and administers the law. They bind nobody - a taxpayer may object to a treatment set out in one. In the hierarchy of authority they sit below statute, case law and Board of Review decisions.

questions.question: Which sequence correctly ranks the authority of Hong Kong tax sources, highest first?
options: DIPNs, then statute, then case law
Advance rulings, then DIPNs, then statute
Statute, then case law, then Board of Review decisions, then DIPNs, then advance rulings
Case law, then statute, then DIPNs
questions.answer: Statute, then case law, then Board of Review decisions, then DIPNs, then advance rulings
questions.explain: Statute is supreme, followed by subsidiary legislation and case law, then Board of Review decisions, then DIPNs, with advance rulings least persuasive because they turn on their own facts.

questions.question: What distinguishes tax avoidance from tax evasion?
options: They are the same thing
Avoidance is illegal; evasion is lawful
Avoidance applies to companies and evasion to individuals
Tax avoidance uses lawful means; tax evasion is illegal
questions.answer: Tax avoidance uses lawful means; tax evasion is illegal
questions.explain: Avoidance arranges affairs lawfully to reduce tax; evasion involves deceit, concealment or false statements and is criminal. Note that general and specific anti-avoidance provisions are excluded from the TX-HKG syllabus.

questions.question: What is the effect of a specific advance ruling issued by the Commissioner?
options: A ruling applies only to the applicant and the arrangement described
A ruling binds all taxpayers in a similar position
A ruling is published and may be relied on by anyone
A ruling is binding on the courts
questions.answer: A ruling applies only to the applicant and the arrangement described
questions.explain: A specific ruling may be relied on only by the applicant, and only for the arrangement and period described. Published versions are anonymised and are persuasive at best.

questions.question: Who is empowered to assess and collect tax under the Inland Revenue Ordinance?
options: The Financial Secretary
The Commissioner
The Chief Executive
The Board of Review
questions.answer: The Commissioner
questions.explain: The Commissioner of Inland Revenue, who is also Collector of Stamp Revenue and Commissioner of Estate Duty.

questions.question: What is the Board of Review?
options: A division of the Inland Revenue Department
A committee of the Legislative Council
An independent statutory body that hears tax appeals
A branch of the District Court
questions.answer: An independent statutory body that hears tax appeals
questions.explain: An independent statutory body constituted under s.65, with a chairman, deputy chairmen with legal training, and up to 150 members appointed by the Chief Executive. It hears appeals against the Commissioner's determinations.

questions.question: On what basis may a Board of Review decision be appealed to the Court of First Instance by way of case stated?
options: Any question of fact or law
Questions of fact only
Only the amount of the assessment
A point of law only
questions.answer: A point of law only
questions.explain: The Board is the final arbiter of fact. An appeal by case stated under s.69 lies on a question of law only.

questions.question: For 2025/26 profits tax returns with Accounting Date Code 'D', what were the extended lodgement dates announced by the Commissioner on 14 July 2026?
options: 31 August 2026 for paper filing and 2 October 2026 for electronic
17 August 2026 and 17 September 2026 respectively
30 April 2026 and 31 May 2026 respectively
There is no extension for 'D' code returns
questions.answer: 31 August 2026 for paper filing and 2 October 2026 for electronic
questions.explain: Code 'D' covers accounting dates from 1 to 31 December. The paper deadline moved from 17 August to 31 August 2026, and the electronic deadline from 17 September to 2 October 2026. Codes 'N' and 'M' were unchanged.

questions.question: When is a newly incorporated Hong Kong company normally issued with its first profits tax return?
options: Within 1 month of incorporation
Around 18 months after incorporation or commencement of business
Within 4 months of the first year end
Only after the company notifies chargeability
questions.answer: Around 18 months after incorporation or commencement of business
questions.explain: Usually about 18 months after incorporation or commencement. The company must still notify chargeability under s.51(2) within 4 months of the basis period end if no return has arrived by then.

questions.question: Besides simply processing what a return states, what compliance activity does the Inland Revenue Department carry out?
options: IRD only ever reviews a return if the taxpayer itself requests it
Every return is manually checked line by line before assessment
Field assessments/audits, and desk audits and field investigations into offshore claims and transfer pricing risk
Reviews are limited to companies with a history of late filing
questions.answer: Field assessments/audits, and desk audits and field investigations into offshore claims and transfer pricing risk
questions.explain: IRD runs a risk-based programme of field audits and investigations - including into offshore profits claims and transfer pricing - as well as desk-based reviews, quite separately from the routine processing of assessments.

questions.question: What must generally accompany the first return filed by a newly registered taxpayer, in addition to the return itself?
options: A passport is always sufficient on its own
No form of identification is ever required to file a return
Only a bank statement is required
A Hong Kong identity card, or - for a company - its certificate of incorporation and business registration certificate, plus supporting documents as requested
questions.answer: A Hong Kong identity card, or - for a company - its certificate of incorporation and business registration certificate, plus supporting documents as requested
questions.explain: Basic identification and registration documents - an HKID for an individual, or the certificate of incorporation and business registration certificate for a company - together with any supporting schedules IRD specifically requests.

questions.question: Under the totality of facts test in Goepfert, which three factors principally determine whether an employment is a Hong Kong employment?
