She is single and claims only the basic allowance ($145,000 for 2026/27); she has no mortgage on either property and no other income, deductions or losses.
questions.question: Ignoring any election for personal assessment, what is Fiona's salaries tax payable for the year?
questions.explain: Progressive rates on net chargeable income ($1,056,000 − $145,000 allowance = $911,000) give $136,870; the standard rate on net income before allowances ($1,056,000) gives $158,400. Salaries tax payable is the lower of the two: $136,870. Applying the standard rate to income after allowances instead of before (giving $136,650) is a close-looking but wrong alternative route to this figure.

questions.scenario: Fiona Ng is employed as marketing manager by Silverline Retail Ltd, a company centrally managed and controlled in Hong Kong. Her annual salary for the year of assessment 2026/27 is $960,000. Silverline provides her with a self-contained flat, rent free, for the whole year; Fiona has no outgoings deductible under s.12(1)(a) against her salary. Separately, Fiona wholly owns a second residential flat, which she lets out (unconnected with her employer) for the whole year at $18,000 a month. She personally paid rates of $6,500 for the year on that flat. She is single and claims only the basic allowance ($145,000 for 2026/27); she has no mortgage on either property and no other income, deductions or losses.
questions.question: Should Fiona elect personal assessment for the year?
options: No — total tax without electing ($162,010) is lower than with personal assessment ($165,362): there is no mortgage interest or loss for the election to unlock, and her income already sits in the 17% marginal band
Yes — personal assessment always reduces tax for a taxpayer with property income
Yes — electing lets her claim both the basic allowance and a separate property allowance
It makes no difference either way
questions.answer: No — total tax without electing ($162,010) is lower than with personal assessment ($165,362): there is no mortgage interest or loss for the election to unlock, and her income already sits in the 17% marginal band
questions.explain: Without electing: salaries tax $136,870 + property tax $25,140 = $162,010. Electing aggregates both incomes ($1,223,600) less the same one basic allowance, computed at progressive rates capped by the standard rate on reduced total income: $165,362. Aggregating drags the property income into her 17% marginal band, above the flat 15% property tax rate, and there is nothing else (no mortgage interest, no loss) for the election to unlock — so electing costs her $3,352 more, not less. Compute both ways; never assume personal assessment helps.

questions.scenario: Golden Horizon Ltd, a Hong Kong trading company, reports an accounting profit before tax of $5,000,000 for the year ended 31 March 2027. Its accounts include depreciation of $300,000 and a fine of $20,000 for a pollution control breach, and it paid $150,000 in approved charitable donations, all charged as expenses. During the year Golden Horizon bought qualifying plant for $500,000 (the 20% pool's written-down value brought forward was $200,000, and there were no disposals), and incurred $1,000,000 of qualifying Type B R&D expenditure, which is included in the $1,000,000 already charged as an expense in arriving at the accounting profit above. The company has no connected entities for the two-tier regime.
questions.question: What is the total depreciation allowance available on the plant pool for the year?
questions.explain: Initial allowance: $500,000 additions × 60% = $300,000. Reduced pool: $200,000 + $500,000 − $300,000 = $400,000. Annual allowance at 20%: $80,000. Total = IA $300,000 + AA $80,000 = $380,000. Taking the IA alone, the AA alone, or computing the AA on the pool before deducting the IA, each give one of the other three options.

questions.scenario: Golden Horizon Ltd, a Hong Kong trading company, reports an accounting profit before tax of $5,000,000 for the year ended 31 March 2027. Its accounts include depreciation of $300,000 and a fine of $20,000 for a pollution control breach, and it paid $150,000 in approved charitable donations, all charged as expenses. During the year Golden Horizon bought qualifying plant for $500,000 (the 20% pool's written-down value brought forward was $200,000, and there were no disposals), and incurred $1,000,000 of qualifying Type B R&D expenditure, which is included in the $1,000,000 already charged as an expense in arriving at the accounting profit above. The company has no connected entities for the two-tier regime.
questions.question: Beyond the $1,000,000 already charged as an expense in the accounts, what additional deduction is available for the qualifying Type B R&D expenditure?
questions.explain: Type B R&D is enhanced at 300% on the first $2,000,000: $1,000,000 × 3 = $3,000,000 total allowable deduction. $1,000,000 of that is already in the accounting profit, so the additional deduction still to be made in the computation is $3,000,000 − $1,000,000 = $2,000,000. Stating the total enhanced deduction ($3,000,000) as if it were the additional amount is the commonest error - it double-counts the $1,000,000 already expensed.

questions.scenario: Golden Horizon Ltd, a Hong Kong trading company, reports an accounting profit before tax of $5,000,000 for the year ended 31 March 2027. Its accounts include depreciation of $300,000 and a fine of $20,000 for a pollution control breach, and it paid $150,000 in approved charitable donations, all charged as expenses. During the year Golden Horizon bought qualifying plant for $500,000 (the 20% pool's written-down value brought forward was $200,000, and there were no disposals), and incurred $1,000,000 of qualifying Type B R&D expenditure, which is included in the $1,000,000 already charged as an expense in arriving at the accounting profit above. The company has no connected entities for the two-tier regime.
questions.question: What is the maximum charitable donation deduction Golden Horizon may claim?
questions.explain: The allowable deduction is the lower of the amount paid ($150,000) and 35% of assessable profits before donations ($1,081,500), so the full $150,000 paid is deductible — well within the $1,081,500 cap. Stating the cap itself, rather than the lower of the two, is a common error.

questions.scenario: Golden Horizon Ltd, a Hong Kong trading company, reports an accounting profit before tax of $5,000,000 for the year ended 31 March 2027. Its accounts include depreciation of $300,000 and a fine of $20,000 for a pollution control breach, and it paid $150,000 in approved charitable donations, all charged as expenses. During the year Golden Horizon bought qualifying plant for $500,000 (the 20% pool's written-down value brought forward was $200,000, and there were no disposals), and incurred $1,000,000 of qualifying Type B R&D expenditure, which is included in the $1,000,000 already charged as an expense in arriving at the accounting profit above. The company has no connected entities for the two-tier regime.
questions.question: What is Golden Horizon's assessable profit for the year?
questions.explain: $5,000,000 accounting profit + $300,000 depreciation + $150,000 donations + $20,000 fine = $5,470,000. Less the additional R&D deduction $2,000,000 = $3,470,000. Less depreciation allowances $380,000 = $3,090,000 (the base for the donation cap). Less the donation deduction $150,000 = assessable profit $2,940,000. Stopping before deducting the donation, or before deducting the depreciation allowances, gives one of the other two wrong figures.

questions.scenario: Golden Horizon Ltd, a Hong Kong trading company, reports an accounting profit before tax of $5,000,000 for the year ended 31 March 2027. Its accounts include depreciation of $300,000 and a fine of $20,000 for a pollution control breach, and it paid $150,000 in approved charitable donations, all charged as expenses. During the year Golden Horizon bought qualifying plant for $500,000 (the 20% pool's written-down value brought forward was $200,000, and there were no disposals), and incurred $1,000,000 of qualifying Type B R&D expenditure, which is included in the $1,000,000 already charged as an expense in arriving at the accounting profit above. The company has no connected entities for the two-tier regime.
questions.question: What is Golden Horizon's profits tax payable for the year?
questions.explain: The two-tier rates apply to the final assessable profit of $2,940,000: ($2,000,000 × 8.25%) + ($940,000 × 16.5%) = $320,100. Applying a flat 16.5% or flat 8.25% to the whole profit, or applying the two-tier rates to the wrong (pre-donation) profit figure of $3,090,000, each give one of the other three options.

questions.scenario: Harbour Partners is a Hong Kong partnership with two partners: Mr Tam, an individual, holding a 60% profit share, and Silver Bay Ltd, a corporate partner, holding the remaining 40%. The partnership's assessable profit for the year is $4,000,000, allocated in that profit-sharing ratio, with each partner's two-tier $2,000,000 band apportioned in the same ratio. Mr Tam's own tax on his share remained unpaid more than six months after the due date - specifically 7 months overdue when he finally settled it.
questions.question: What is Mr Tam's share of the partnership's assessable profit?
questions.explain: $4,000,000 × 60% = $2,400,000. Using Silver Bay's 40% share instead, using the whole partnership profit unallocated, or misapplying a 50:50 split, each give one of the other three options.

questions.scenario: Harbour Partners is a Hong Kong partnership with two partners: Mr Tam, an individual, holding a 60% profit share, and Silver Bay Ltd, a corporate partner, holding the remaining 40%. The partnership's assessable profit for the year is $4,000,000, allocated in that profit-sharing ratio, with each partner's two-tier $2,000,000 band apportioned in the same ratio. Mr Tam's own tax on his share remained unpaid more than six months after the due date - specifically 7 months overdue when he finally settled it.
questions.question: What is Silver Bay Ltd's own profits tax payable on its 40% share, applying the two-tier rates to its apportioned band?
questions.explain: Silver Bay's share is $1,600,000, with an apportioned first-tier band of $800,000 ($2,000,000 × 40%) at the corporate rates: ($800,000 × 8.25%) + ($800,000 × 16.5%) = $198,000. Applying a flat 16.5% or flat 8.25% to the whole share, ignoring the apportioned band, or stating Mr Tam's figure instead, each give one of the other three options.

questions.scenario: Harbour Partners is a Hong Kong partnership with two partners: Mr Tam, an individual, holding a 60% profit share, and Silver Bay Ltd, a corporate partner, holding the remaining 40%. The partnership's assessable profit for the year is $4,000,000, allocated in that profit-sharing ratio, with each partner's two-tier $2,000,000 band apportioned in the same ratio. Mr Tam's own tax on his share remained unpaid more than six months after the due date - specifically 7 months overdue when he finally settled it.
questions.question: What is Mr Tam's own profits tax payable on his 60% share, applying the two-tier rates to his apportioned band?
questions.explain: Mr Tam's share is $2,400,000, with an apportioned first-tier band of $1,200,000 ($2,000,000 × 60%) at the unincorporated rates: ($1,200,000 × 7.5%) + ($1,200,000 × 15%) = $270,000. Applying a flat 15% or flat 7.5% to the whole share, or stating Silver Bay's figure instead, each give one of the other three options.

questions.scenario: Harbour Partners is a Hong Kong partnership with two partners: Mr Tam, an individual, holding a 60% profit share, and Silver Bay Ltd, a corporate partner, holding the remaining 40%. The partnership's assessable profit for the year is $4,000,000, allocated in that profit-sharing ratio, with each partner's two-tier $2,000,000 band apportioned in the same ratio. Mr Tam's own tax on his share remained unpaid more than six months after the due date - specifically 7 months overdue when he finally settled it.
questions.question: What is the total profits tax payable in respect of Harbour Partners' profit for the year?
questions.explain: The partnership is not itself taxed; the total is simply the sum of what each partner pays on their own apportioned share: $270,000 + $198,000 = $468,000. Applying one flat rate to the whole $4,000,000 as if it were a single corporate taxpayer (16.5%), a single unincorporated taxpayer at the flat rate, or the two-tier corporate rates without regard to Mr Tam's individual rate, each give one of the other three - and each ignores that a mixed partnership has more than one type of partner.

questions.scenario: Harbour Partners is a Hong Kong partnership with two partners: Mr Tam, an individual, holding a 60% profit share, and Silver Bay Ltd, a corporate partner, holding the remaining 40%. The partnership's assessable profit for the year is $4,000,000, allocated in that profit-sharing ratio, with each partner's two-tier $2,000,000 band apportioned in the same ratio. Mr Tam's own tax on his share remained unpaid more than six months after the due date - specifically 7 months overdue when he finally settled it.
questions.question: Mr Tam's own tax of $270,000 on his share was paid 7 months after the due date. What is the total amount he actually had to pay, including surcharges?
questions.explain: A 5% surcharge arises on the due date: $270,000 × 1.05 = $283,500. Because it remained unpaid beyond 6 months, a further 10% is charged on the tax plus that first surcharge: $283,500 × 1.10 = $311,850. Stopping at the first 5% surcharge, applying a flat 10% instead of the compounding two-step charge, or applying the second 10% to the original tax rather than to tax-plus-first-surcharge, each give one of the other three options.

questions.scenario: Kenneth Lau runs Lau's Trading as a sole proprietorship. Its accounts for the year show a net profit of $1,800,000, after charging the following as expenses: a monthly “salary” of $50,000 drawn by Kenneth himself ($600,000 for the year), a salary of $240,000 paid to his wife, who works full time managing the shop, and depreciation of $80,000. Depreciation allowances for the year have been computed at $120,000. Kenneth also made the mandatory MPF contribution of $18,000 in respect of himself as a self-employed person; this was not charged in the accounts above.
questions.question: How much must be added back in respect of the salaries paid to Kenneth and to his wife?
questions.explain: Both are added back: $600,000 (Kenneth) + $240,000 (his wife) = $840,000. A sole proprietor cannot be their own employee, and s.17(2) extends the same treatment to a payment to the proprietor's spouse — however genuinely she works in the business, husband and wife are not treated as at arm's length for this purpose. Adding back only one of the two is the error this question tests.

questions.scenario: Kenneth Lau runs Lau's Trading as a sole proprietorship. Its accounts for the year show a net profit of $1,800,000, after charging the following as expenses: a monthly “salary” of $50,000 drawn by Kenneth himself ($600,000 for the year), a salary of $240,000 paid to his wife, who works full time managing the shop, and depreciation of $80,000. Depreciation allowances for the year have been computed at $120,000. Kenneth also made the mandatory MPF contribution of $18,000 in respect of himself as a self-employed person; this was not charged in the accounts above.
questions.question: What deduction may the business claim for Kenneth's own mandatory MPF contribution as a self-employed person?
questions.explain: Section 16AA allows the proprietor's own mandatory contribution as a deduction in the profits tax computation, capped at the statutory maximum of $18,000. It was not charged in the accounts, so it is deducted in the computation. Answering nil — on the reasoning that a proprietor's own payments are never deductible — confuses this with the s.17(2) salary rule; MPF is the deliberate exception.

questions.scenario: Kenneth Lau runs Lau's Trading as a sole proprietorship. Its accounts for the year show a net profit of $1,800,000, after charging the following as expenses: a monthly “salary” of $50,000 drawn by Kenneth himself ($600,000 for the year), a salary of $240,000 paid to his wife, who works full time managing the shop, and depreciation of $80,000. Depreciation allowances for the year have been computed at $120,000. Kenneth also made the mandatory MPF contribution of $18,000 in respect of himself as a self-employed person; this was not charged in the accounts above.
questions.question: What is Lau's Trading's assessable profit for the year?
questions.explain: $1,800,000 net profit + $840,000 salaries added back under s.17(2) + $80,000 depreciation = $2,720,000; less depreciation allowances $120,000 and the s.16AA MPF deduction $18,000 = $2,582,000. Forgetting the MPF deduction, forgetting the wife's salary, or forgetting the depreciation allowances each give one of the other three options.

questions.scenario: Kenneth Lau runs Lau's Trading as a sole proprietorship. Its accounts for the year show a net profit of $1,800,000, after charging the following as expenses: a monthly “salary” of $50,000 drawn by Kenneth himself ($600,000 for the year), a salary of $240,000 paid to his wife, who works full time managing the shop, and depreciation of $80,000. Depreciation allowances for the year have been computed at $120,000. Kenneth also made the mandatory MPF contribution of $18,000 in respect of himself as a self-employed person; this was not charged in the accounts above.
questions.question: What is the profits tax payable by Lau's Trading?
questions.explain: A sole proprietorship is an unincorporated business, so the two-tier rates are 7.5% and 15%, not the corporate 8.25%/16.5%: (2,000,000 × 7.5%) + ($582,000 × 15%) = $237,300. Using the corporate rates gives $261,030 and is the commonest slip here.

questions.scenario: Kenneth Lau runs Lau's Trading as a sole proprietorship. Its accounts for the year show a net profit of $1,800,000, after charging the following as expenses: a monthly “salary” of $50,000 drawn by Kenneth himself ($600,000 for the year), a salary of $240,000 paid to his wife, who works full time managing the shop, and depreciation of $80,000. Depreciation allowances for the year have been computed at $120,000. Kenneth also made the mandatory MPF contribution of $18,000 in respect of himself as a self-employed person; this was not charged in the accounts above.
questions.question: Suppose instead that Lau's Trading had made a loss for the year, and Kenneth also had salary income from a part-time job. What could he do to relieve the loss against that salary in the same year?
options: Nothing — a sole proprietor's loss can only ever be carried forward against future profits of the same business
Carry the loss back against the previous year's profits
Surrender the loss to his wife against her own income
Elect personal assessment, which lets the current-year business loss be set against his salary in the same year
questions.answer: Elect personal assessment, which lets the current-year business loss be set against his salary in the same year
questions.explain: Within profits tax alone the loss is simply carried forward (s.19C) and cannot touch his salary. Electing personal assessment aggregates all his chargeable income, letting the current-year business loss shelter the salary. Hong Kong has no carry-back and no transfer of losses between spouses.

questions.scenario: Priya Sharma has a Hong Kong employment with an annual salary of $1,200,000 for the year of assessment 2026/27. During the year she exercised a share option granted to her by her employer in an earlier year. The market value of the shares on the date of exercise was $850,000 and she paid the exercise price of $500,000. On completing her fixed-term contract she also received a gratuity of $200,000, payable under the terms of that contract. She paid $135,000 of mortgage interest on the flat she lives in herself, and made the mandatory MPF contribution of $18,000. She is married and her husband has no income; the married person's allowance is $290,000.
questions.question: What amount of the share option gain is assessable to salaries tax?
options: Nil — a gain on shares is capital
questions.explain: The charge falls on exercise, on the gain: market value at exercise $850,000 less the exercise price paid $500,000 = $350,000. Assessing the full market value, or treating the gain as a capital gain outside the charge, are both wrong — an employee share option gain is specifically brought into charge by s.9(1)(d).

questions.scenario: Priya Sharma has a Hong Kong employment with an annual salary of $1,200,000 for the year of assessment 2026/27. During the year she exercised a share option granted to her by her employer in an earlier year. The market value of the shares on the date of exercise was $850,000 and she paid the exercise price of $500,000. On completing her fixed-term contract she also received a gratuity of $200,000, payable under the terms of that contract. She paid $135,000 of mortgage interest on the flat she lives in herself, and made the mandatory MPF contribution of $18,000. She is married and her husband has no income; the married person's allowance is $290,000.
questions.question: How is the $200,000 contract-completion gratuity treated?
options: Not assessable — it is compensation for loss of office
Assessable in full — it is payable under the contract, so it rewards services
Assessable at 50% as a terminal payment
Not assessable because it was paid after the contract ended
questions.answer: Assessable in full — it is payable under the contract, so it rewards services
questions.explain: A gratuity payable under the contract on completing it is a reward for services and is fully assessable. Contrast a genuine statutory severance or long service payment under the Employment Ordinance, which is compensation for loss of office and is not assessable — that is the distinction being tested.

questions.scenario: Priya Sharma has a Hong Kong employment with an annual salary of $1,200,000 for the year of assessment 2026/27. During the year she exercised a share option granted to her by her employer in an earlier year. The market value of the shares on the date of exercise was $850,000 and she paid the exercise price of $500,000. She paid $135,000 of mortgage interest on the flat she lives in herself, and made the mandatory MPF contribution of $18,000. questions.question: What deduction may Priya claim for the $135,000 of home loan interest?
questions.explain: Home loan interest on the taxpayer's own dwelling is deductible but capped at $100,000 a year (the $120,000 figure applies only where there is a qualifying child), so $100,000 of the $135,000 paid is allowed and the excess simply lapses.

questions.explain: Assessable income $1,200,000 salary + $350,000 option gain + $200,000 gratuity = $1,750,000; less the capped home loan interest $100,000 and MPF $18,000 = $1,632,000.

She is married and her husband has no income; the married person's allowance is $290,000.
questions.question: What is Priya's salaries tax payable for the year?
questions.explain: Progressive rates on net chargeable income ($1,632,000 − $290,000 allowance = $1,342,000) give $210,140; the standard rate on net income before allowances ($1,632,000 × 15%) gives $244,800. The lower of the two is $210,140.

questions.scenario: Wong Kwok-keung owns two properties in Hong Kong, both let in his own name. Flat A was let for the whole year at $30,000 a month. Wong paid rates of $12,000 on it. The tenant defaulted and $60,000 of the year's rent was proved to be irrecoverable during the year. Flat B was let under a new four-year lease granted at the start of the year, for which Wong received a premium of $360,000. No periodic rent is payable on Flat B, and the tenant pays the rates on it direct to the Government.
questions.question: What is the assessable value of Flat A for the year, before deducting rates and the statutory allowance?
questions.explain: Rent for the year $360,000 ($30,000 × 12) less the $60,000 proved irrecoverable during the year = $300,000. Section 7C(1) gives the deduction in the year the rent is recognised as irrecoverable, not the year it accrued.

questions.scenario: Wong Kwok-keung owns two properties in Hong Kong, both let in his own name. Flat A was let for the whole year at $30,000 a month. Wong paid rates of $12,000 on it. The tenant defaulted and $60,000 of the year's rent was proved to be irrecoverable during the year. Flat B was let under a new four-year lease granted at the start of the year, for which Wong received a premium of $360,000. No periodic rent is payable on Flat B, and the tenant pays the rates on it direct to the Government.
questions.question: What is the property tax payable on Flat A?
questions.explain: Assessable value $300,000; less rates paid by the owner $12,000 = $288,000; less the 20% statutory allowance $57,600 = net assessable value $230,400; × 15% = $34,560.

questions.scenario: Wong Kwok-keung owns two properties in Hong Kong, both let in his own name. Flat A was let for the whole year at $30,000 a month. Wong paid rates of $12,000 on it. The tenant defaulted and $60,000 of the year's rent was proved to be irrecoverable during the year. Flat B was let under a new four-year lease granted at the start of the year, for which Wong received a premium of $360,000. No periodic rent is payable on Flat B, and the tenant pays the rates on it direct to the Government.
questions.question: How much of Flat B's premium falls into the assessable value for this year?
questions.explain: A premium is spread over the lease term or 36 months, whichever is shorter. The lease runs four years (48 months), so the 36-month cap bites: $360,000 ÷ 36 × 12 = $120,000 for the year. Spreading over the full 48 months gives $90,000 and is the error the cap exists to catch.

questions.scenario: Wong Kwok-keung owns two properties in Hong Kong, both let in his own name. Flat A was let for the whole year at $30,000 a month. Wong paid rates of $12,000 on it. questions.question: What is Wong's total property tax liability for the year on both properties?
questions.explain: Property tax is computed property by property, each with its own rates deduction and its own 20% allowance: Flat A $34,560 + Flat B $14,400 (net assessable value $96,000 × 15%) = $48,960. Flat B has no owner's rates to deduct because the tenant pays them direct.

questions.scenario: Wong Kwok-keung owns two properties in Hong Kong, both let in his own name. Flat A was let for the whole year at $30,000 a month. Wong paid rates of $12,000 on it. Flat B was let under a new four-year lease granted at the start of the year, for which Wong received a premium of $360,000. questions.question: Suppose Flat B were instead owned by a Hong Kong company carrying on business here. What relief from property tax would be available?
options: Nothing — a company pays both property tax and profits tax on the same rent with no relief
Apply for exemption under s.5(2)(a), the rental income being included in its profits tax computation instead
Claim depreciation allowances on the building against the property tax
Pay property tax at the corporate rate of 16.5% instead of 15%
questions.answer: Apply for exemption under s.5(2)(a), the rental income being included in its profits tax computation instead
questions.explain: A corporation carrying on a trade or business in Hong Kong may apply under s.5(2)(a) for exemption from property tax where the income is brought into its profits tax computation. Without that application property tax is charged and then set off against the profits tax payable under s.25 — so the rent is not taxed twice either way, but the exemption is the cleaner route.

Daniel Lau is an individual resident in Hong Kong. In May 2026 he bought three adjacent mini-storage units in Kwun Tong for $3,200,000. profitsTax.caption: Two-tiered profits tax rates (from YA 2018/19, current)
profitsTax.text:
2. Rates & Recent Changes Schedule 8B

Two-tiered profits tax rates (from YA 2018/19, current)

Taxpayer type | First HKD 2,000,000 of assessable profits | Remainder
Corporations | 8.25% | 16.5%
Unincorporated businesses (sole proprietors / partnerships) | 7.5% | 15%
Legislated via s.14(2)/(3) referring out to Schedule 8B (two-tiered rates) — Schedule 8 sets the flat standard/corporate rate that continues to apply where a group of connected entities has more than one entity in Hong Kong (only one connected entity per group may be nominated each year to access the discounted first-tier rate; s.14AAC deals with connected entities generally).

Recent changes to watch

- Refined FSIE regime — effective 1 January 2023 (Division 3A of Part 4, added by 17 of 2022) — see §6 below.

- Patent Box concession — 5% concessionary rate on qualifying IP income from YA 2023/24 (Inland Revenue (Amendment) (Tax Concessions for Intellectual Property Income) Ordinance 2023).

- Pillar Two — Income Inclusion Rule + Hong Kong Minimum Top-up Tax for in-scope MNE groups, effective for fiscal years beginning on/after 1 January 2025.

- One-off relief — Inland Revenue (Amendment) Ordinance 2026 (gazetted 22 May 2026): 100% profits tax reduction for YA 2025/26, capped at HKD 3,000 per taxpayer. (Source: PwC Tax Summaries, reviewed 22 Jul 2026 — verify against the gazetted ordinance before relying on this for a filing.)

Bills in progress — not yet law (as at 24 September 2026)

- Funds / FIHV / carried interest — Inland Revenue (Amendment) (Preferential Tax Regimes for Funds, Family-owned Investment Holding Vehicles and Carried Interest) Bill 2026, gazetted 12 June 2026, first reading 24 June 2026. Widens the definition of "fund", broadens the schedule of qualifying assets (notably to support private credit), removes the 5% cap on incidental transactions, relaxes the exemption conditions for special purpose entities and family-owned SPEs, and enhances the carried interest regime — but adds a tax reporting mechanism and economic substance requirements modelled on the FIHV regime. (Gazettal press release, 12 Jun 2026; FSTB response on carried interest, 12 Aug 2026.)

- Shipping & physical commodity trading — Inland Revenue (Amendment) (Tax Concessions for Shipping-related Activities and Physical Commodity Trading) Bill 2026, gazetted 12 June 2026. Offers shipping-related companies an elective 15% concessionary rate (elected annually) as a BEPS 2.0-aware alternative to the existing 0%/8.25% concessions, and creates a new half-rate (8.25%) concession for physical commodity trading. (Press release, 10 Jun 2026.)

- Corporate treasury centres — the Government published an Action Plan to Promote Development of Corporate Treasury Centres (9 Jun 2026) and launched a consultation on enhancing the CTC tax concession regime (27 Jul 2026). Expect the qualifying-activity and safe-harbour conditions for the 8.25% CTC rate to change — check before advising a group treasury structure.

- Qualifying debt instruments — the list of debt instruments and sovereign bonds eligible for profits tax concession or exemption was refreshed on 30 June 2026. The list is the operative test — do not rely on an older copy.

- Pillar Two filing — IRD published the GIR XML schema and user guides for the GloBE Information Return on 8 June 2026. In-scope MNE groups now have the machine-readable filing format. (IRD BEPS 2.0 page.)

salariesTax.caption: Progressive rates on net chargeable income (2025/26 and continuing into 2026/27 basis) — Schedule 2
salariesTax.text:
2. Rates & Standard Rate Cap IRO s.13, Schedule 2

Progressive rates on net chargeable income (2025/26 and continuing into 2026/27 basis) — Schedule 2

Band | Rate
First HKD 50,000 | 2%
Next HKD 50,000 (50,001–100,000) | 6%
Next HKD 50,000 (100,001–150,000) | 10%
Next HKD 50,000 (150,001–200,000) | 14%
Remainder (above 200,000) | 17%
Under s.13, tax computed progressively on net chargeable income (i.e. after allowances) is capped at a standard-rate calculation applied to net total income (i.e. before personal allowances, but after concessionary deductions): 15% on the first HKD 5,000,000, 16% on the remainder. The taxpayer pays whichever of the two computations is lower — this matters most for higher earners with large personal allowances.

One-off relief
Inland Revenue (Amendment) Ordinance 2026 (gazetted 22 May 2026): 100% reduction of salaries tax/personal assessment tax for YA 2025/26, capped at HKD 3,000. (Source: PwC, reviewed 22 Jul 2026 — verify against the gazetted ordinance.)

propertyTax.text:
1. Overview & Charging Basis IRO s.5

Property tax is charged for each year of assessment on every person who owns land or buildings in Hong Kong, computed at the standard rate on the net assessable value — regardless of whether the owner carries on any trade or business. It is a tax on ownership + letting, not on trading profit as such.

Statutory text — s.5(1)
"Property tax shall...be charged for each year of assessment on every person being the owner of any land or buildings or land and buildings wherever situate in Hong Kong and shall be computed at the standard rate on the net assessable value of such land or buildings..."

Current rate

Standard rate applied to net assessable value | 15%
Owner-occupied property generates no rental consideration and therefore has no assessable value — no property tax arises. Where the owner of the land is not the owner of the buildings on it, separate assessments are made for each (s.5(1)(b)).

stock.text:
2. Share Transfers SDO s.19 (contract notes), First Schedule Head 2(1)

Ad valorem duty on transfer of Hong Kong stock | 0.2% of consideration or market value, whichever is higher (split 0.1% buyer / 0.1% seller, plus a small fixed contract note duty)
Contract notes are charged under s.19 (First Schedule Head 2(1)); s.21 prohibits stock being passed through without duty on the intervening step, s.22 covers consideration paid in stock/securities, and s.23 covers periodical-payment consideration. s.20 (formerly a related contract-note provision) has been repealed (33 of 2024 s.5) — do not cite it. Reliefs exist for stock borrowing/lending transactions (s.19(11) excludes a stock borrowing/return from the charge; s.19(12A) sets the borrower's return conditions; registration fee currently $270, must register within 30 days) and for intra-group ("associated companies") transfers under s.45 (§6 covers this in more detail) — see SOIPN 2.

New — RMB settlement of stamp duty on dual-counter stock
The Stamp Duty (Amendment) (No. 2) Ordinance 2026 (Bill passed 8 July 2026, gazetted 17 July 2026) lets stamp duty on a transfer of dual-counter stock traded at the RMB counter be calculated and paid in Renminbi, so an investor settles the trade and the duty in the same currency at the same counter. The 0.2% rate is unchanged — this is a settlement-currency and administration change only. Commencement is on a day to be appointed by the Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury, pending HKEX system readiness, so it is not yet in force.
Source: Government welcomes passage of Stamp Duty (Amendment) (No. 2) Bill 2026, 8 Jul 2026.

property.text:
3. Property Transfers — Ad Valorem Duty (AVD) First Schedule Head 1(1)/(1A); ss.29AI, 29AJ, 29AK

Correction vs. common assumption
AVD Scale 1 is not a flat 15% on residential property. The flat-15% Scale 1 that applied from 5 Nov 2016 was superseded by a 2023 reform that made Scale 1 a graduated table matching Scale 2's bands (top rate 4.25%) — the only remaining difference is a new top band the Stamp Duty (Amendment) Ordinance 2026 added above ~$109.57M (see below). If your prior understanding was "flat 15% for non-HKPR/company buyers," that is now out of date except at the very top of the market.

AVD has three rate tables, all graduated (not flat), all sharing the same lower bands:

Scale | Applies to | Top rate
Scale 1 (First Schedule Head 1(1)/(1A), default table — s.29AI) | Residential property, buyer not qualifying for the Scale 2 concession (incl. companies, non-HKPRs) | 4.25% up to $100,000,000; a transitional band charging $4,250,000 + 30% of the excess from $100,000,000–$109,574,470; 6.5% flat above $109,574,470 (new top bands added by the Stamp Duty (Amendment) Ordinance 2026, s.14)
Scale 2 (s.29AJ concession) | Hong Kong Permanent Resident buying their sole residential property, or a qualifying closely-related-person reassignment | 4.25% — unchanged by the 2026 amendment
Scale 3 (s.29AI(b) default for non-residential; also s.29AK for a car park bought alongside a Scale-2 residential purchase) | Non-residential property | 4.25% — unchanged by the 2026 amendment
All three scales start at a flat $100 for low-value transactions and climb through the same intermediate bands (1.5% / 2.25% / 3% / 3.75%) before reaching their respective top rate. Duty is charged on consideration or market value, whichever is higher. "Closely related persons" (for Scale 2 eligibility and for the close-relative exemptions on BSD/SSD) is defined at s.29AD — broadly parent/spouse/child/sibling. Reliefs: replacement of a sole residential property (refund window), exchange/partition ("equality money" only), court orders, mortgagee sales, associated-company transfers under s.45 (§6) — see SOIPN 8, though note SOIPN 8 (Nov 2018) predates the 2023 Scale 1 reform and the 2026 amendment.

buyersAndSpecial.text:
4. Buyer's Stamp Duty (BSD) & Special Stamp Duty (SSD) First Schedule Head 1(1AAB)/(1C) [BSD]; Head 1(1AA) [SSD]

Correction vs. common assumption
There is no "Part IIIAA" or "Part IVA" for BSD/SSD in the current ordinance structure — Part IVA is actually the unrelated Unit Trusts/Open-ended Fund Companies part (ss.37A–41). BSD and SSD are instead defined as separate Heads of charge in the First Schedule, cross-referenced from Part IIIA.

Duty | Applies to | Rate
Buyer's Stamp Duty (BSD) — Head 1(1AAB) conveyance / Head 1(1C) agreement for sale | Residential property acquired by a non-HKPR (companies are always treated as non-HKPR); subject to ss.29C, 29CB, 29CC | 0% — reduced from 15% in stages (L.N. 148 of 2023; 3 of 2024 s.14; L.N. 26 of 2024; 8 of 2024 s.6)
Special Stamp Duty (SSD) — Head 1(1AA), Part 4 (property disposed of on/after 28 Feb 2024) | Residential property resold within the holding-period window; subject to ss.29D, 29DA | 0% — reduced from up to 20% (L.N. 26 of 2024; 8 of 2024 s.6)
Note
BSD and SSD remain fully defined in the First Schedule with their mechanics unchanged (liable party, timing, holding-period tiers for SSD) — only the rate was reduced to 0% as a market-support measure from 28 February 2024. Head 1(1AA)'s historical Parts 1–3 are preserved verbatim for legacy holding-period windows still being assessed (20 Nov 2010–27 Oct 2012 at 15/10/5%; 27 Oct 2012–25 Oct 2023 and 25 Oct 2023–28 Feb 2024, both at 20/15/10%) — relevant only if assessing an old disposal that hasn't yet been finalised. Both duties could in principle be reactivated at a non-zero rate by future amendment — see SOIPN 5 (SSD) and SOIPN 7 (BSD), noting both predate the current 0% rate and Head numbering nuances above.

leases.text:
5. Leases SDO Head 1(2)

Lease term | Duty
Not defined or uncertain / ≤ 1 year | 0.25% of average annual rent (plus any premium, taxed as a sale)
Between 1 and 3 years | 0.5% of average annual rent
Over 3 years | 1% of average annual rent
A premium paid for a lease is chargeable as if it were a sale consideration, separately from the rent-based duty above — see the interaction with Property Tax/Profits Tax premium-spreading rules on the Property Tax page.

buildings.text:
2. Industrial & Commercial Buildings IRO ss.33A, 34, 36, 37

Building type | Initial allowance | Annual allowance | Balancing allowance/charge
Industrial building or structure (mills, factories, docks, utility undertakings, qualifying storage/farming/R&D buildings) | 20% (1/5) of cost, year of first use | 4% (1/25) straight-line on cost | On sale/lease termination/demolition — balancing charge capped at total allowances previously granted
Commercial building or structure (all other non-excluded buildings) | None | 4% (1/25) straight-line on cost, from 1998/99 | Same balancing mechanism as industrial buildings, from 1998/99
"Industrial building or structure" is narrowly defined (DIPN 2) — it excludes dwellings, retail shops, showrooms, hotels, and offices. Where a building is used partly for a qualifying industrial purpose and partly not, a 10% de-minimis rule applies: if the non-qualifying use is no more than 10% of the whole, the building is treated as wholly industrial. On a sale, the buyer's future annual allowance is recalculated as the residue of expenditure after sale, spread over the remaining years to the building's 25th year from first use.

Historical note
Before 1998/99, commercial buildings only qualified for a much smaller "rebuilding allowance" (0.75% pre-1990/91, then 2% from 1990/91–1997/98) rather than the modern 4% annual allowance — relevant only when tracing the residue of expenditure on a very old building still being written down today.

plantAndMachinery.text:
3. Plant & Machinery — Pooling System IRO ss.39B–39E

Since YA1980/81, plant and machinery of the same annual-allowance rate class is pooled together rather than tracked asset-by-asset (the old asset-by-asset method under ss.37–39 survives only for hire-purchase assets, mixed business/private-use assets, and a few other special cases).

Initial allowance | 60% of cost, given once on acquisition
Annual allowance | Reducing-balance on the pool's "reducing value," at 10%, 20% or 30% depending on asset class (Board of Inland Revenue rates)
Common annual allowance rate classes (Appendix A(i), DIPN 7)

Rate | Asset examples
10% | Air-conditioning plant, lifts, cables, ships
20% | Furniture, fixtures, domestic/room air-conditioners — the general residual rate for unlisted items
30% | Motor vehicles, computer/EDP equipment, textile/electronics manufacturing plant, tractors/bulldozers
Balancing allowances only arise when the trade/pool ceases altogether. Balancing charges can arise at any time disposal proceeds exceed the pool's reducing value, but are capped at the total allowances previously granted for that asset (you can never be charged more than you were originally allowed). Hire-purchase assets, and assets moved between private and business use, are excluded from pooling and calculated separately with notional allowance adjustments.

Child allowance claim period for the enhanced "year of birth" rate was extended from 1 to 2 years effective YA 2026/27 — check whether this affects the year you're computing.

Proposed — 2026 Policy Address, 16 September 2026
The Chief Executive announced that child allowance will rise from HKD 140,000 to HKD 160,000 for a taxpayer's second and subsequent children born on or after 16 September 2026 (claimable until age 25, on the usual full-time education / disability conditions). The enhanced additional child allowance for the year of birth and the following year rises to HKD 160,000 on the same basis, so those two years give HKD 320,000 per qualifying child. Intended to take effect from YA 2026/27, but it requires an amendment ordinance — until that is enacted, the enacted figure for every child remains HKD 140,000. First-born children are not covered by the increase.
Source: IRD — 2026 Policy Address, Tax-related Policy Measures (on Individuals), published 16 Sep 2026.
